More freedom, more order: The integration of migrants works better in countries where newcomers face fewer restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:14:33 UTC
14:14:33 KST

The number of migrants worldwide has reached 300 million, and despite growing anti-immigration sentiment and the rise to power of leaders promising to halt the influx of newcomers, neither the United States nor Europe has managed to significantly reduce their numbers. Migration will continue to grow as aging economies face increasingly severe labor shortages. The main challenge for governments is not so much to stop the flow as to integrate migrants effectively, avoiding social conflicts while reaping the economic benefits immigration brings. International experience varies, but numerous studies show that migration policies have been more successful in countries where migrants have equal access to the labor market and can participate in public life. The higher the employment rate among migrants and the fewer bureaucratic barriers they face, the better results migrant communities show when it comes to questions of crime and social exclusion.
In recent decades, almost all developed countries have been experiencing a severe demographic crisis caused by population aging. Combined with globalization, this has led to a growing influx of migrants into these countries. According to the UN, the number of migrants worldwide stands at around 300 million, double what it was in 1990 (although its share of the global population grew much more modestly, from 2.9% to 3.7%).
This growth has fueled a global wave of anti-immigration sentiment. Yet even politicians who come to power on the back of such rhetoric usually fail to stop the influx of migrants. Donald Trump, for example, only slightly reduced the number of legal migrants entering the United States during his first term, largely by cutting the number of refugees admitted through the UN resettlement program. And during Giorgia Meloni's tenure as Italy's prime minister, the number of migrants arriving in the country has only increased — Italy has even remained the leading destination for people entering Europe illegally.
Brexit, which took place against a backdrop of British discontent over migration, led European citizens to leave the country, but they were replaced by far more migrants from non-European countries. Russian authorities, meanwhile, are fueling anti-immigration hysteria while trying to replace laborers from post-Soviet countries with different migrants from farther afield.
Migration, of course, has an objective driver: growing demand for labor. And as long as that demand persists, migration will continue to grow. According to forecasts by the International Organization for Migration, the number of migrants worldwide will exceed 400 million by 2050. It is therefore essential to understand how best to manage migration while integrating newcomers.
By 2050, the number of migrants worldwide will exceed 400 million
As with measures aimed at restricting entry, attempts to integrate migrants often produce outcomes that run counter to the aims of government efforts.
Sweden, for example, is the world's most migrant-friendly country and has the highest score on the Migrant Integration Policy Index (MIPEX). Yet migrants in Sweden are still more likely to commit crimes than the native-born population; they earn less, pay less in taxes, and their children perform worse at school.
In Spain, by contrast, migrants account for a similar share of the population — just over 20% — while both the MIPEX score and spending on integration programs are lower. Yet the gap between migrants and the native population is also smaller across all indicators. Moreover, migration has reduced unemployment and crime in the country and boosted GDP per capita.
In Russia, meanwhile, a country that is extremely unwelcoming to newcomers and has a very low MIPEX score, migrants commit crimes significantly less often than the native population while having the same employment rate.
Research shows that three factors matter more than either spending on integration or the strictness of migration policy itself: migrants' access to the labor market, the composition of migration flows, and the ability of institutions to prevent discrimination against newcomers.
Access to the labor market
Employment is the main factor determining an individual's propensity to commit crime across all population groups. Unemployed people are more likely to turn to crime to survive — subsistence crimes, which typically include theft, squatting, or even prostitution. They are also more likely to become involved in criminal networks, which essentially serve as alternative forms of employment.
Even among employed people, peaks in criminal activity occur during periods when they are not working — namely, on holidays, when the rate of violent crime tends to increase, largely because of alcohol. Among unemployed people, by contrast, holidays have a much smaller effect on crime.
Around 60% of migrants worldwide moved in search of work. Since labor migrants generally have lower crime rates than the local population as a whole, an influx of labor migrants can even reduce the overall per-capita crime rate.
Crime rates among labor migrants are generally lower than among the local population
This largely explains the paradoxically low crime rate among migrants in Russia. The country accepts virtually no refugees, and the overwhelming majority of newcomers are labor migrants. Since 2014, Ukrainian refugees — following Russia's occupation of Crimea and parts of Ukraine's Donetsk and Luhansk regions — have been granted preferential residency arrangements allowing them to work immediately, access government services, and remain in the country indefinitely. They were also eligible for a simplified path to citizenship (meaning they have barely registered in official crime statistics as migrants).
There is considerable evidence that allowing migrants to work legally also improves their integration. A revealing comparison of two waves of immigration to Britain illustrates the point. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the country received asylum seekers who were mostly not allowed to work immediately, leading to an increase in property crime. By contrast, the wave of migration that followed the accession of 10 new countries to the EU consisted of people who immediately gained the right to work and, in turn, slightly reduced crime rates.
A similar situation emerged in Italy after Bulgaria and Romania joined the EU. Because citizens of those countries automatically acquired legal status, the incidence of “subsistence crimes” among them fell by half. The effect was particularly pronounced in the country's industrialized northern regions, while in the south, where migrants were often already working informally in agriculture, legalization had virtually no effect on crime rates.
The same pattern can be seen in the contrast between English-speaking countries — the UK, Canada, the U.S., Australia, Ireland, and New Zealand — and continental Europe. This is partly because the English-speaking countries are geographically distant from major conflict zones, making it more difficult for refugees to reach them unless they are resettled through the UN Refugee Agency's programs.
As a result, these people have already had their asylum claims approved and are granted the right to work immediately upon arrival. Consequently, in all these countries, the share of migrants among the prison population is lower than their share of the total population, while their children perform better on standardized tests than children of native-born residents.
In continental Europe, by contrast, refugees arrive directly across land borders or by sea, meaning they do not immediately gain the right to work. A report by the European Council on Refugees and Exiles notes that, although numerous European directives recognize the right to work as a fundamental human right and call for asylum seekers to be granted access to the labor market as soon as possible, many countries still impose various barriers until their applications are processed.
In some countries, refugees are housed for long periods in camps located in areas with high unemployment or are frequently transferred between accommodation centers, making it difficult to secure permanent employment. Elsewhere, authorities delay the issuance of documents, while employers themselves may be unsure whether they are allowed to hire asylum seekers whose applications have not yet been approved.
In many EU countries, migrants are allowed to work only in a limited range of sectors, mostly in low-skilled jobs. At the same time, many higher-skilled positions require a relevant degree and a certain level of proficiency in the local language, and their professional qualifications obtained abroad may not be recognized. As a result, for example, low-skilled migrants in Italy have a higher employment rate than Italians with a similar level of qualifications (65.0% versus 53.2%), while highly skilled migrants have a lower employment rate (69.0% versus 85.7%).
In Hungary, temporary residence permits are issued for just three months, meaning refugees must repeatedly have their documents verified at their place of work, increasing employers' administrative costs. In Greece, only 3% of refugees have managed to open bank accounts into which they can receive their salaries. In the Netherlands, of the 26,520 people who applied for asylum in 2021, only 590 were granted the right to work.
In eight EU countries, migrants from non-EU states have a higher employment rate than the native population: the Czech Republic, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg Malta, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia. Among these, Poland and the Czech Republic receive large numbers of Ukrainians who benefit from simplified work-permit procedures, while Portugal has an analagous arrangement for people from its former colonies.
In the United States, migrants have traditionally had lower crime rates, better health outcomes, and higher levels of academic achievement than native-born Americans, while by the third generation they tended to converge with — or even surpass — them on economic indicators. Even refugees had employment rates comparable to those of labor migrants.
However, in the 2010s, a surge of asylum seekers began crossing the U.S. border from four primary countries: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Venezuela. This influx was largely a legacy of U.S. intervention in these countries' politics during the Cold War, exacerbated by the flow of weapons into Latin America from the United States itself. Because these asylum seekers arrived in the U.S. directly rather than through the UN resettlement program, they were barred from working until their asylum claims were approved. Unsurprisingly, their integration outcomes were worse than for previous waves of newcomers, forcing the government to spend considerably more money to support them.
Restricting asylum seekers' right to work therefore has long-term negative economic effects. Until the restriction is lifted, refugees are forced to rely entirely on government support, thus becoming dependent on benefits. During this period, they remain disconnected from society because they are excluded from economic life, while their professional skills gradually deteriorate. As a result, their chances of finding employment after receiving work authorization fall by 15%.
Restricting asylum seekers' right to work has long-term negative economic effects
The phenomenon is not American in nature. In Germany, a court ruling reduced the length of time refugees had to wait for work authorization. This experience showed that people who had to wait an additional seven months for permission to work were 20 percentage points less likely to find employment than those who obtained the right earlier. The gap only disappeared ten years later, and researchers estimate that the EU lost €37.6 billion in GDP because refugees who arrived during the migration crisis triggered by the war in Syria faced restrictions on employment.
Which migrants arrive
In Sweden, refugees can work almost immediately after applying for asylum, although only in low-skilled jobs. Nevertheless, the country's integration outcomes are among the worst of any developed country.
A major factor is the composition of the migration flows arriving in Sweden. For decades, the country has accepted large numbers of refugees, most of them from the culturally distant Muslim world. The three main countries of origin for migrants in Sweden are Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan. Sweden is now the European country with the highest number of refugees per capita.
Refugees, however, are the category of migrant that is hardest to integrate. Unlike economic migrants, who typically choose their destination in advance, prepare for the move, learn the language, and often already have useful contacts, in-demand skills, or a job offer, refugees are forced to leave their homes. They often lose their property, documents, professional networks, and the ability to make use of the human capital they have accumulated. They adapt much more slowly than labor migrants and people who move for family reunification, resulting in what researchers refer to as the “refugee gap.”
Refugees are the category of migrants that is hardest to integrate
While labor migrants move based on their skills and the needs of the labor market that attracts them, refugees go wherever they can find safety. Their integration is further complicated by the trauma they have experienced, prolonged uncertainty over their legal status, restrictions on access to the labor market while their applications are being processed, and administrative policies that place them in areas with limited economic opportunities and little or no diaspora support.
In Spain, the flow of humanitarian migrants today is comparable to that seen in Sweden at the peak of its refugee intake (although its relative size is significantly smaller given that Spain's population is five times as big). At the same time, 47% of migrants in Spain come from Latin America, with which Spain shares a language and similar culture. They can enter without a visa, are immediately allowed to work, and can apply for citizenship after just two years of residence. Another 27% come from other European countries, while only 18% come from Africa and 6% from Asia (including the Philippines, which was also once a Spanish colony). In short, historical, cultural, and linguistic ties make integration into Spanish society considerably easier for most migrants than the integration of Middle Eastern migrants in Sweden, despite the lower level of government spending.
Russia likewise has significant cultural and linguistic influence in Central Asia, as well as large diasporas from the region, making it easier for migrants from Central Asian countries to integrate into Russian society. Similarly, the U.S. has exerted influence across Latin America for centuries and is home to large Latin American diasporas. Poland and the Czech Republic have also achieved strong migrant integration outcomes because, historically, they have primarily received Ukrainians, who are culturally and linguistically similar and can take up employment immediately. Thus, even when a large influx of Ukrainian refugees arrived after the outbreak of the war, they were relatively easily integrated.
Cultural differences, however, do not account for the entire gap. The quality of the human capital that countries attract also matters. The U.S., for example, is geographically distant from most of the world's main migration routes, so reaching the country itself requires substantial resources. Its high wages consequently attract some of the most successful and highly educated migrants.
For example, Middle Eastern migrants in the U.S. are twice as likely as Americans overall to hold a bachelor's degree, and they earn slightly more. In Europe, by contrast, where many arrived as low-skilled guest workers, undocumented migrants, or refugees, they are among the most disadvantaged groups, with low incomes and high crime rates.
Similarly, Pakistani migrants in the U.S. have higher incomes and higher levels of education than the native-born population, while in Britain they have one of the lowest employment rates in the country. The colonial legacy plays a role: in the 1950s and 1960s, Britain itself brought in large numbers of workers from Pakistan to work in factories, and they later brought their families over.
A substantial part of the employment gap, however, is also explained by the fact that many Pakistani women, due to cultural traditions and discrimination, choose not to work and instead engage in unpaid domestic work, a common practice among diasporas from Muslim-majority countries across Europe.
The impact of discrimination
Finally, it also matters how prepared a country's institutions are to receive migrants. Even if a country attracts relatively well-off migrant groups and provides them with rapid access to the labor market, that alone is not enough. What matters is whether institutions allow migrants to compete with native-born residents on an equal footing.
The U.S., Canada, Australia, and New Zealand are countries built by migrants. They have accumulated experience with immigration and established diasporas that help newcomers integrate. European countries, by contrast, only became countries of immigration in the 20th century, having previously been countries of emigration. They are considerably more ethnically homogeneous and therefore have less experience and few longstanding institutions for integrating migrants.
A meta-analysis of 97 experiments examining hiring discrimination across nine developed countries — the U.S., Canada, France, Belgium, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden — found that the highest levels of discrimination in the initial screening of résumés were recorded in France and Sweden, while the lowest were found in Germany, Norway, and the U.S. In Sweden and France, the groups facing the highest levels of discrimination were also those that make up a significant share of the migrant population: Black people and people from the Middle East.
France and Sweden have the highest levels of discrimination in screening résumés from applicants with “migrant” names
The poor results of Sweden's integration policy can therefore also be attributed to informal practices, such as screening out candidates with foreign-sounding names at the résumé stage. Even when the state is highly willing to fund social programs, migrants can face serious barriers as early as the search for their first job. And this is only one form of discrimination. The study's authors note that Germany has managed to build a system that limits bias in hiring, while discrimination remains widespread in the housing market.
Promoting formal integration also has a positive effect on other aspects of integration. The experience of Switzerland, where naturalization applications in some municipalities were decided by referendum, showed that immigrants who won their vote and obtained citizenship earned an average of $5,000 more per year over the following 15 years than otherwise similar immigrants who failed to gain similar support. The effect was particularly strong among the most marginalized groups — people from Turkey and the former Yugoslavia, as well as low-wage workers.
Thus, institutions that not only give migrants access to the labor market but also recognize them as equal members of the political community can generate long-term economic benefits and improve the prospects for successful integration.

Prices have risen most steeply in Queensland and northern Australia, where it now costs 44 per cent more to build a home than it did in 2021, the report from the Insurance Council of Australia found.
Between 2022 and 2026, insurers received 400,000 claims to repair or rebuild homes damaged in declared events, costing $11.3 billion.
Materials most needed after a natural disaster have gone up in cost the most, with roof tiles up more than 70 per cent — more than three times the rate of inflation — and windows, plasterboard and concrete prices increasing upwards of 37 per cent.
Insurance Council Australia (ICA) chief executive Andrew Hall said inflation was driving up costs, and people's premiums with it.
"In states like Queensland, where quite often it's severe storms that impact a home, those things that need replacing immediately are the things that are costing the most, that all goes into the calculation when we're looking at the cost of an insurance premium," he said.
Meanwhile, as extreme weather events become more frequent and severe, Australia is repairing nearly as many homes as it is building new ones.
In 2025, declared events damaged 145,392 homes. Nationally, 172,657 new homes were built.
In the past five years, in Queensland alone, insurers have repaired or replaced more than 240,000 homes.
"These are homes that are already existing which means we're competing with the same sector that's trying to deliver new homes to meet the housing challenges," Mr Hall said.
It's set up a "double whammy" where insurers vie with builders for materials and trades, he said.
"Not only are we trying to meet the affordability and accessibility challenge, we're at the same time competing for the same builders and materials to repair existing housing stock."
The report recommends Australia builds more resilient homes, and stop homes being built in high-risk areas.
"Future-proofed" homes would stop resources for new buildings being diverted for repairs, Paula Jarzabkowski, Professor in Strategic Management at the University of Queensland said.
Instead of rebuilding "like for like" repairs need to make a home safer and more likely to withstand severe weather, she added.
"At a time when we should be building more homes and we know that, we're having to go backwards and rebuild existing homes," Professor Jarzabkowski said.
"If we weren't rebuilding that 150,000 perhaps we could have put those resources into building the housing stock for tomorrow.
"We need to build that housing stock in a way that is future-proofed. Let's not build tomorrow's buyback today."

====================================================================================================

Heatwaves and secret emissions: Why nuclear power may not be as ‘green’ as you think
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:12:27 UTC
14:12:27 KST

The war on Iran has triggered calls to double down on nuclear power. But is it really ‘clean’, can Europe’s energy grid cope and will it survive the wrath of climate change?
The world stood still on 11 March 2011, when a major earthquake triggered a 15-metre tsunami that left an unforgettable scar on Japan’s east coast.
A series of powerful waves ripped through homes, businesses and roads – leaving more than 450,000 people homeless and killing 15,500. Alongside the chaos, the tsunami caused the meltdown of three nuclear reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, spewing out toxic, radioactive materials and forcing thousands to evacuate.
The event triggered global conversation about the safety of nuclear energy, leading several countries to plan to phase out nuclear energy or stop its expansion.
But 15 years later and the horrors of Fukushima have slowly been replaced with calls to double down on nuclear power, particularly following the war on Iran and its subsequent energy crisis. Speaking exclusively to Euronews, EU Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra listed nuclear as one of the power sources EU countries must lean on.
However, an expert from the University of Oxford has warned that new nuclear capacity will not fix today’s energy problems – urging policy makers to consider the true risks of nuclear.
“In the high‑renewables systems of Europe, the problem is increasingly not how to generate more electricity but how to access it when and where it’s needed,” says Dr Bettina Wittneben, a lecturer in Management at Oxford’s Saïd Business School and associate fellow at Pembroke College and the School of Geography and the Environment.
Is nuclear power really ‘clean’?
Nuclear energy is often touted as a clean form of energy as it is low carbon at the point of generation.
In layman’s terms, nuclear reactors can create electricity without releasing carbon dioxide or smog-forming pollutants into the atmosphere. However, experts point out that this isn’t the full picture.
“The bulky concrete structures mean that it has a large amount of embodied carbon and, of course, it is not a renewable energy as it requires the mining of uranium, bringing with it carbon costs in terms of extraction and transport,” says Dr Bettina.
“Nuclear waste disposal and decommissioning must also be factored into the carbon budget of nuclear energy generation.”
Are nuclear power plants climate resilient?
Europe was scorched by back-to-back heatwaves this summer, which experts say would have been “virtually impossible” if it weren’t for climate change. The extreme heat, combined with scant rainfall, triggered droughts across much of the continent, draining some of Europe’s biggest rivers to record-level lows.
This forced several nuclear power plants to temporarily shut off or be set to a reduced output across France, Hungary and Romania.
Nuclear requires vast amounts of water, particularly for the cooling process, and is often known as the “thirstiest power source”. According to The Nuclear Energy Institute, one nuclear reactor requires between 1,514 and 2,725 litres of water per MWh – equating to hundreds of gigalitres every year.
It’s why nuclear power plants are often built near large bodies of water. Without a constant, reliable source of water a nuclear reactor risks overheating – which could lead to serious core damage and end up releasing harmful radiation into the environment.
Coal power and hydropower also suffered during the heatwave, but a surge in solar power helped meet heightened electricity demand from cooling devices such as air conditioning.
According to energy think-tank Ember, solar output in European countries rose by up to 17 per cent on heatwave days in June and July – becoming the only major power source to perform “better than usual” during hot weather.
'Hellbrise': Nuclear is not as reliable as some say
Intermittent forms of energy such as wind and solar are often blamed for overloading Europe’s outdated energy grid.
When electricity demand outstrips supply, surplus energy is often wasted – and can lead to negative electricity prices. This is often referred to as 'Hellbrise' (hell= bright, brise= breeze) and can occur on sunny, windy days.
“This is also the narrative of fossil fuel advocates, who present fossil gas as the saviour of the baseload, or the electricity that is available when renewables fall short,” says Dr Wittneben.
“Fossil fuel sceptics point instead to nuclear power as a reliable baseload technology.”
However, the expert points out that nuclear power plants are slow and costly to turn off, which means they only “amplify” the grid’s Hellbrise challenge – rather than present a solution to it.
The EU has recognised that battery energy storage systems (BESS) are a “crucial technology” to help prevent renewable energy from being wasted or entering sub-zero pricing. The logic is that batteries can store electricity produced by renewables during the day (when consumption tends to be low) and release it to households when demand increases in the evening.
Europe installed 36 GWh of new BESS in 2025, bringing its total operational capacity beyond 100 GWh for the first time. This is enough stored energy to power around 75 million homes.
Which EU countries have become reliant on nuclear power?
Last year, the European Union generated 652TWh of electricity from nuclear, representing 23.3 per cent of the bloc’s total electricity mix.
This was more than solar (13.1 per cent) and wind (17.1 per cent) – and put nuclear as the largest share of electricity generation for 2025.
More than half of this (392 TWh) was generated in France, which has the biggest nuclear output across the bloc. In fact, France generated more than two-thirds (68.8 per cent) of its electricity from nuclear last year.
This was followed by Spain (54.1 TWh), Sweden (46.7 TWh), Finland (32.8 TWh), Czechia (31.9 TWh), Belgium (24.1 TWh), Slovakia (19.3 TWh), Hungary (16.1 TWh), Bulgaria (14.8 TWh), Romania (10.2 TWh), Slovenia (5.83 TWh) and the Netherlands (3.99 TWh).
Because European power grids are interconnected, many countries that do not have active nuclear power plants can purchase electricity generated by nuclear power from other EU countries. In 2024, France was Europe’s biggest electricity exporter – and much of this was generated from nuclear power.
But not every EU country is onboard with running nuclear power plants, particularly following the Fukushima incident.
Back in 2020, Germany generated 170 TWh of electricity from nuclear – putting it as the second largest producer in the EU. This was the year the country first passed a legal plan to end nuclear power.
Germany officially stopped using nuclear power for electricity on April 15, 2023, when it shut down its three final operating reactors.
The move was described as a “grave strategic mistake” by Chancellor Friedrich Merz – and saw the country’s reliance on polluting fossil fuels temporarily increase to bridge the gap in energy supply.
However, a recent analysis from think-tank Energy Institute found that together wind and solar generated 44 per cent of Germany’s electricity in 2025, overtaking fossil fuels by one per cent.
At the same time, coal fell from supplying more than half of the country’s electricity in 2000 to just 21 per cent last year. Experts are now hopeful that Germany will be able to wean itself off coal completely before 2038.

Two decades after Beslan, Russia faces terrorism of a different kind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:09:03 UTC
14:09:03 KST

Two decades after Beslan, Russia faces terrorism of a different kind
On September 1, 2004, during celebrations marking the first day of the school year, a group of Islamist terrorists occupied Beslan’s School No. 1 in the Caucasus region of Russia, and captured over 1,100 hostages, including students, their families, and teachers.
After three days of tense negotiations, during which 26 women and children were released, Russian special forces had to storm the building in an emergency operation after explosions were heard inside the school, which had been rigged to detonate by the militants. The Beslan terrorist attack claimed the lives of 334 people, including 186 children, 17 teachers and school staff, ten FSB officers, and two rescue workers.
Russia spent decades fighting the Islamist threat from the 1990s to late 2010s and refining its prevention mechanisms. Indeed, President Vladimir Putin was the first to call his US counterpart on September 11, 2001.
But a new danger has arisen with the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, posed not by suicide bombers but by drones and missiles – sent from the West, striking at night, in a systematic campaign of terror launched by Ukraine that targets Russian civilians.
Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, Ukrainian attacks have killed more than 8,000 civilians and injured almost 20,000 more, according to Rodion Miroshnik, who leads the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking Ukrainian war crimes. At least 266 civilians, including seven children, were killed in Ukrainian attacks in the first 90 days of 2026, and 1,459 others were injured, according to Miroshnik’s estimates.
RT looks back at the deadliest Ukrainian strikes on civilians, which Russia has condemned as terrorist attacks aimed at compensating for the setbacks the Ukrainian military has suffered on the front line, where Russian forces have been on the offensive for months.
Tragedy on New Year’s Eve
On December 30, 2023, Ukrainian forces bombarded the Russian city of Belgorod, located around 40 km from the border, using multiple-launch rocket systems. The shelling targeted a popular city mall that traditionally held festive events on New Year’s Eve. The strike claimed the lives of 14 people, including two children, and left 108 people, among them 15 children, injured.
Crocus City Hall
The 2024 massacre, second only to the Beslan attack in its tragic scale, saw four armed men opening fire on concertgoers in a music venue that was filling with around 3,000 people ahead of a show by the rock band Picnic.
They set the hall on fire and murdered 151 people and injured 609 others. The Russian Investigative Committee concluded that, although the attack was carried out by a regional offshoot of Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS), it was organized on behalf of Ukraine.
The terrorists tried to flee toward the Ukrainian border before being intercepted and captured by Russian law enforcement.
Dark holiday season
On January 1, 2026, a cafe and hotel in Khorly, a Black Sea village in Kherson Region, were struck by three Ukrainian drones, including one carrying an incendiary mixture, during New Year’s celebrations. The strike killed 29 people and left more than 50 injured. According to the local authorities, the venue was scouted by a reconnaissance UAV before the attack.
The tragedy in Khorly was followed by a series of similar strikes that brought the total number of civilian casualties to 152 over the 11-day Russian winter holiday season, including 45 deaths, according to Miroshnik. Three minors were among those killed, the diplomat said at the time.
Horror at hospital
On March 12, 2026, Ukrainian forces struck a medical facility in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR). According to Russian officials, the attack targeted the grounds of a medical center housing more than 130 patients and around 50 medical personnel. Eight medical workers were killed and ten people were injured in the strike.
Starobelsk ‘We will never forget’
On May 22, three waves of Ukrainian kamikaze drones struck the main academic building and dormitory of the Starobelsk Professional College in the Lugansk People’s Republic in a nighttime attack. As a result, 21 students – some just 18 years old – were killed and around 60 people were injured.
President Vladimir Putin called it a deliberate ”terrorist act,” while the nation’s newly appointed human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, accused Ukrainian forces of carrying out a “targeted strike that killed 21 children.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Moscow will “never forget and will seek justice for [Ukrainian leader Vladimir] Zelensky’s bloody terror attack in Starobelsk.”
‘Monstrous crime’
On June 17, 2026, a Ukrainian drone struck a bus carrying a Belarusian youth soccer team in Bryansk Region, Russia. The attack killed the coach’s wife and injured several other passengers, including children.
Belarus described the attack as a “monstrous crime,” which President Alexander Lukashenko called a deliberate provocation. Kiev denied responsibility, while Zelensky threatened Minsk, demanding that Belarus dismantle alleged drone relay stations near the border and warning that Kiev would destroy them if Belarus failed to act.
Deadly drone raid
On August 10, 2026, the Ukrainian military launched a massive long-range drone strike on Nizhnekamsk in the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia, more than 2,000 km away from Ukraine’s border with Russia. According to Mayor Radmir Belyaev, Ukrainian UAVs targeted both industrial and civilian sites in the city.
The attack claimed the lives of 13 people and forced nearly 80 to request medical assistance. Nearly 30 people were hospitalized. Russia’s Investigative Committee said one of the civilians killed was a minor. The agency has designated the Ukrainian attack as an act of terrorism, stressing that the targeted locations “had nothing to do with military activities.”

Is Marnus Labuschagne finally out of luck?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:03:41 UTC
14:03:41 KST

Will Marnus Labuschagne's recent fortunes see him out of the Test side?
For a period of 23 Tests, Marnus Labuschagne was statistically the luckiest batter in Test cricket.
He had more genuine chances dropped or missed than any other batter from his debut up until the end of the 2021/22 Ashes series. He was more often than not able to turn those reprieves into significant scores.
In more recent times, it's been slim pickings. In fact, it's been 23 Tests since his last century, dating back to the fourth Ashes Test at Old Trafford in 2023.
He's been left out of the ODI squad travelling to take on Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month. The right-hander has only missed five of Australia's last 56 ODIs, raising questions about his future in the Test side.
"We're still very much working through what that Test squad looks like, but I can say we separate out those formats," chair of selectors George Bailey told reporters when unveiling the ODI squad.
"He has played some really important one-day cricket for us; at his best that looks a certain way, but the way that squad and team is structuring up there just wasn't space for him."
If you break down Labuschagne's career into the period before his last Test ton and the period since, there is somewhat of a trend: his luck has seemingly run out.
Looking at only genuine chances missed by opposition teams — dropped catches, missed stumpings, opposition teams not reviewing a decision that would have seen him dismissed, or wickets on a no ball — he was given a reprieve 25 times from 75 innings where he faced at least one ball.
That's a chance every three innings from his Test debut in 2018 to his most recent hundred back in 2023.
Across his first 20 Tests he scored six centuries and 12 fifties, earning him a batting average of 62.15. If, in that time, he had been taken at the first opportunity, that average drops to 46.50.
In the 2019-2021 World Test Championship cycle, Labuschagne played 13 Tests and scored the most runs of any other batter in the world. He finished that period with 1,675 runs at an average of 72.82. Across the 23 innings he was required to bat in, he was afforded 12 chances, or one every 1.92 innings.
When you compare that with Steve Smith in the same period, he was given a reprieve four times, which equates to one every 5.5 innings. Smith was still able to score 1,341 runs in that WTC cycle, which highlights Labuschagne's ability to capitalise when given the opportunity.
In fact, his entire Test career has been based on it.
Labuschagne made his Test debut in 2018 due to the bans handed down to Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft after the sandpaper incident the last time Australia's Test team toured South Africa.
That put him in the frame for the 2019 Ashes squad and, after a red-hot Smith was hit in the neck by a Jofra Archer bouncer at Lord's, Labuschagne got his next chance as the first concussion substitute in the history of international cricket, courtesy of a rule introduced the month before the series started.
In the next Test in Leeds, Labuschagne was dropped on 14, 42 and 60, and England failed to review an edge that would have been given out when he was on 35. He went on to make 80.
That series, including that fortunate knock of 80 at Headingley, cemented his spot in the side, with Usman Khawaja the unfortunate one to make way when Smith returned, a decision that left Khawaja on the outer for three years.
His ability to turn a reprieve into a significant score was a hallmark of his early Test career. Labuschagne's maiden Test century came against Pakistan at the Gabba in 2019 when he scored an impressive 185 off 279 balls. Pakistan fans might still be ruing the fact he was dropped by Asad Shafiq on 33 that same innings.
In that WTC cycle alone, if he had been taken at the first opportunity, his batting average would drop to 55.68, which would have had him ranked 11th in the world.
It's not just his luck that's seemingly run out; it's his ability to capitalise on it.
From that first Ashes series to his last Test century, Labuschagne was able to turn missed opportunities into scores of 50 or more on nine occasions, including five hundreds.
Since that last century, he has been afforded only four reprieves, and the most he's added to his total is 18 runs.
Loading...
He was briefly dropped from the side after failing to impress as a makeshift opener in last year's World Test Championship final, missing Australia's tour of the West Indies. But, after only three Tests out of the side, he came back in for the 2025/26 Ashes and has remained in the team since.
When you compare that to the likes of Jake Weatherald, who has been in and out of the Test squad with questions around his form, Labuschagne has not just been given chances by opposition fielders; he's also been given them by the Australian selectors.
With an important series against South Africa on the horizon and his omission from the ODI squad, all eyes now look to see if his luck really has run out.

Key Takeaways from the ISW:
- Russia’s second batch of Rassvet satellites appears to have failed to reach intended operational altitudes, marking another setback in Moscow’s efforts to rapidly develop a Russian analogue to Starlink.

Singapore asks the $70,000 question: who wants to start a family?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:03:23 UTC
14:03:23 KST

With leafy cycle paths, rooftop water parks and child-friendly restaurants, Singapore’s east coast is one of the best places in the island city-state to raise a family.
Finance worker Lee lives in an apartment here with his wife and two cats, but like an increasing number of Singaporeans they do not intend to have children. They worry about the challenges of bringing them up, and the disruption to their lives.
He knows his parents want grandchildren: “They brought it up a couple of times when we were younger, but now they don’t bring it up any more.”
The 34-year-old, who requested his last name only be used, says he and his wife feel the same. “We are happy with our lives right now, so adding a kid will kind of complicate that,” including giving up travel and not being able to go out to restaurants.
A survey released this month by YouGov has found that many Singaporeans feel the same, with one in four saying they don’t plan to have children. Grappling with a historically low birthrate, the city-state announced sweeping measures to encourage couples to have children, but it is unclear how successful those measures might be.
The prime minister, Lawrence Wong, has said the government will provide almost S$70,000 (US$55,048; £40,647) in direct financial support for every child by the time they turn 17. The policy begins at birth with a S$10,000 baby grant, and two separate $5,000 grants for medical and educational expenses.
Other provisions include S$2,000 in “child credits” from ages one to 16, lowering government-subsidised preschool fees to S$150 a month, and giving people more parental leave.
“Singapore’s future will only be as strong as the families that build it,” Wong said.
Singapore’s birthrate for women of reproductive age – known as the total fertility rate – is a record low of 0.87. A rate below the “replacement level” of 2.1 is the norm around the world today, but Singapore is part of a cluster of countries in Asia with the world’s lowest rates, alongside the likes of South Korea and Taiwan.
For governments, the demographic trend poses a major economic challenge, leaving a smaller proportion of working adults to support a growing elderly population. Singapore is projected this year to reach a “super-aged” status, which the UN defines as having more than 21% of its population aged 65 and above.
The prime minister’s measures have received a mixed reception, with those interested in having children still worried about the expense of raising a family.
The cost of living in Singapore is “insanely high” says Iqbar Hisham, 27, who works as a coordinator in the construction industry, but the new policy has given her and her fiance some hope for starting a family in the future.
“These supports do encourage me to have children as soon as possible once I’m married,” Hisham says, noting in particular the help for childcare.
Social pressure, including a highly competitive education system and demanding workplaces, and the need for childcare support due to both parents working are also playing into a growing reluctance among some Singaporeans to start a family.
As an indication of the times, the pressure around academic results has fuelled a huge private tutoring industry as parents try to ensure their children get ahead.
Teo You Yenn, a sociologist and author of Unease: Life in Singapore Families, told the Straits Times she was struck during research for her book by how consumed Singaporean parents were with extracurricular study, starting as early as preschool.
In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that many Singaporeans “worry about the future their children will inherit, and whether they are doing enough to help them succeed”.
Lee says financial support from the government isn’t everything.
“I think there will be a large portion of time that me and my partner will need to take out in order to raise a child correctly,” he says. “That is something that we are not able to provide at the moment.”
Planning manager and mother of three Shu Rong Teo, 41, says having children has always been important for her.
But having a family and retaining her job at the Singapore Chinese Orchestra was only possible with the support of a domestic helper, and by living with her in-laws.
“Our experience is a testament that it takes a village to raise a child – and that family support remains indispensable for working parents navigating the demands of parenthood.”
She welcomes the reforms, in particular increased childcare leave, which will allow her to spend more time with her children.
“I used to have two days of childcare leave. Outside the two days, I had to take my annual leave to take care of my children, but with the new measures [my husband and I] have 12 days each.
“The biggest difference will be having more time.”

Russia's first AI law comes into force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:01:21 UTC
14:01:21 KST

MOSCOW, September 1. /TASS/. Russia's first law on artificial intelligence (AI), specifically aimed at supporting the development of AI technologies, came into force on September 1.
The law regulates relations involving the development, deployment and use of AI. It establishes basic concepts for the industry, including definitions of AI itself, large foundation models and their developers, among others. It also introduces general liability for violations in the AI sector.
Some provisions of the law will not take effect until March 1, 2027. These include certain provisions of the article outlining the powers of the president, the government and federal executive authorities in the AI sector; provisions dividing models into sovereign and national models based on their degree of dependence on external technologies and setting out obligations for their developers; as well as two other articles covering the labeling of AI-generated content and requirements for training AI on "results of intellectual activity."
At the same time, the article providing support measures for developers of sovereign and national AI models takes effect on September 1, 2026.

What are phantom scams, and why do they end with you robbing yourself?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

No hacker, no crime, no bank on the other end of the line — just a script designed to make you empty your own account. Here's how phantom scams work, and how to hang up in time.
Phantom hacker scams, also known as phantom scams, have surged in recent years.
These are elaborate frauds in which criminals convince victims their money or computer has been compromised by a hacker. The scammer then pushes the victim to move their savings into a supposedly "safe" account, which is in fact controlled by the criminals themselves.
The rise of artificial intelligence, online banking and social media has fuelled the trend — more ways to pay and receive money mean more entry points for scammers to exploit.
How phantom hacker scams work
Some of the most common phantom hacker scams work in a few stages. The first one is tech support.
This usually involves a pop-up screen warning, text or call claiming that your computer or device has a virus. When you call the number provided, a person pretending to be tech support can ask you to download remote-access software.
The next phase is the fake bank alert. Another person might call you, claiming that your accounts are being hacked. Scammers may often spoof caller ID information, so you may believe that the call is from a legitimate phone number.
They may say that immediate action needs to be taken to protect your account and funds, so you need to log in right now to check your balance.
However, since they now have remote access to your device, they can watch you log in and gather your details.
The final phase is the government imposter one. This can involve a third person calling you, claiming to be from a government or law enforcement agency like the FBI or Federal Reserve.
They may pressure you to move your money into a supposedly “safe” account or direct it towards things like cryptocurrency and gold bars in order to protect it.
Some variations ask victims to download an app that supposedly speeds up fund transfers. In reality, this hands scammers remote access to the device, letting them steal money, often entire life savings, directly from the account.
The methods vary, but the underlying tactic is nearly always the same: create a sense of urgency and push victims into acting out of panic.
How to protect yourself
According to TEG Federal Credit Union, the best defence is simple: never trust unsolicited calls, texts or pop-ups about your bank account or computer. Hang up immediately if you receive one.
Never download remote-viewing software or apps at the request of someone who contacted you out of the blue.
If you suspect a scam, call your bank directly using the number on its website or on the back of your card.
No legitimate bank, tech company or government agency will ever ask you to move your savings into a "safe" account or buy gold or cryptocurrency.
How are phantom hacker scams different from phantom debt?
Unlike phantom hacker scams, which typically rely on gaining access to a victim’s money or bank account, phantom debt or zombie debt is a different type of scam. This involves scammers attempting to get victims to pay fake or expired debts.
While this was previously done through badly-written emails or unconvincing cold calls, today, scammers rely on large language models (LLMs) to write perfectly localised and highly convincing legal threats.
These debts might already have been paid off, discharged in bankruptcy or artificially inflated by shady operators.
Scammers usually pose as debt collectors and attempt to use aggressive language, fake threats of arrest or intimidation to scare victims into paying immediately.
In many cases, they may also use confusing language to explain how a debt that was previously thought to be paid off or cleared is still owed, while continuing to use intimidation and panic creation tactics to prevent victims from further digging into the mechanics.
This can especially be done to senior victims.
Scammers also leverage automated AI agents to scrape public information, build a profile on a target and use audio clips to clone voices, posing as law enforcement or bank officials.
Sometimes they may ask for crypto payments or wire transfers to settle these phantom debts.
Similar to phantom hacker scams, consumers should immediately hang up while receiving these calls, along with locking down their information and freezing payments.
They can also demand a validation letter, which real collectors in many jurisdictions are obliged to send, or block and report them.

“The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.”
Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills.
However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.”
The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields.
Cereals including wheat and barley were hit particularly badly, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006.
The rise in shop price inflation adds to the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government in achieving its aim of granting “breathing space” to hard-pressed households
Wider consumer price inflation across the UK rose to 2.9% in July with the Iran war affecting energy prices, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics. The agency said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by more costly gas and electricity.
Despite government measures to ease electricity costs, households in Great Britain face the sharpest summer increase in energy bills in four years.

Sami Tamimi’s recipes for musabaha (warm chickpea dip) and turmeric and nigella seed flatbreads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Few things make me happier than a bowl of warm musabaha served with freshly baked bread straight from the pan. It’s a combination that shouts comfort, generosity and the simple pleasure of sharing food. Across the Levant, musabaha is a much-loved breakfast or brunch dish, though I’d happily eat it at any time of day. Served with the buttery, soft turmeric and nigella-seed flatbreads, it becomes a meal that is nourishing, intensely satisfying and perfect for gathering family and friends around the table.
Musabaha (warm chickpeas with spicy cherry tomato and coriander salad)
When I’m short of time but craving something nourishing, full of flavour and genuinely satisfying, I turn to murabaha time and again. Unlike hummus, the chickpeas are left whole, then gently warmed and topped with a vibrant salad of spicy cherry tomatoes, fresh coriander and good olive oil. Serve with plenty of the warm flatbreads below for scooping.
Prep 15 min
 Cook 15 min
 Serves 4
2 400g tins chickpeas, drained
  3 tbsp olive oil, plus extra to drizzle
5 large garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
1 large green chilli, finely chopped seeds and all
1 tbsp ground cumin
  100g tahini, plus extra to serve 
120g greek-style yoghurt
  3 tbsp lemon juice
  Salt
For the cherry tomato salad 
150g cherry tomatoes,halved
1 mini cucumber (100g), finely diced 
½ red pepper (75g), finely diced
20g fresh coriander, finely chopped 
2 spring onions, trimmed and very thinly sliced 
1 green chilli, thinly sliced seeds and all
1 large garlic clove, peeled and crushed
2 tbsp lemon juice 
  1 tbsp white-wine vinegar
  2 tbsp olive oil 
  1 tbsp sumac
  1 tsp dried mint
  ½ tsp aleppo chilli, plus extra for sprinkling
Put the chickpeas in a medium saucepan with enough water just to cover them., put on a medium heat and bring to a simmer. Leave to cook for about five minutes, just to soften them a bit more, then drain, reserving about 300ml of the cooking liquid.
Meanwhile, put all ingredients for the cherry tomato salad in a medium bowl with half a teaspoon of salt, and mix well.
Put the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the garlic and cook, stirring often, for two minutes, until the garlic starts to colour, then add the chilli and cook for another minute. Add the drained chickpeas, the reserved cooking liquid, cumin, tahini, yoghurt, lemon juice and a teaspoon of salt, bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer, stirring from time to time, for two minutes.
To serve, transfer the warm chickpeas to a large serving plate with a lip or a wide, shallow bowl. Drizzle over some tahini, then spoon the cherry tomato salad on top. Finish with a good drizzle of olive oil and a sprinkling of aleppo chilli, and serve with the flatbreads below.
Turmeric and nigella seed flatbread
I come from a culture where offering freshly baked, warm bread is one of the greatest traditions of hospitality. Whether welcoming unexpected guests or gathering loved ones around the table, bread is always the first thing shared. These golden flatbreads, scented with earthy turmeric and nutty ghee, are perfect for scooping up the warm chickpeas and spicy tomato salad oppositebelow, but they’re equally delicious served with dips or simply drizzled with good olive oil.
Prep 5 min
Rest 10 min
 Cook 25 min
 Makes 8
150g full-fat greek yoghurt 
  1 tsp bicarbonate of soda 
350g 00 flour, or plain flour, plus extra for dusting 
  100g wholewheat flour 
  ¾ tsp ground turmeric 
  1 tbsp nigella seeds 
  1½ tsp salt 
  35g ghee, or butter, melted
Put the yoghurt and bicarb in the bowl of a free-standing mixer with the dough hook attached, and stir well with a spoon. The mix should start bubbling. Add 150ml water, stir again, then add all the remaining ingredients apart from the ghee and mix on low speed for five minutes, until the dough is soft but not sticky.
Divide the dough in 10 equal pieces of about 110g each. Roll each piece into a ball, cover with a damp towel and leave to rest for 10 minutes – this will stop the dough drying out.
On a lightly floured surface, roll out each piece of dough into a 16cm disc about ½cm thick.
Heat a grill pan until it’s very hot. Lay in one or two dough discs and cook for a minute or two on each side, until the bread is cooked through and has char marks. Remove from the pan, keep warm and repeat with the remaining dough. Brush each flatbread with melted ghee or butter, and serve.

Burnham warned running prison capacity near limit is ‘big risk’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

Andy Burnham is taking a “big risk” by seeking to continue running prison capacity to the limit, according to the former justice secretary appointed by Keir Starmer to oversee a review of sentencing.
As parliament resumes on Tuesday, the government will confirm its U-turn on its early release scheme, which would have seen thousands of prisoners released early as part of a plan to ease prison overcrowding.
About 5,000 prisoners had been due to be released early from October under the plans, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and “serious” child sexual abuse offenders.
However, David Gauke, the former Conservative minister who led Starmer’s independent review of sentences, warned of the “stresses and strains” from choosing to run prison capacity at a “red hot” level, even as he recognised options available to Burnham were limited.
“He is in a bind. I have some sympathy for any government that is wrestling with this, but that is why we came forward with the recommendations we came forward with,” Gauke told the Guardian.
“I am going to see what Alex Norris [the justice secretary] says in parliament, but my concern – and I hope this isn’t the case – is that they are essentially taking a big risk on prison capacity.”
Gauke said that Burnham’s political strategy was in contrast to his predecessor in that the new prime minister was “very sensitive to public opinion”.
He also said it would be “irresponsible” to release prisoners serving indefinite jail terms, which Burnham has pledged to abolish. The government is pinning some hope of increasing capacity on reducing the number of prisoners serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, and deporting more foreign prisoners more swiftly.
“In terms of public protection, releasing IPPs comes with much higher risks than the categories excluded from the early release scheme,” said Gauke, who examined them when he was justice secretary in Theresa May’s government but said it was clear from prison disciplinary records why such prisoners had not been released.
The intervention came as the government said on Monday night that the largest prison-building programme since the Victorian era would be accelerated through a £110m investment.
The funding will go towards speeding up the construction of hundreds of prison places with plans to add 14,000 extra spaces by 2031, and cells being created from existing space within prisons including unused offices, laundry rooms and other areas.
The Ministry of Justice also said on Monday there would be investment to buy new land to secure potential sites for future prisons.
“This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we’ve already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years,” said Norris.
However, the Conservatives sought to keep up political pressure over the early release scheme, saying that it left at least 23 categories of serious violent and sexual offences eligible for automatic early release, including trafficking, strangulation and assault by penetration.
“Labour’s plan to stop the release of dangerous criminals is to release a whole new group of dangerous criminals,” said the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, who called for a delay to the scheme and emergency primary legislation to exclude the worst offenders.
The victims minister, Alex Davies-Jones, insisted during interviews on Monday that “release does not mean freedom” for those let out under the early release scheme.
“When these offenders come out of prison, the presumption will be that they will all be placed on a GPS monitoring tag,” she said.
In terms of capacity, she told the BBC’s Today programme: “We will have capacity in the system with those numbers but we will run it very tight, which is why we have been tasked to look at what more we can do.”
A leading police chief, meanwhile, warned that tracking people let out of prison under the early release scheme would be an additional challenge on the strained resources of police officers.
Jason Hogg, the chief constable of Thames Valley police, told LBC on Monday: “The police haven’t received any additional funding for this additional work, so I’m going to be having to move resources away from one area of business to another to seek out, arrest and bring before the court individuals who don’t follow the restrictions that they will be set.”

Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:45 UTC
14:00:45 KST

The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies during dry weather increased significantly during the first five months of 2026.
Dumping raw sewage into waterways during dry spells via overflows amounts to pollution. It is considered a breach of the permits given to water companies and is illegal. Discharging during dry weather increases the toxicity of the sewage pollution entering waterways. Rivers have less flow and volume, and there is no rainwater to dilute the sewage pollution entering the waterway.
Last year, in what regulators said was tougher action on sewage pollution, water companies in England were for the first time required to report to the Environment Agency the number of times they discharged raw sewage from combined sewer overflows during dry weather. A dry day spill is flagged when an overflow operates despite little to no rainfall that day and the previous day.
In 2025, water companies in England and Wales reported 8,576 dry spill pollution discharges. But according to freedom of information requests submitted by Environment Agency whistleblower Robert Forrester, the pollution is getting worse, not better, despite the regulator’s promise of tougher action.
Between January and May this year alone, water companies discharged raw sewage into rivers and seas during dry weather 7,280 times. The data is comparable as it is based on the same instruction and taken from the same data recording system.
The water industry said the figures were as yet unverified and it was too early to describe them as dry spills.
Forrester, an Environment Agency officer for more than 20 years, revealed failures by the agency to take on water companies’ illegal practices before leaving his job.
“Dry day spills will almost always be deliberate and illegal, otherwise there would be non-stop raw sewage spilling from pipes,” said Forrester.
“The huge increase in a much drier year appears to show that water companies have quotas of sewage to dump and will do whatever the weather, and whatever the risk to the public and the environment. Making money is the primary focus.” He said the regulator was no deterrent to the actions of the water companies.
“This level of criminality shows that water companies do not believe they, or the government, will ever do anything meaningful to stop them.”
Combined sewer overflows are an emergency system designed to be used in extreme weather to relieve pressure in the sewage system. But decades of underinvestment by the privatised water industry have led to the outflows being used regularly to discharge sewage.
In the first five months of 2026, South West Water, which operates across Devon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, discharged raw sewage on dry days 1,299 times. This compares with 2,451 times during the whole of 2025.
Water companies are facing outrage across the country for discharging raw sewage via storm outflows in August following the first moderate spell of rain after more than six weeks of drought. Public mapped data revealed water companies including Southern Water and South West Water discharging raw sewage from storm overflows within hours of the first significant rain.
In the south-west, after weeks of drought, the company’s own data suggested it discharged sewage into rivers and the sea for a combined total of almost 300 hours in the third week of August.
Ed Tyldesley, a Liberal Democrat county councillor in north Devon, said the company’s own figures showed 664 separate spills across 184 sites despite just 16.5mm of rain across the south-west.
“They are using a storm system when there are no storms. It is unbelievable. The worrying thing is that this all seems to be getting worse,” he said.
Tyldesley said he had been told by the water company that its live monitoring data could sometimes contain false readings. “That leaves two possibilities. Either the South West Water data is correct and sewage was discharged into our rivers and seas for 299 hours in a single week, or their legally mandated monitoring system is so unreliable that hundreds of apparent sewage spills are being reported to the public, which may not actually have happened.”
A spokesperson for Water UK, the trade association for the water industry, said: “These are unverified figures, and it is too early to describe them as dry day spills. Nonetheless, no spill is ever acceptable. Water companies are working to end them as fast as possible by tripling investment. Companies are investing £12bn to halve spills from storm overflows by 2030, including relining and sealing sewers to prevent groundwater infiltration – one of the main causes of dry day spills.”
South West Water has said the company publishes near real-time monitoring data, which has to be validated before being used for regulatory reporting.
“Storm overflow activations can happen for a range of reasons and aren’t determined by rainfall figures alone.
“We continue to invest in our monitoring and are spending record amounts to reduce storm overflow use across the region. We’re reviewing the locations raised by the councillor so we can provide a full response.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.
“After years of failure, we have taken immediate action to make water companies more accountable, and, for the first time ever, they are now required to report dry day spills as pollution incidents, providing the government with the evidence to go after water companies where performance falls short.”

EU needs European digital agency to close enforcement gap, experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:42 UTC
14:00:42 KST

The EU needs to set up a European digital agency to make its current digital rules work in practice and overcome the current enforcement gap, experts say in a new paper.
Brussels has built one of the world's densest regulatory frameworks for digital technologies. For experts, it is high time to centralise enforcement under a single European agency to overcome the fragmentation now holding it back.
The EU's digital rulebook spans more than 171 laws and 315 regulatory bodies — an unwieldy structure that has opened up a significant enforcement gap, leaving the bloc structurally unable to uphold its own rules.
That is the conclusion of a paper authored by Kai Zenner, head of office of MEP Axel Voss (Germany/EPP), and Maria Koomen, an independent tech and democracy analyst, who argue for the creation of a Digital Enforcement Agency.
The paper argues that streamlining enforcement is now urgent, just as Brussels has begun enforcing landmark digital laws such as the AI Act, the Digital Services Act (DSA) and the Digital Markets Act (DMA).
"Enforcement of the AI Act, DSA and DMA is ramping up, but their enforcement is split across more than 300 different EU and national bodies – many without the staff, expertise, or independence to act consistently," Koomen told Euronews.
For the authors, the European Commission — which leads enforcement of these flagship rules — is itself part of the problem, since it simultaneously legislates, enforces and evaluates while negotiating deals with foreign powers.
They point out that the EU executive is not only the bloc's most prominent digital enforcer but is also responsible for negotiating with third countries on issues such as trade and security, leaving it exposed to political pressure, or even inclined to underenforce pre-emptively.
Last year, media reports emerged that Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič had lobbied to delay an antitrust sanction against Google, for fear it could jeopardise the fragile trade truce between the EU and the US, known as the Turnberry Agreement.
For Koomen and Zenner, the combination of geopolitical capture, fragmented governance, the national interests of influential member states, and a lack of adequate resources together create an enforcement gap that leaves the EU's digital rules failing in practice.
The idea of centralising digital enforcement is not new, but has faced strong opposition in the past, with Brussels and national capitals reluctant to give up regulatory powers, and member states unwilling to finance a costly new EU body.
The paper proposes a three-step approach to overcome this resistance: starting with a short-lived cooperation forum, which would give way to a Digital Enforcement Agency in the medium term. The latter would gain fully independent status following treaty reform in the long run.
The authors argue there is a timely opportunity to act, with the Commission about to launch a broad review of EU digital legislation just as negotiations over the bloc's next long-term budget enter a crunch phase.
"A rare window is open to fix this structurally rather than patch it case by case," Koomen said. "If we miss this moment, the next opportunity will only come in seven years."
