Schengen strained, solidarity broken and return hubs disputed: EU struggles again with migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:37 UTC
14:00:37 KST

After a troubling summer marked by Ceuta's crisis, EU countries are scrambling to find solutions for migration management. The reintroduction of border checks, deportation centres outside the bloc, and redistribution of migrants will feature in a heated debate this autumn.
Migration is taking center stage again in the European Union, as Brussels returns to work after a summer marked by the major crisis of recent years.
Over 70,000 irregular migrants entered the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in a single day on 30 July, more than all other irregular entries across all European borders so far in 2026, sparking a political crisis in Spain and putting other member states on alert.
The Ceuta crisis increased pressure on the EU to implement its strategy to tighten the rules for asylum seekers and speed up returns, but it also highlighted the shortcomings of the new migration rules as they face their first real stress test.
EU leaders are expected to debate the topic in October at the European Council in Brussels, the culmination of a season of heated discussions through formal and informal meetings of interior ministers and ambassadors.
Schengen in trouble
The first impact of the domino effect was on free movement within the EU.
After the Ceuta crisis, Italy reintroduced air and maritime border controls with Spain for a month, while other countries such as Denmark and Finland called for Spain to be temporarily suspended from the Schengen area, where citizens and residents have been able to move since 1985 without border checks.
Spain answered with a mirror retaliatory measure towards Italy, even copy-pasting the wording of the official notification, reintroducing border checks until 7 September. At the end of the month, both countries decided to extend the suspension for further 15 days.
And the Italian government is not the only one concerned that Schengen rules could indirectly benefit irregular movement.
In an extraordinary online meeting in Brussels in early August, EU interior ministers initiated a discussion over the future of free movement. Twenty-two governments stated that any "necessary measures" will be taken into account "to safeguard public order and address risks arising from secondary movements [of migrants]", envisaging a wider reinforcement or reintroduction of border controls.
"The Schengen system has become one of the main victims of the internal political dynamics and concerns by member states around migration," Davide Colombi, researcher on migration at Brussels-based think tank CEPS, told Euronews.
EU member states may unilaterally reintroduce temporary, ad hoc border checks at their borders for a period of up to six months — renewable up to two years — on security grounds.
Currently, nine EU countries — Germany, Spain, Italy, Denmark, Austria, the Netherlands, Poland, France and Sweden — plus Norway have temporarily reintroduced border controls, citing concerns over irregular migration or terrorism threats.
Member states started to retain their own border controls in 2015, with the so-called European refugee crisis, as the removal of internal checks within the EU is widely considered to be closely intertwined with the surveillance of external borders.
"Migration will have broad repercussions on internal movements. For the moment, the Commission is choosing diplomatic ways rather than enforcing EU law and challenging the reintroduction of border checks," Colombi said.
Where is the solidarity?
Far from expressing solidarity, other EU countries accused Pedro Sánchez’s government, in the aftermath of the mass entry, of failing to sufficiently protect Europe’s external borders.
Solidarity is — on paper — one of the pillars of the new EU migration rules, which entered into force on 12 June.
The EU Migration and Asylum Pact entails a mandatory mechanism to assist the EU's frontline members, through a “solidarity pool” that defines the help countries need to offer each other for the following year. Member states have to choose among relocating a number of asylum seekers to their territory, paying a financial contribution, or financing personnel and other operational costs.
Redistribution of migrants across Europe is the most contentious point, as governments have little appetite for it and have managed to significantly reduce the numbers in the pool for 2026, asking for exemptions.
Relocations only apply to asylum seekers and people who have already been granted protection, therefore excluding most of the irregular Moroccan migrants who entered Ceuta in July, who have been or are set to be returned to their country of origin.
However, Spain is among the countries considered "under migratory pressure" because of last year's arrivals and will benefit from help this year. A total of 8,878 migrants who have applied for asylum in Spain, Italy, Greece, Cyprus and Malta will be taken in by other countries.
On the other hand, those countries will send back to frontline states the so-called "secondary movement" migrants — people who have entered the EU through a certain member state and then managed to move irregularly to another, asking for asylum there. According to EU rules, the first-entry country still has the responsibility to assess the request.
The first cracks are beginning to appear in the new solidarity system, as seven countries asked Italy to take back migrants and the Italian government invoked further compensation — which is not foreseen by EU rules — for migrants rescued at sea by NGO ships and disembarked on Italian shores.
A bilateral meeting between Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt in early September will kick off the debate on solidarity, which is set to continue at the Home Affairs Council at the beginning of October.
The crucial point will be the definition of the solidarity pool for 2027, which could see Italy and Spain on the same side, asking for more contributions from other countries after a summer of diplomatic spats between Rome and Madrid.
The uncertain future of return hubs
A key part of the EU strategy on migration concerns the return of irregular migrants, through a new regulation finalised last June and considered the strictest ever.
It introduces the possibility for member states to send people to a country with which they have no direct or indirect connection, provided that there is a bilateral agreement to set up deportation centres in the non-EU country.
These "return hubs" can be either places of transit, where a person is placed while waiting to be returned to their country of origin, or locations where a person is expected to stay with no guarantee of onward returns.
Some European governments are actively looking for partner countries, focusing on Asia and central Africa, intending to have the first partnership agreed by the end of the year, a diplomat told Euronews.
Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are working together on this project and are reportedly in talks with Uganda and Rwanda. Immigration ministers from the five countries are due to take stock of progress at a meeting in Copenhagen on 4 September.
The five-country working group could pave the way for a new model at EU level, despite criticism from civil society, operational difficulties and possible legal challenges.
"So far, it's not quite clear who is responsible for the migrants in a return hub, how long they can remain there and who monitors their conditions and provides effective remedies in case of human rights violations," Colombi said, pointing out that the EU legislation is vague on purpose to give states a free hand.
"I think there will be legal cases against the hubs once they are implemented on the ground, with a risk of a complete dismissal by the Court, as it happened with the UK-Rwanda migration scheme," he said.

Spa weekends: Where to go in Europe for a relaxing wellness escape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:13 UTC
14:00:13 KST

In need of a reset? These European destinations offer the perfect choice for rest and relaxation alongside mineral springs, forest escapes and Mediterranean sunshine.
Picture a getaway: rest, relaxation, rejuvenation and much-needed treatments against the backdrop of serene surroundings and no dings from urgent notifications. Sign me up, I say…
Hollywood has captured my sentiment in 'Spa Weekend', a new comedy film that hit big screens earlier in August.
It follows the misadventures of four lifelong friends who realise that in between juggling careers with everyday responsibilities, they lost track of taking care of themselves and each other. As burnout reaches breaking point, they all go for a – you guessed it – spa weekend.
With the trend now going beyond cinema theatres, luxury travel specialists Virtuoso reports that wellness bookings have increased by 28% year-on-year.
Now, I’m not someone who needs even an iota of convincing to indulge in spa treatments, but if you need a little push, these are the ideal European destinations where rejuvenation can easily fit into your itinerary.
A spa tour of Europe
If you're stumped on where to go for your spa weekend, you're in luck. There's actually a map of UNESCO World Heritage Sites to help you choose
The continent is home to 11 towns spread across seven countries that UNESCO has crowned as part of the “Great Spa Towns of Europe”.
According to the UN, each town has created its own "spa architecture”, pioneering a style of urban design centred on medical care as well as modern health and wellness tourism.
Out of the hundreds of spa towns across Europe, this handful were selected for their “outstanding universal value”, and they are:
- Baden bei Wien, Austria
- Spa, Belgium
- Františkovy Lázně, Czechia
- Karlovy Vary, Czechia
- Mariánské Lázně, Czechia
- Vichy, France
- Bad Ems, Germany
- Baden-Baden, Germany
- Bad Kissingen, Germany
- Montecatini Terme, Italy
- City of Bath, UK
Europe’s top spa hotels and resorts
Even though the 11 towns above are recognised by UNESCO and, in many cases, are filled to the brim with wellness spots, Europe has myriad spas across its territories, and these are some of the best.
Finn Lough, Northern Ireland
This self-styled 'luxury hideaway' is secluded in the ancient Irish woodland on the edge of the Lough Erne lake system. The spa experience is centred around reconnecting with nature, and offerings include a soak at the Shoreline Spa, which sits on the banks of Lough Erne or a sauna session with panoramic lake views.
Lefay Resort & Spa Lago di Garda, Italy
This Gargnano property in Italy offers a “temple of wellness” which stretches over 4,300 square metres. Promising a synergy of East meets West, the treatments on offer range from Thalassotherapy, including seaweed facial purifying, to Western massages for tension relief as well as Eastern massages and rituals such as Chinese Gua Sha or Tibetan hot sponging and cupping.
AMARA, Limassol, Cyprus
The five-star AMARA Hotel in Limassol is located on Cyprus’ southern coast. Its spa hosts three-and five-day wellness retreats centred around the resort's adults-only seawater infinity pool. Away from the water, the spa also offers a range of therapies which highlight local ingredients like organic olive oil and citrus, and there are also countless rituals, therapeutic massages and facials to experience.
ZEM Wellness Clinic Altea, Alicante, Spain
For travellers looking to take the wellness element of their getaway up a notch, Alicante’s ZEM Wellness Clinic Altea features an expansive 4,000 square metre wellness and spa facility. Guests can choose from Signature treatments which spotlight Mediterranean tradition in wellbeing, to technology-based therapies which boost metabolism and promote physical recovery, as well as aquatic and manual therapies and facial treatments.
Other destinations to go for a spa weekend
Velingrad, Bulgaria
Home to more than 700 mineral springs, which are known for their healing properties, Bulgaria has seen growing interest from tourists seeking spa tourism offerings, with demand rising by 15%, according to Irena Georgieva, Bulgaria's Deputy Tourism Minister.
If your aim is to immerse yourself completely in rest and relaxation, Bulgaria Travel describes Velingrad as the “spa capital of the Balkans”. Located 130 kilometres away from the capital Sofia, and tucked away in the Rhodope Mountains, the Bulgarian town is home to some 80 springs, including the country’s largest karst spring, Lake Kleptuza.
For a thermal retreat in the pine-topped Rhodope Mountains, Velingrad’s Spa Hotel Santé’s array of rooms and apartments comes alongside various wellness offerings, including steam bathing facilities, halotherapy (salt therapy) in the salt room, as well as a Turkish bath facility.
Guests can also take their pick from the hotel’s array of pools, all filled with mineral-rich water. All pools are set to a temperature of at least 33C; the outdoor dipper pool, however, is set to 38C, and is best for quick dips. Another “dipping-style” option is the contrast pools, divided into two temperature zones, a 40C section for brief relaxation and the 18C section to stimulate blood circulation.
Hiiumaa Island, Estonia
Encircled by the Baltic Sea and a destination of natural beaches, small harbours and hiking routes, Estonia’s Hiiumaa Island is an ideal island escape.
Accessible by land, air and sea, its slow rhythm is marked by nature reserves and coastal forests of dense woodland environments, so it’s no surprise why it's a perfect “forest bathing” destination.
Between forest and sea, the Eha Retreat is earmarked to open its doors in autumn. It will be shaped around Estonia’s so-called “five seasons”, and everything here is designed to support deep rest and regenerative wellbeing.
Guests will be able to choose between a three-, five- or seven-night experience which begins with a consultation to create a personalised programme for individualised wellbeing.
The Thermal Suite invites guests to Eha’s wellness offerings, including multiple saunas, steam rooms and hydrotherapy pools within the Thermal Suite.
Eha Retreat also facilitates nature-immersive experiences, such as foraging for ingredients to learn about food as medicine, and exploring Estonian food conservation techniques, tending land, gardening, going on guided walks through its estate, as well as engaging in forest tea ceremonies.

Shortages or ‘social dumping’: Lithuanian businesses and govt clash over migrant quotas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania’s annual quota for employing foreign workers has already been exhausted, prompting business groups to call for changes to the system, while the government says there is no reason to increase the quota next year and may consider reducing it.
Lithuania set this year’s quota at 24,700 foreign workers, but business representatives say it was exceeded in July.
Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė said, however, that only about 10,000 new workers actually entered Lithuania this year, suggesting the quota system may be allowing the same worker to account for multiple quota places.
“About 10,000 new workers have actually entered this year, so we need to look at why businesses have already run out of the quota,” Ruginienė said. “Perhaps we need some adjustments. If we fixed this system, we would see that a much smaller quota would be needed next year.”
The International Transport and Logistics Alliance said reducing the quota would hurt not only the transport sector but the wider economy.
About 80,000 third-country nationals work in the sector and pay more than 700 million euros in taxes annually through Lithuania’s State Tax Inspectorate and Social Insurance Fund, according to alliance head Povilas Drižas.
“If it is not possible to employ at least another 5,000 to 6,000 workers, we can calculate that the state will again lose about 40 million euros in tax revenue,” Drižas said.
Some workers are already being employed through companies established abroad, he insisted, potentially reducing Lithuania’s tax revenue further if the quota is cut.
The Business Confederation has urged the government to review the quota, arguing that the current system does not reflect labour market needs and that existing legislation allows a higher quota than the one set this year.
“There is room to increase the quota,” said Ineta Rizgelė, the confederation’s director general. She argued businesses facing higher taxes and other economic pressures needed government support as the quota had been exhausted unusually early.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas opposes an increase, arguing that businesses should make greater use of Lithuania’s domestic workforce.
“Unskilled labour from third countries is a form of social dumping,” Katelynas said, arguing that some employers prefer foreign workers because they can pay lower wages.
The quota does not apply to workers whose employers pay them more than 1,750 euros net per month, he said, questioning whether some companies are addressing genuine labour shortages or simply seeking cheaper workers.
Rita Karavaitienė, head of communications at the Employment Service, said Lithuania nonetheless faces significant labour shortages because of its aging population and demographic trends.
More than 168,000 third-country nationals currently work in Lithuania. About half are employed in transport, one-fifth in construction and one-tenth in manufacturing.
Ukrainians and Belarusians make up the largest groups, followed by citizens of Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and India. The number of workers arriving from the Philippines is growing particularly rapidly.
About 80% of third-country nationals working in Lithuania are classified as medium-skilled workers.

Who can still get a free COVID vaccine? Australia's new rules explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:59:12 UTC
13:59:12 KST

IN BRIEF
- Experts warn younger people with chronic conditions could face new barriers to accessing free COVID vaccines.
- Australia has yet to see a clear winter COVID peak in 2026, despite cases rising over the past fortnight.
Australia is preparing to wind back its universal COVID-19 vaccination program, but experts warn the change shouldn't be interpreted as a sign the virus is no longer a public health concern.
From 1 October, the National COVID-19 Vaccine Program will transition into the National Immunisation Program (NIP), with free COVID-19 vaccines becoming limited to people considered most at risk of severe disease.
But professor Adrian Esterman, chair of biostatistics and epidemiology at the University of Adelaide, said the new eligibility rules could leave some people vulnerable.
"There are lots and lots of people with diabetes, with other chronic conditions, autoimmune conditions, that would be hundreds of thousands of people who were getting a free shot and aren't getting one now," Esterman said.
The change comes as the latest federal government surveillance data shows COVID-19 cases increased over the past fortnight.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
However, experts say 2026 has been unusual, with Australia yet to experience the clear winter COVID peak seen in previous years.
SBS News has contacted the Department of Health for comment, but it previously told the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners that COVID-19 is now endemic in Australia and that vaccination policy should focus on maintaining protection among those most vulnerable to severe disease.
Which Australians can still get free COVID vaccines?
From 1 October, free COVID-19 vaccination under the NIP will be available to adults aged 75 and over every six months, and adults aged 65 to 74 every 12 months.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 to 74 will also remain eligible for an annual dose, as will adults aged 18 and over who are severely immunocompromised.
People outside those groups will still be able to access COVID-19 vaccines, but may have to pay for them.
Catherine Bennett, chair of Epidemiology at Deakin University, said the change should be viewed alongside Australia's broader vaccination program.
She said COVID-19 was now behaving differently from earlier in the pandemic, with population immunity helping to reduce severe illness.
"It's important that this is actually now being taken into a national immunisation program because that means that we have a sustained commitment to COVID alongside the other respiratory diseases," Bennett said.
She told SBS News that the lower vaccination rates among healthy adults had not translated into a comparable increase in severe disease.
Are the people most at risk getting vaccinated?
Esterman said a bigger concern was whether Australians who most need protection were actually taking up the vaccines already available to them.
He said just 25 per cent of people aged 75 and over had received a COVID-19 vaccine in the previous six months, while only 30 per cent had received one in the past year.
Among people aged 65 to 74, uptake was around 19 per cent over the past year.
"The issue here is the people at the highest risk aren't actually taking the vaccine," Esterman said.
He said the change could also leave some younger people with chronic health conditions without access to free vaccination.
People under 65 with conditions including diabetes, chronic lung disease or autoimmune conditions may not meet the new definition of severe immunocompromise, despite potentially facing a greater risk from COVID-19.
Esterman said healthcare and aged-care workers could also face new barriers, particularly if they are expected to pay for vaccination themselves or rely on their employers to provide it.
His concern is that cost and access could further discourage people who would otherwise benefit from a booster.
"We've got groups who desperately need the COVID vaccine missing out," he said.
What does Australia's COVID vaccine change mean for public health?
Experts emphasised that communication around the change would be important.
Esterman warned that winding back universal access could reinforce the perception that COVID-19 is no longer a significant health concern.
He said that would be a "very poor message" to send, particularly given the virus continues to cause serious illness and deaths.
Bennett agreed that COVID should not simply disappear from the public health conversation, but said the focus should now be on clearly communicating who remains at greatest risk and ensuring they know they are still entitled to free vaccination.
She said the transition to the NIP could actually help by putting COVID vaccination alongside other routine immunisations, rather than treating it as a separate pandemic-era program.
States and territories will take responsibility for ordering, distributing and reporting COVID-19 vaccines under the new arrangements.
Bennett said having the Australian Centre for Disease Control provide national guidance would be important to ensure messaging remains consistent, even if individual states respond differently to local outbreaks.
What Australia's 2026 COVID case trends reveal
Australia has recorded 64,357 COVID-19 cases so far this year, which is 56 per cent fewer than the 146,232 cases notified over the same period in 2025.
But the most unusual feature of 2026 has been the absence of a clear winter peak.
Bennett said that could partly reflect the same COVID variant continuing to circulate, allowing people's existing immunity to remain effective against it.
The variant NB.1.8.1 has dominated in Australia, while new variants have not produced the dramatic shifts in transmission seen earlier in the pandemic.
Esterman similarly expects COVID to continue producing smaller waves rather than the large peaks seen in previous years.
He said a major new wave would be more likely if there was a significant genetic shift in the virus.
Could Australia face another COVID wave in 2026?
Neither expert expects an immediate major COVID wave as Australia heads into spring and summer, although both say the virus will continue circulating.
Bennett said a new variant could still trigger an increase in cases, but summer generally brings lower transmission because people spend more time outdoors and have better ventilation.
For now, experts say the challenge may be less about preparing for another pandemic-scale wave and more about ensuring people at greatest risk do not become complacent.
As Australia moves away from universal COVID vaccination, experts agree that as the virus changes, so too must the way the country communicates about it.

Nearly three million Israeli students begin school year with AI, financial education at center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:56:19 UTC
13:56:19 KST

Some 2.6 million students are expected to begin the 2026-2027 school year in Israel’s schools and kindergartens on Tuesday, including some 180,000 first-graders, as the Education Ministry launches new programs and expands initiatives introduced in recent years.
The ministry is placing particular emphasis on strengthening students’ sense of belonging and resilience, deepening studies of identity and heritage, introducing financial education into the school system, and expanding the use of artificial intelligence in both learning and examinations.
As students return to classrooms, the ministry said it would focus the school year on three areas: belonging and security, identity and roots, and knowledge and tools for coping with a changing world.
“We are opening the year with great responsibility and with a clear direction: to strengthen the sense of belonging and resilience of Israel’s students, deepen identity, values, and heritage, while at the same time giving them the knowledge and tools that will enable them to lead and succeed in a rapidly changing world,” Education Minister Yoav Kisch said.
First week to focus on belonging, resilience, preventing ostracism
During the first week of school, the Education Ministry plans to focus on strengthening social ties and trust among students and between students and teaching staff.
Alongside reacquainting students with their schools and classrooms, staff will be asked to conduct emotional and social discussions, identify students’ needs, and strengthen both individual and group resilience.
Special emphasis will be placed on preventing violence, social rejection, and ostracism, both in physical spaces and online. The ministry said the initiative is based on the view that academic achievement cannot be separated from a student’s social and emotional condition, and that a sense of security and belonging is a prerequisite for learning and perseverance.
The school system’s annual theme will be “Roots of AMI: Future, Heritage and Entrepreneurship,” and will run from kindergarten through 12th grade. Through the program, the ministry aims to connect identity and heritage with initiative, leadership, personal responsibility, and social involvement.
The “Heritage Paths” field of study will also be expanded this year to Druze elementary schools and to seventh-grade classes in the state and state-religious education systems.
Preparing students for adulthood and the workforce with financial education
One of the most prominent innovations in the 2026-2027 school year will be the introduction of financial education as a subject for the first time.
In its initial phase, the subject will be taught in ninth grade and will be expanded to 10th grade beginning next school year.
According to the ministry, the program is intended to provide students with knowledge and tools for independent financial management, develop critical thinking about financial issues, and prepare them for adulthood and the workforce. In addition to financial knowledge, the program is also expected to address personal, social, and civic responsibility.
“This year we will continue to connect roots with the future: We will expand STEM and artificial intelligence studies, introduce financial education for the first time, and continue to promote innovative and personalized learning,” Kisch said.
Artificial intelligence will play an even larger role in classrooms this year.
As part of the expansion of the “Realistic Israel” reform, intended to strengthen science, technology, engineering, and mathematics education, the 720 program will expand to adapt teaching and assessment methods to the AI era.
This year, the program will run in English studies in all middle schools and will also expand to about 140 schools in STEM fields.
More than 12,000 English, science, and technology teachers are expected to undergo training in artificial intelligence. Students will also receive dedicated training.
Eighth- and ninth-grade students will take part in a 20-hour program using personalized AI-based learning systems. Among other things, they are expected to learn how to use artificial intelligence thoughtfully and creatively, develop critical thinking, identify false information, and become familiar with the ethical issues involved in the use of the technology.
The change will not be limited to classroom instruction. AI tools will be incorporated into matriculation assignments in more than 10 STEM study tracks this year.
According to the Education Ministry, the move is intended to adapt assessment methods to the growing use of artificial intelligence in academia and the research world.
At the same time, 27 schools across the country, from Dimona to Majdal Shams, will open a dedicated artificial intelligence sciences track. Graduates of the program will be eligible for a technological certification.
“Behind the opening of the school year is an entire system that has worked in recent months to bring the schools and kindergartens to this moment. Our mission continues every day, in supporting the teams and ensuring that policy and resources reach the classroom and every student,” Education Ministry Director-General Meir Shimoni said.
The Education Ministry has set a target of returning Israel to the top 10 in the international Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study examinations by 2029. Israeli students are expected to take the tests this year for the first time since the reform began.
“We are opening the school year with an approach that connects roots with the future: a foundation of values and a sense of belonging alongside innovative learning, knowledge, and skills for a changing world. The goal is to give every student the tools to develop, create, and lead,” Ina Zaltzman, senior deputy director-general and head of the ministry’s Pedagogical Administration, added.
What about the Gaza border communities?
The school year will open in the Tekuma region with 22,233 students across the area’s five local authorities: the city of Sderot and the Eshkol, Hof Ashkelon, Sdot Negev, and Sha’ar HaNegev regional councils.
The figure represents an increase of approximately 9% compared with the period before October 7, 2023, amounting to an additional 1,802 students.
The growth in the education system comes as communities in the region continue returning to their homes.
During the summer months, residents began returning to Kibbutz Kissufim, where more than 95% of residents have returned so far. The communities of Holit and Kfar Aza have also returned, as have teenage students from Kibbutz Be’eri, who resumed their studies in the Eshkol Regional Council area.
The continued return to these communities, together with the rise in the number of students in the region’s local authorities compared with the previous school year, is another indication of the process taking place in the Tekuma region, from rehabilitation and returning home to renewed stability and growth.
Alongside the increase in the number of students and the continued return of communities to their homes, the Tekuma Administration is continuing its efforts in 2026 to strengthen the education system as a central pillar of community resilience and regional growth.
During the year, the administration is advancing eight major education projects with a combined budget of NIS 364 million.
The investment focuses on developing educational excellence, expanding holistic services, and implementing supportive tools to strengthen stability and the quality of education while advancing students throughout the region.
The plan places special emphasis on strengthening English and technology studies, recruiting and retaining high-quality personnel, and developing a pipeline of future education system managers.
The measures are part of an effort to create conditions for the region’s long-term growth, retain the existing population, and attract new families to the area.
Among the main investments in 2026 are NIS 184 million for the “Tekuma Education Basket,” which allows local authorities to advance educational responses according to local needs; NIS 103 million for additional education facilities; and NIS 54 million to support informal education programs.
Alongside investments in infrastructure and educational services, the plan emphasizes developing educational excellence and expanding opportunities for students, strengthening English and technology studies, recruiting and retaining high-quality personnel, and building a pipeline of future administrators.
These measures are intended not only to strengthen the existing education system, but also to create conditions that will support the region’s long-term growth, retain its population, and attract new families.
“The increase in the number of students in all the region’s local authorities compared with last year is far more than a numerical figure. It reflects the return home, the strengthening of communities, and the transition of the Tekuma region from rehabilitation to growth," Tekuma Administration head Aviad Friedman said.
"The education system is one of the most important anchors in building the future of the region, and therefore we are investing in it not only to address today’s needs, but with a view years ahead. Our goal is for the children of the region to receive an excellent education here, for families to choose to continue building their lives here, and for the region’s communities to continue growing and becoming stronger. That is our mission, and that is the renewal we are working to achieve.”

KKL-JNF unveils archival photos showcasing Israeli classrooms in honor of new school year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:55:26 UTC
13:55:26 KST

In honor of Israel’s new school year beginning on September 1, the Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael–Jewish National Fund (KKL-JNF) Photo Archive has unveiled five rare photographs showing what Israeli classrooms looked like throughout the past century, with images spanning from 1925 to 1963.
The oldest photograph shows what it was like to study in the moshav Kfar Hasidim in August 1925, nearly 20 years before the founding of the state of Israel. With no traditional classroom, the children gathered beneath the shade of a tree to listen to their teacher.
Fifteen years later, a photograph from 1940 depicts the library of the Spitzer Girls School in Jerusalem, showing a range of girls reading together, while a photo taken in Kibbutz Mishmar HaEmek in 1944 shows a young boys’ school where the students appear to be practicing their penmanship.
The final two photos are from 1961 and 1963. The first shows a student from Tzur Hadassah solving a math problem on a chalkboard, while the second, taken in Jerusalem, shows a crowded classroom of children excitedly opening and reading letters.
Showcasing how students learned in a time before smartphones
The photographs show how children learned before modern technology, whiteboards, and even before they had classrooms.
“These photographs allow us to step for a moment into the classrooms of the past and see not only how children learned, but also what the society being built here looked like,” Efrat Sinai, Director of KKL-JNF, said.
“Through the blackboard, the books, the desks, and even the lesson held beneath a tree, they reveal the deep connection between education, community, and a love of the land. It is a privilege to preserve these moments and share them with the public, especially as a new school year begins.”

Israel moves Palestinian journalist, detainee Bushra al-Tawil to solitary confinement in Ramla prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:53:24 UTC
13:53:24 KST

Mohammad Sio
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Israeli authorities have moved Palestinian journalist and detainee Bushra al-Tawil, 33, to solitary confinement at Ramla prison, nearly six months after her arrest and transfer to administrative detention, the Palestinian Prisoner Society said Monday.
The group said al-Tawil, from the West Bank city of Al-Bireh, was arrested in February and later placed under administrative detention. She had previously been detained several times, most of them under the same procedure, it added.
Al-Tawil first experienced detention in 2011, when she was 18, according to the society. Her father, Jamal al-Tawil, also remains in an Israeli prison and is among Palestinian detainees who have spent extended periods under administrative detention.
The society said the family has faced repeated raids and harassment, including deliberate damage to their home during the arrests of Bushra and her father.
Al-Tawil had also been placed in solitary confinement several times during her current detention at Damon prison, the group said, describing the latest transfer as part of a broader pattern of punitive measures against her.
The transfer comes amid worsening conditions for Palestinian women held in Israeli prisons, including food deprivation, denial of medical care, solitary confinement, and poor detention conditions. It also said scabies had spread among female detainees amid inadequate hygiene and health care.
About 90 Palestinian women are currently held in Israeli prisons, according to the society.  
‘Unprecedented level of brutality and disrespect’
The group said al-Tawil’s transfer followed a visit Sunday by extremist Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to the women’s section of Damon prison. Ben-Gvir posted footage from the visit “in a scene that embodies an unprecedented level of brutality and disrespect for the dignity and rights of female prisoners,” the society said.
The society accused Israeli authorities of subjecting female detainees to systematic raids, filming, and invasive searches, including forced strip searches.
It said solitary confinement, denial of medical treatment, food deprivation, and harsh detention conditions form part of policies imposed on Palestinian prisoners since Israel launched its genocide on Gaza in October 2023.
The group described Israeli prisons as having become “grounds for torture as one of the most prominent aspects of the ongoing crime of genocide” and held Israel fully responsible for the safety of al-Tawil and other Palestinian female detainees.
It called on international and human rights groups to work urgently to halt the violations and protect the prisoners.
About 9,500 Palestinians are held in Israeli prisons, including around 90 women and more than 350 children, who face food deprivation, torture, and medical neglect, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups.

OPEC+ seven's quota rises by 188,000 bpd in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:52:23 UTC
13:52:23 KST

MOSCOW, September 1. /TASS/. The oil production quota for the OPEC+ seven (Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman) increases by 188,000 barrels per day (bpd) in September compared with August, to 31.01 mln bpd as the group completes the phaseout of its 1.65 mln bpd voluntary production cut, according to OPEC data and TASS calculations.
At their latest meeting, the seven leading OPEC+ countries decided to increase oil production by 188,000 bpd in September compared with August, bringing the group's oil production quota for the month to 31.01 mln bpd. OPEC+ countries had also previously extended until the end of 2026 the period during which they can compensate for earlier overproduction, though an updated compensation schedule has yet to be published. The previous schedule called for the compensation period to end in June 2026.
Starting in April 2025, the OPEC+ eight gradually began returning previously withheld barrels to the market, and in September 2025 the group fully unwound its voluntary production cuts of 2.2 mln bpd, a year ahead of the original schedule. In October 2025, OPEC+ began gradually unwinding another oil production cut of 1.65 mln bpd. Following the UAE's withdrawal from OPEC and OPEC+ on May 1, 2026, the group has operated as a seven-country format, with this production cut amounting to around 1.5 mln bpd excluding the UAE's share.
In September of this year, the OPEC+ seven will complete the phaseout of the voluntary oil production cut of 1.65 mln bpd, or 1.5 mln bpd excluding the quota of the UAE, which withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ on May 1, fully returning the withheld volume to the market.
The OPEC+ seven will continue to hold monthly meetings to assess market conditions, with the next meeting scheduled for September 6.

Jury finds ex-gang leader guilty of murder in Tupac case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:51:07 UTC
13:51:07 KST

Jury finds ex-gang leader guilty of murder in Tupac case
Aug 31 - An ex-street gang leader accused of orchestrating the drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur three decades ago in Las Vegas was convicted of murder on Monday for his role in a long-unsolved crime that silenced one of rap music's most influential voices.
A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours before finding Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a downtown Las Vegas courtroom. Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13.
Davis told the judge "he plans to appeal this matter." Several people in the gallery wiped away tears and hugged a prosecutor as the court adjourned.
Representatives of the Clark County District Attorney's Office and Davis' lawyer did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
Binu Palal of the Clark County District Attorney's Office told jurors that under the code of respect in street gangs, Davis could not let the beating of his nephew slide.
"So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together, and went hunting for Mr. Shakur," Palal said.
Police say they long suspected Davis but did not have enough evidence to charge him until he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir, which, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, make up most of the prosecution’s case.
'FICTION, NOT FACT'
Davis' lawyer Michael Sanft told jurors during his closing argument that his client's story could not be corroborated by evidence and should not be trusted. He also said the case was tainted by police corruption, mismanagement and missing files.
“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact, but the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession," Sanft said, referring to Davis' 2019 memoir "Compton Street Legend."
Over the past two weeks, prosecutors played hours of recordings for jurors in which Davis said he was enraged after Shakur and his entourage beat up Davis’ nephew.
Davis and three other men, including his nephew, went looking for Shakur and his record executive Marion “Suge” Knight in a white Cadillac on the night of the beating, he told police during an unrelated investigation. Davis said he passed a gun to the backseat, and when they found Knight and Shakur’s car, one of the two men in the back opened fire.
Prosecutors have not named the shooter, and the three other men in the car have since died. Under Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder even if he did not pull the trigger.
Davis was a leader of the South Side Compton Crips, a Los Angeles-area street gang that feuded with rival gang Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur and his record label Death Row Records.
Shakur's 1996 killing became a seminal moment in rap history and heightened hip-hop culture's violent image during “gangsta” rap’s heyday, an era defined by feuding between East and West Coast artists. REUTERS

Ex-official among 33,019 who failed to complete eTAX filings amid unclear wording
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:50:54 UTC
13:50:54 KST

Ex-official among 33,019 who failed to complete eTAX filings amid unclear wording
Former Hospital Authority executive Dr Luk Che-chung calls on government to learn from incident and respond faster to user complaints
More than 33,000 people failed to submit completed tax returns because of unclear wording in Hong Kong’s eTAX system, the ombudsman has found, with nearly 5,200 receiving penalty notices and two prosecuted.
Dr Luk Che-chung, a former chief executive of the Hospital Authority’s Hong Kong East area, was among the affected taxpayers and urged the government on Tuesday to learn from the incident.
In a report released on Monday, the Office of the Ombudsman said ambiguous instructions on the eTAX submission and signature interface led many users to believe that signing via the “iAM Smart” platform completed their filing, when in fact they had to return to eTAX until a confirmation page appeared.
Between May 2 last year and January 31 this year, 489,425 taxpayers attempted to submit electronic returns using a digital signature on iAM Smart, the investigation found.
Of these, 33,019 did not complete the submission process; 5,169 received penalty notices and two were prosecuted. About 14,000 successfully resubmitted on the same day as their initial attempt.
Under Hong Kong law, taxpayers must file returns within one month of issue so the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) can prepare assessments and approve deductions.

“In Russia, we do not forget your personal contribution to the development of friendly, allied relations between our countries,” Putin wrote.
He wished Kocharyan “good health, spiritual strength and resilience in the face of the trials that you and members of your family are currently facing.”
Kocharyan, who served as Armenia’s president (a largely ceremonial role with little executive power) from 1998 to 2008 and now leads the opposition Armenia Alliance, was detained on Aug. 25 after authorities searched businesses linked to his family.

His detention came amid rising tensions between Pashinyan’s government and Armenia’s pro-Russian opposition as Yerevan increasingly distances itself from Moscow and seeks closer ties with the West.
Putin’s unusually pointed birthday message came just before his scheduled Sept. 1 meeting with Pashinyan on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
European Ministers Boycott Russian Counterpart After Surprise US G20 Invitation
Kocharyan has long maintained close personal ties with Putin and advocated preserving Armenia’s strategic relationship with Russia.
Putin has publicly supported Kocharyan during previous legal troubles as well. When Kocharyan was jailed in an earlier criminal case, Putin continued sending him birthday and holiday greetings, gestures that Kocharyan described at the time as a sign of “serious support.”
Moscow losing its grip
US analyst Paul Goble told Kyiv Post that Armenia’s broader shift away from Moscow reflects Russia’s declining influence in the South Caucasus.
According to Goble, the shift extends beyond Pashinyan personally and reflects a broader change in Armenia’s understanding of its place in the region.
Armenia may continue cooperating with Moscow where its interests require it, he said, but is increasingly unwilling to accept what Goble called Russia’s “imperial approach of total dominance.”
Kocharyan’s arrest adds to a growing list of setbacks for longtime Kremlin partners and Putin-aligned leaders far beyond the former Soviet space – from Bashar al-Assad, ousted in Syria and forced into exile in Moscow, to Nicolás Maduro, removed from power in Venezuela earlier this year.
For Moscow, the pattern underscores a broader erosion of influence, as leaders once close to the Kremlin increasingly find that Russian backing is no guarantee of political survival.

Drone crossed Estonia's border in southeast, says air force commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01

Drone crossed Estonia's border in southeast, says air force commander
One drone crossed Estonia's border in the southeast and another flew towards the eastern border city of Narva on Tuesday morning, said Air Force Commander Brigadier General Riivo Valge after potential air threat alerts were issued across the country.
The warnings were sent to residents in eight regions of Estonia between 3 a.m. and 4 a.m. Tuesday morning. Turkish Air Force fighter jets stationed at Estonia's Ämari Air Base as part of NATO's rotation air defense mission were scrambled in response. The threat had passed by 5.30 a.m.
Valge told ERR's morning TV show "Terevisioon" at around 2 a.m. it became clear Ukraine was carrying out drone strikes in western Russia. Approximately a dozen drones could be seen moving close to Estonia's border.
"Unfortunately, at around 3 a.m., one of those drones headed towards Narva, and as a result we issued an alert to the population. The first thing we did was activate our air defence units on the ground, and immediately after that, fighter jets took off from Ämari," he said.
The drone did not enter Estonia's airspace and veered back towards Russia, but alerts were sent in Ida-Viru and Lääne counties.
"But about half an hour later, there was another incident involving a drone in southeastern Estonia. It also crossed the Estonian border and remained close to the border zone. However, its behaviour was unpredictable, and I would remind you that there were even more of these drones just beyond our border," Valge told the show.
The Estonian Defense Forces then issued a second alert in southern Estonia for Tartu, Jõgeva, Viljandi, Valga, Võru and Põlva counties.
"Fortunately for us, the drones did not fall in Estonia, the aircraft did not open fire, so we don't have a missile lying around somewhere either. By 5 a.m., things had become calm or quiet on the other side of the border, and we were able to lift the alert," he said.
The Air Force commander confirmed that the situation is currently calm and that people in Estonia should focus on getting their children to school.
Previous alerts have been issued when Ukrainian attack drones strayed off course, often due to GPS jamming, when attacking Russia's oil infrastructure on the Baltic coast.
Leningrad Oblast regional Governor Alexander Drozdenko said 38 drones had been destroyed over Leningrad Oblast, which borders Estonia, early on Tuesday morning and confirmed damage at the Port of Ust-Luga.

Couple who survived Tai Po fire await trial for fraud, cannot leave Hong Kong
Wang Fuk Court residents allegedly obtained more than HK$330,000 in government-backed loans by overstating drop in revenue of their business
A couple who survived the deadly Tai Po blaze last year have been barred from leaving Hong Kong pending trial for allegedly obtaining more than HK$330,000 (US$42,000) in government-guaranteed loans by overstating the decline in revenue of their decoration business.
Former Wang Fuk Court residents Jason Kong Cheung-fat, 65, and Rosanna Cheung Yeuk-lan, 62, appeared in Sha Tin Court on Tuesday to face two counts of fraud and one of money laundering.
The couple were not required to enter a plea as prosecutors applied a five-week adjournment to prepare the necessary paperwork to transfer the case to the District Court for trial.
According to a charge sheet available for press viewing, the defendants misrepresented to HSBC the decline in sales of Ace Interior Design & Engineering Company, of which they are directors, to support two applications under the 100 per cent Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme between February 8 and June 30, 2022.
The scheme was a relief measure introduced in 2020 to provide fully government-guaranteed loans to companies struggling to stay afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Prosecutors also accused the couple of laundering the HK$331,300 they dishonestly obtained between April 4 and July 25 that year.

European gas price hits highest August level since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:37:32 UTC
13:37:32 KST

MOSCOW, September 1. /TASS/. The average monthly gas price in Europe reached its highest level since late 2022 in August, at $744 per 1,000 cubic meters, amid record-low gas inventories ahead of the coming winter and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, according to futures data from London's ICE exchange and TASS calculations.
European gas prices nearly doubled in August compared with the same month a year earlier and were also 17% above the July average.
While gas futures traded at around $709 per 1,000 cubic meters on July 31, trading closed at about $840 on August 31, up 18.5% from the end of the previous month.
The price of gas at European hubs averaged $481 per 1,000 cubic meters in the first quarter of this year and $550 in the second quarter, while the third-quarter average currently stands at $691.
In January 2025, the average gas price in Europe was around $517 per 1,000 cubic meters (up 53% year-on-year from 2024), followed by $542 in February (+88%), $467 in March (+55%), $409 in April (+28%), $412 in May (+15%), $439 in June (+14%), $410 in July (+12%), $394 in August (-10%), $393 in September (-5.5%), $384 in October (-16%), $368 in November (-25%), $334 in December (-32%), $415 in January 2026 (-20% year-on-year from 2025), $396 in February (-27%), $632 in March (+35%), $544 in April (+33%), $570 in May (+39%), $534 in June (+22%), $638 in July (+55%), and $744 in August (+89%).
Reasons behind gas price increase
The rise in gas prices in the second half of the summer was primarily driven by a new phase of the Middle East conflict and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of global supplies pass. This pushed up gas prices in Europe and Asia, which compete for available supplies on the market, driving prices higher.
The latest escalation in the US-Iran conflict began on July 8. For the first time since Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum, the US Armed Forces carried out several waves of strikes on the Islamic Republic, purportedly in response to an attack on a merchant vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. On the same day, US President Donald Trump announced the end of the ceasefire with Iran. In response, Tehran began striking US facilities in the Middle East located in Bahrain, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE and Oman.
Meanwhile, Europe is continuing to inject gas into storage facilities ahead of winter. As TASS previously reported, Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. The average rate of replenishment at underground gas storage facilities in EU countries in July was among the lowest recorded since data collection began in 2011, accelerating only slightly in August. At these rates, Europe's storage facilities may be only 70-75% full by the start of the fall-winter period, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the beginning of a heating season.
The Guardian, citing experts, reported that Europe's gas market is experiencing a bout of panic over hydrocarbon inventories in storage facilities falling to their lowest level in 13 years. According to their estimates, gas inventories in European storage facilities are set to reach a 13-year low ahead of colder weather, raising the risk of "winter panic" among traders.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. As a result, net injections into European storage facilities ahead of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period must total at least 68 bln cubic meters to meet the storage target. So far, Europe has injected only 59% of the volumes needed for the coming winter.
Storage-filling rates this year have been significantly affected by Europe's lost "battle" with Asia for available LNG supplies during the Middle East conflict, higher fuel prices, and extreme heat in June and July. During such hot summer periods, demand for electricity to power cooling and air-conditioning systems rises sharply. Gas is one of the main sources of electricity generation, alongside nuclear, wind and solar power.

One person killed as woman randomly stabs two people in Times Square before being fatally shot by police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:33:58 UTC
13:33:58 KST

The woman behind the attack has reportedly had a history of mental health issues with New York police but no arrest record prior to her stabbing attacks on Tuesday.
A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.
The shooting happened just before 4:30 pm local time, next to a New York Police Department (NYPD) substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city’s annual New Year’s Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in all of New York.
The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference.
Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman also in the abdomen, Tisch said. Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died and the man is in stable condition, according to police.
Police didn’t say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents. Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives.
Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said. The woman told them: “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” according to Tisch.
The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly toward the officers while waving the knives in front of her.
Two officers then shot the woman, according to police. In videos posted by eyewitnesses, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid.
“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said.
The woman has a “documented mental health history with the NYPD,” which include incidents in 2018 and 2019 but no arrest history with the department, said Commissioner Tisch without adding further details, but ruling out terrorism.
“We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment," said Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Both Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions.
The NYPD temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby.
Violent crime has fallen sharply in the City so far this year, with homicides down 24% and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. But this is the second killing this year in Times Square. Earlier in May, a man was fatally stabbed in the same area.

AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:32:00 UTC
13:32:00 KST

AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
September 1, 2026
All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of a state election on Sunday that could trigger a political earthquake across Germany.
Though the state is small, with a population of just 2 million — and with economic strength and life expectancy the lowest of any of Germany's 16 federal states — a victory for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could usher in the first far-right government in the history of post-World-War-II Germany.
The AfD's lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, and polls show him well in the lead. The only open question seems to be whether the AfD will be able to secure an absolute majority of the seats in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which would allow it to govern alone. This would appear to be Siegmund's only path to the state premiership, as the other parties have said they will not enter a coalition with the AfD.
Things are going well for the 35-year-old Siegmund. As he tours his state on the campaign trail, he draws crowds — even in small towns. He's often surrounded by a swarm of international journalists: from Canadian and Danish television, Swiss broadcasting, the BBC and the British magazine The Economist, alongside dozens of reporters from across Germany. Everyone wants to know: Who is Ulrich Siegmund?
The candidate was born in the small town of Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, in 1990. He joined the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at age 19, only to leave the party five years later and join the AfD. A former perfume salesman, he cuts a dynamic and athletic figure: slim, handsome and fresh-faced.
Above all, he is cheerful — playing the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances. When he steps into town squares to a cheering crowd, he beams back, shaking hands and cracking jokes. Nothing about him seems forced; he visibly enjoys the campaign grind.
"I don't know when there was last such a high approval rating, even among young people," Siegmund told DW. "It's simply enormous." He speaks quickly, articulately and with practiced ease.
AfD campaign pushes policies with 'high-gloss marketing'
Even critical observers in Saxony-Anhalt can't help but admit that the AfD has all the momentum in this election.
"The AfD's campaign events run like clockwork, both logistically and in terms of political strategy," observed David Begrich of Miteinander, an organization based in the state capital of Magdeburg that fights right-wing extremism. "It is high-gloss marketing of their own policies."
But what exactly do the AfD's policies aim to achieve? To judge by Siegmund's campaign speeches, the goal is a return to a bygone era — a time before Germany viewed itself as a country of immigration, when electricity came from nuclear power plants rather than wind turbines, and when LGBTQ+ rights were not yet recognized. Siegmund wants to pursue, as he says in his campaign speeches, politics "from the people, for the people!"
Apparently, that doesn't include all the people living in the state. The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains some radical policies, including a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay, but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons, many of whom have found work and established their lives in Germany.
The action plan also calls for funding cuts to pro-democracy NGOs, forcing refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity. There are significant legal doubts, however, about whether a state government actually has the authority to implement all these pledges.
Controversial figures behind the scenes
There are also doubts over the "clean" image that Siegmund has cultivated. He has not been able to escape the allegations of cronyism that have dogged the AfD, after it was reported that several of the party's state and federal lawmakers secured well-paid jobs for their friends and relatives in the offices of other AfD officials.
Siegmund himself found a position for his own father. While not illegal, the move was poorly received, even within his own party.
Then there are the people behind Siegmund, those who support him as leader of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt. According to the daily newspaper Die Welt, the group employs four former members of a now-banned neo-Nazi organization, the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend (German Youth Loyal to the Homeland). Before it was outlawed, the group openly admired Adolf Hitler's Nazism and adhered to his racial ideology, one that led to the murder of 6 million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma in the Holocaust.
Siegmund himself appears to have no qualms about associating with supporters who have tattoos or clothes with neo-Nazi symbols. DW observed him appearing arm-in-arm with men wearing neo-Nazi attire and sporting tattoos such as the Black Sun, a recognized symbol among neo-Nazis.
AfD wants to 'turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground'
But what would all this mean if the AfD actually did take power after the September 6 election?
"There are clear indications that if the AfD were to enter government, it would turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground for the whole country," said Begrich. "Just how far can one go in overriding the written — and perhaps even more importantly, the unwritten — rules of democratic culture in a federal state?"
For that reason, many churches, trade unions, civil society organizations and political parties have warned against an AfD victory. Begrich shares their concerns.
"Naturally, things will become difficult, above all, for those in society who either belong to minorities or do not fit into the AfD's ideological worldview," he said. "The social climate would inevitably shift to an authoritarian regimentation — and that poses a problem for people who need liberal openness in society as they need air to breathe."
Like many critics, Begrich believes that winning Saxony-Anhalt is only the first step for a party that wants to take over the entire country.
This article was originally published in German.

S. Korea proposes record budget plan for 2027 to drive growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
12:29:59 CST
13:29:59 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The South Korean government proposed its record budget plan for 2027 on Tuesday to drive economic growth through aggressive fiscal expansion, utilizing a semiconductor-led tax windfall.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung presided over a cabinet meeting to endorse the budget proposal of 820.9 trillion won (about 598.8 billion U.S. dollars) for next year, up 12.8 percent compared to the previous year.
If confirmed by the National Assembly, the 2027 fiscal spending would mark the fastest single-year growth, topping the previous record of 10.6 percent set during the 2009 global financial crisis, according to the Ministry of Planning and Budget.
The unprecedented fiscal expansion was funded by the semiconductor boom, which was projected to push national tax revenues up by 194.2 trillion won to 584.4 trillion won next year.
Aggregate revenues, including tax and non-tax revenues, were forecast to surge 30.4 percent over the year to 880.8 trillion won in 2027.
"We are now standing at the crossroads between structural low growth and a rebound in our potential growth rate," Lee said at the cabinet meeting, emphasizing the need for the expansionary budget.
Acknowledging the "unavoidable" interest rate hikes, Lee stressed the need for the fiscal expansion to minimize the financial pain inflicted by the monetary tightening.
The country's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3 percent in August, delivering back-to-back rate hikes amid rising worries about inflationary pressure and household debts.
To foster future growth engines, the budget focused on industrial revitalization and future technologies. The research and development budget was set at 39.5 trillion won, up 11.2 percent compared to this year.
The double-digit increase aimed to secure technological sovereignty and drive future growth by aggressively scaling up investments in 10 next-generation strategic technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), advanced robotics and semiconductors, and accelerating AI integration across all major industries.
Budget for industry, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and energy jumped 29.7 percent to 41.2 trillion won for 2027 to speed up manufacturing AI transformation, shift toward renewable energy, boost regional economies and support supply chain diversification.
Next year's environment budget gained 5.2 percent to 14.6 trillion won to accelerate decarbonization and reinforce safety against climate disasters, while budget for culture, sports and tourism soared 20.4 percent to 11.6 trillion won to enhance cultural soft power, bolster regional tourism and improve sports competitiveness.
For national defense, 73.3 trillion won was allotted for 2027, up 8.2 percent from a year earlier.
Budget for health, welfare and employment grew 9.3 percent to 289 trillion won, and education budget expanded 10.8 percent to 110.7 trillion won.
The country's national debt-to-GDP ratio was expected to drop 3.3 percentage points to 48.3 percent in 2027. ■

TEHRAN, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei on Monday condemned the EU's support for a U.S. economic operation against Iran, saying that Europe could no longer claim "strategic autonomy."
Baghaei made the remarks in a post on the social media platform X in response to an EU statement issued Monday at the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors meeting in Asheville, the United States.
The EU said it "welcomes efforts (aimed) at ensuring that Iran ceases its destabilizing activities and engages in peace negotiations with good faith, also through additional economic pressure, including through the U.S.-led Operation Economic Outcast."
"Europe can no longer speak of 'strategic autonomy' while merely executing Washington's orders," Baghaei said.
The EU called for continued diplomacy with Iran to ensure regional stability and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that it remained ready to take further measures and maintain pressure on Tehran together with the United States and other partners.
On Aug. 19, U.S. President Donald Trump announced what he called "the most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country," warning that countries providing a lifeline to Iran would face "tremendous economic consequences." ■

Charges filed in absentia against Russian general and colonel over attacks on Okhmatdyt and Reuters journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
04:28:00 UTC
13:28:00 KST

Charges filed in absentia against Russian general and colonel over attacks on Okhmatdyt and Reuters journalists
According to Ukrinform, the SSU reported this.
“According to the case file, one of the suspects is Russian Major General Mykola Varpakhovych, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division of the Russian Armed Forces. The investigation established that on July 8, 2024, the officer issued a combat order to carry out a missile strike on the “Okhmatdyt” National Children’s Specialized Hospital in Kyiv,” the statement reads.
The SSU noted that at that time, long-range aviation units under Varpakhovich’s command carried out a precision strike on the medical facility using an “Kh-101” air-to-ground cruise missile, which was launched from a Russian Tu-95MS missile-carrying bomber.
“At the time of the attack, there were over 600 patients in the hospital. Two people were killed, including a doctor, and dozens more were injured. The missile completely destroyed the toxicology wing and damaged four other buildings where surgical operations were being performed and children with cancer were being treated,” the SSU reported.
Another suspect is Russian Colonel Alexander Lutovinov, commander of the missile brigade of the 49th Combined Arms Army of the Russian Federation’s Southern Military District.
According to the investigation, he organized a missile strike on the “Sapphire” hotel complex in Kramatorsk on August 24, 2024. As a result of this attack, a security advisor for the international news agency Reuters was killed, and five of his colleagues sustained injuries of varying severity.
According to the investigation, the decision to carry out the strike was made by Colonel General Alexei Kim, deputy chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, whom the SSU has already notified of the charges against him in absentia.
“In accordance with his criminal order, Lutovinov directly ordered his subordinates to launch an ‘Iskander-M’ ballistic missile from the Rostov region,” the SSU emphasized.
Investigators from the SSU’s Main Investigative Directorate have charged Varpakhovych and Lutovinov in absentia under Part 2 of Article 438 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (war crimes resulting in loss of life).
Comprehensive measures are underway to bring them to justice.
As previously reported, on July 8, 2024, Russia carried out a terrorist attack on the Okhmatdyt National Children’s Specialized Hospital. The strike killed two people and injured 35, including nine children.
The hospital’s toxicology wing was destroyed, and the surgical and new wings, as well as the Ministry of Health’s pediatric cardiology center, were damaged.
Five buildings of the medical facility were damaged, including the toxicology wing, the Soviet-era surgical wing, and the new treatment and diagnostic wing, as well as a transformer substation.
On the night of August 24, 2024, Russian forces launched a missile strike on a hotel in Kramatorsk where Reuters journalists were staying. Reuters security adviser Ryan Evans, a former British military officer, was killed.
