Injuries cloud tennis as US Open gets under way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:26 UTC
01:47:26 KST

After Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner split last year’s Grand Slams, the two superstars were expected to continue their see-saw rivalry this year.
That has not happened. Instead, injuries have foreclosed the possibility of a clash between the two champions in three of the four Grand Slams, with the Spaniard missing the French Open and Wimbledon due to a wrist injury and the Italian absent from New York because of a knee injury.
Alcaraz and Sinner are far from alone among top players missing big tournaments this year due to injury, a trend that has been a source of growing alarm in the sport.
Photo: Reuters
Italy’s Lorenzo Musetti and France’s Arthur Fils missed earlier Grand Slams this year due to injury but are playing in New York, while women’s No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina is nursing a heel injury as she prepares for her first round. Canada’s Victoria Mboko missed Wimbldedon and the US Open due to injury, along with Britain’s Jack Draper. Compared with earlier generations, today’s best tennis players have access to more sophisticated practices in fitness and nutrition, greater candor about mental health, and improved technology in detecting and treating injuries.
“We’re losing the battle overall despite the advances in sports medicine,” said Neeru Jayanthi, who leads the tennis medicine program at Emory Healthcare in Atlanta, Georgia.
The injury problem points to the downside of the greater physicality needed to compete at the highest levels of a sport where play is becoming faster and more powerful all the time, enabled by racquet innovations that allow for wicked topspin shots that did not exist in earlier tennis eras.
“The game has gotten more intense, because the players have gotten bigger, faster and stronger,” said Mackie Shilstone, a longtime fitness expert who worked with Serena Williams for 14 years.
The faster pace places greater strain on the body when it changes direction, while more severe weather due to climate change also takes a toll, Shilstone said.
Adding to that, the big business of tennis is played over 11 months of the year, highlighted by the four Grand Slams and a series of mandatory 1,000-level tournaments.
“You can’t go 11 months straight and travel all over the world,” Shilstone said. “There has to be planned recovery built in.”
Extreme topspin is a factor in the rising incidence of wrist injuries seen at all levels of tennis, said New York hand and wrist surgeon Remy Rabinovich at Northwell Health, who perceives a silver lining in that players are opting to rest rather than playing through pain.
“There is a big element of preventative medicine and more strategic ways of playing in the hopes of having a longer career,” Rabinovich said.
Alcaraz on Friday said he decided to rest until he was ready to come back to “hopefully have a really long career.”
Novak Djokovic has had injuries in the past few years, but at 39, was a contender at this year’s US Open, but he crashed out in the first round.
Injuries in tennis are not new. Among the group of recently retired greats, Rafael Nadal was out of commission for significant stretches in his peak years due to injury, while hip problems largely derailed Andy Murray’s career after he won Wimbledon and the Olympics in 2016.
Roger Federer, who avoided major injury for most of his career, retired in 2022 after realizing “the knee can’t do it anymore,” he said last week.
Since Federer retired, the tours have shifted many of the 1,000-level tournaments to two-week coed events with 96-player draws, which the “players are probably mentally and physically adjusting to,” Federer said, adding that not overplaying is “easier said than done.”
A 2024 study by the European Journal of Sport Science in pro matches from the 1970s through 2019 pointed to an overall increase in match retirements.
However, a 2016 study showed no increase in injuries at Wimbledon between 2003 and 2012, while ruing “a paucity of published data describing the incidence of injury in elite tennis.”
Mitigating injuries is expected to figure into a Grand Slam Player Advisory Council announced earlier this week, according to a news release that identified player welfare as an aspect of the council’s mandate.
Addressing the tennis schedule is the most often-discussed response to the injury problem, but Jayanthi defends a broader approach, maintaining that major injuries are often the result of cumulative wear and tear from more years of intense play in juniors.
“Perhaps we should revisit the way we decide to train our younger players to position them for long-term success,” he said.

At least five leaders skip Pacific Islands summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:24 UTC
01:47:24 KST

At least five leaders would skip the Pacific Island region’s annual summit, officials said yesterday, hours before the opening of talks overshadowed by Taiwan-China tensions.
The gathering aims to grapple with challenges such as climate change, drug crime and the Chinese test-firing of a ballistic missile in July that landed in the Pacific Ocean.
China’s security and economic influence has added resonance this year, because the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum is being hosted by Palau, a diplomatic ally of Taiwan.
Photo: AFP
Beijing has protested against Taiwan’s inclusion among aid partners invited to attend along with China, Singapore, Japan, the UK and the US.
China has also declared Palau an “unsafe” place for tourists.
The Pacific forum, which is to culminate with a leaders’ retreat on Thursday, has been touted for decades as a symbol of regional unity. However, a growing number of leaders are skipping this year’s forum and sending lower-ranked ministers in their place.
Samoa’s government said in a statement its delegation would be led by the deputy prime minister.
The prime minister of Vanuatu and the head of government of the French territory of New Caledonia would also skip the summit, a forum official told journalists.
Kiribati’s president has already said he would not be attending.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale unexpectedly flew out of Palau on Sunday to deal with a political crisis at home after a no-confidence motion was lodged against his leadership.
Solomon Islands had been China’s closest partner in the Pacific until Wale was recently elected, vowing to review a secret security pact with Beijing and repair ties with the US and Australia.
Fiji, a founding member of the forum, said its delegation to Palau would be led by the foreign minister, but it was not known whether the prime minister might join at a later stage.
“The Pacific is our home, not a theater for geopolitical competition,” Palauan President Surangel Whipps said in an interview on Sunday.
Tensions between the Pacific’s partners should not detract from island priorities on renewable energy, drug crime, food security and climate change, he said.
The leaders’ absence might weaken any joint Pacific statement on the Chinese missile test, said Oliver Nobetau, Pacific analyst at the Lowy Institute, a Sydney-based think tank.
“Not having these leaders there really lowers the expectation of whether or not we will see a strong statement come out of the Pacific Islands Forum,” he said.
Some Pacific leaders were staying at home to tackle domestic political priorities, said Nobetau, director of the institute’s Pacific Islands program.
However, the leaders might also have decided that one-on-one discussions with external powers are more useful than forum negotiations in some areas such as security and economic support, he said.
About 110 police officers drawn from various Pacific islands are providing security at the forum, the first large-scale demonstration of Pacific-wide cooperation on policing.
Australia, the biggest forum member and aid donor, has led efforts for the Pacific to provide its own security, arguing there is no need for China to have police in Kiribati and the Solomons.
“Investing in the security and prosperity of our Pacific neighbors makes our region safer and our economy stronger,” Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement.
“The big challenges facing the Pacific require solutions designed and delivered for the Pacific, by the Pacific. And Australia has a key role to play — as a partner and leader,” he said.

信益對上了美翎怒視的眼神。「告訴她你有老婆了。」「不要。」他看著美翎。「別煩我！」一陣尖銳的寒意捏住他的手臂。
他沒有聽到荔芬說「隨便你」，也沒看到她聳聳肩。他只看到她走回舞池。美翎在他身旁的空高腳椅上坐了下來。她的笑容又回到了臉上。「只能跟我在一起」她在他的耳邊輕聲說道。「像一直以來那樣。」
Epilogue 故事討論
Hsin-yi had found a red envelope containing money and a lock of black hair. Then a grieving family appeared and asked him to marry their dead daughter, Mei-ling. Out of pity, he agreed and added her name to his ancestral tablet. He thought it was an old superstition and nothing more. He did not expect a ghost wife to follow him home.
In traditional Chinese society, marriage also determined a woman’s place after death. A woman was said to jia gei (嫁給) a man, “to be married off,” while a man qu hui (娶回) a wife, “to take a wife.” An unmarried woman could be left outside the ancestral line, with no descendants to offer incense, food, or joss paper to her hun (魂, spiritual soul) and po (魄,corporeal soul).
“Ghost marriage” offered her a place in another family’s lineage, where her spirit could be remembered and cared for. In this tradition, peace after death depended partly on still belonging among the living.
信益撿到一個裡面裝有現金與一縷黑髮的紅包。隨後，一個悲痛的家庭找上門，請求他娶他們過世的女兒美翎。出於同情，他答應了，並把她的名字列入了他的祖先牌位。他以為這不過是個過時的迷信，僅此而已。結果萬萬沒想到會有一位鬼新娘跟著他回家。
在傳統華人社會中，婚姻也決定了女性死後的歸宿。女性被說是「嫁給」男性，而男性則是「娶回」妻子。未婚過世的女性往往無法列入本家的祖先牌位，沒有後代能為她的「魂」與「魄」供奉香火、食物或紙錢。
「冥婚」為她提供了融入另一個家族血脈的機會，讓她的靈魂得以被銘記與照顧。在這項傳統中，死後的安寧，某種程度上取決於是否依然在陽世有所歸屬。

Fennec foxes and jackrabbits, both inhabitants of hot desert environments, possess ears that function as natural cooling devices. Meta’s US$18bn settlement could be just the start
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

Not many people would count paying US$18 billion they did not expect to when they woke up that morning as a victory. Yet for Meta Platforms Inc, the owners of Facebook and Instagram, the agreement with 52 US attorneys general to settle claims that it designed its products to be addictive to children and misled people about their safety, could be described as a win of sorts.
Meta denies wrongdoing, and the amount it plans to pay would be spread over a decade. Some of it is contingent on other big tech firms not named in the case coughing up too. The cash is chump change for Meta, which made about US$60 billion in profit last year. More damaging to the tech giant in the long run could be the agreement to unwind some of the mechanics it has spent two decades perfecting to keep users on its platforms.
Children younger than 18 in the US would face a default two-hour daily limit on Facebook and Instagram, with access blocked overnight — unless a parent changes the setting. Teachers will be glad to hear that notifications would be muted during school hours, while teenagers would be nagged as much by the platform itself as their parents about exactly how long they have spent staring at their screens.
Illustration: Yusha
All of these are significant changes that materially change how the company’s products work — and all of them should be welcomed. However, in lots of ways, Meta has got off lightly with this agreement, both in what it has been asked to do and the fine it must pay.
What the decision shows, just months after Meta chose to fight its corner in court, and lost significantly, is how the economics of fighting social media litigation have changed. This settlement signifies an important and deliberate shift in strategy.
Meta last month went to court in New Mexico — a decision that cost it dearly. The judge there ordered the firm to pay US$942 million and overhaul some protections for children — a decision it is appealing.
That Meta lost that case, and was found to have done wrong, was far more damaging than last week’s settlement without liability, even if the amounts involved were smaller. Still, thousands more cases involving social media addiction claims are still wending their way through US courts.
Chastened by a couple of losses, it looks — at least in this instance — like Meta has taken the approach that a Pyrrhic victory is better than the risk of another real loss. Settlements without admission of fault avoid judgements and a legal situation that could quickly spiral out of control for Meta’s product offering.
While Meta has had to make significant changes to its platforms as a result of last week’s settlement, it still ultimately has control over what changes are made, and has sought to limit them to the bare minimum. Settling, however expensive, is a way of protecting its core business proposition.
Meta faces a Hobson’s choice when it comes to litigation. It can gamble on a jury and risk vast damages, damaging internal disclosures and a judge deciding which parts of Instagram or Facebook must change. Or it can pay an eye-watering, but manageable sum to settle, negotiate the product changes on its own terms and staunch the bleeding.
That US$18 billion is certainly more than most companies could pay, but it pales in comparison with the US$1.5 trillion Meta’s own public relations team warned the case could cost it had it gone through the courts — and the more realistic US$200 billion the prosecuting lawyers sought to squeeze from the firm.
Even more than that, Meta has managed to make some of the bill somebody else’s problem. About one-third of the settlement it has agreed to pay is conditional on TikTok and YouTube introducing similar restrictions and each making matching payments. Meta is publicly calling on both companies to sign up.
As this is a negotiated settlement — and one in which no one wins, but Meta certainly does not lose — not everyone has been won over. While attorneys general from 48 US states agreed to Meta’s proposition, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier rejected the deal and intends to continue pursuing Meta. He dismissed the settlement as “peanuts” and said: “We’ll see them at trial.”
Nor is this necessarily just a US story. The settlement formally applies only to the participating US states and territories. A Meta spokesperson said it already offers strong protections for teenagers elsewhere. It would watch how the new measures work before deciding what comes next internationally.
Running substantially different versions of Facebook and Instagram around the world is hardly attractive, and Meta has now demonstrated that putting these restrictions in place is possible. Given the drive toward child safety online in the UK and Australia, it seems likely that politicians would soon ask why American teenagers get them and children in their own countries do not. The UK’s Online Safety Act is a useful stick for the government to wield in this instance, adding extra leverage to bring those changes here, too.
It is that which might prove the settlement’s biggest consequence. Meta has paid billions to manage to duck liability in one court case. However, in doing so, it might have opened up the possibility of change in a raft of other countries.
Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App.

Rescuers race to reach trapped workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:19 UTC
01:47:19 KST

Rescue teams were working to reach more than 900 people thought to be trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of half a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal following the devastating flash floods, ?the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said yesterday.
The death toll from the unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ?and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has risen to 903 people, with 16 more dead reported on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet.
Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves on the plains of the Himalayan region after being swept down the mountains by the torrent.
Photo: Prime Minister Secretariat, Nepal / AFP
Nepali officials yesterday said the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from hydropower projects in the flood-hit region.
Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shoveling mud to try to access the tunnels.
“A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” Nepalese army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet.
Photo: AFP
Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers.
“There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”
On Sunday his team was trying to access Chilime Hydropower in Ruswana, in the worst-hit area.
Photo: Reuters
Mountaineers improvised by grabbing planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as a makeshift bridge, along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe, he said.
“Walking in it is very difficult; at one point it was up to our chests,” Gurung said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 meters in. Inside that far, you could [see further in]; it looked like it was just bodies.”
The hydro company had given his team a map and it looked like there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived by staying inside the internal infrastructure.
“They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”
The Red Cross has estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts linked to the effects of the climate crisis.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and it remained challenging to compile a complete assessment of the damage.
“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he wrote on Facebook late on Sunday.
Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers, he added.
Nepal’s disaster agency yesterday said that 903 deaths had been counted there, with 4,247 people, including 592 foreigners, missing.
As of Sunday, Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, and Chinese state media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalese.
China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing had mobilized more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ?220 million yuan (US$32.7 million) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.
Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search-and-rescue operations, but it has leaned on neighbors India and China for their expertise in tunnel rescues.
Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.
However, the weather was good yesterday and rescue work continued to pick up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hard-hit districts.
In the holy ?town of Devighat, on the banks of the Trishuli River that ?flooded, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ?homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming,” CCTV reported, saying ?it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.
Two ?Nepalese officials told Reuters that China had ?not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels following a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that a lack of data sharing could hamper future disaster preparedness.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment on the meeting.

Ex-health ministry worker indicted in espionage case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:18 UTC
01:47:18 KST

Prosecutors have indicted a former Ministry of Health and Welfare associate researcher for their alleged involvement in a Chinese espionage scheme involving former CTi News anchor and YouTuber Lin Chen-you (林宸佑).
The contracted associate researcher at the Department of Protective Services, a woman surnamed Lin (林), has been ordered to remain in custody on suspicion of leaking confidential documents to hostile foreign forces and handling illicit payments, the Ciaotou District Prosecutors’ Office said yesterday.
Lin Chen-you, also known as Ma Te (馬德), was indicted in May along with six active-duty and retired military personnel on Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), money-laundering and bribery charges; prosecutors also alleged that he helped produced anti-recall videos last year at the direction of a Chinese operative in exchange for cryptocurrency.
Photo: Wu Cheng-feng, Taipei Times
He was charged over alleged contraventions of the Anti-Infiltration Act, Money Laundering Control Act (洗錢防制法) and Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例). Prosecutors requested a combined sentence of 12 years.
The researcher is suspected of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法) for leaking documents to hostile forces, the Anti-Corruption Act for accepting bribes in breach of official duties and helping deliver the bribes, the Money Laundering Control Act and the Criminal Code for disclosing confidential documents unrelated to national defense as a public official, prosecutors said.
Her role at the ministry involved handling subsidies for local governments, the office said, adding that although she is no longer employed by the ministry, prosecutors considered her a public official for the alleged offenses because the position carried statutory authority.
Beginning in May last year, she allegedly made contact with a member of an overseas hostile foreign force known as “Mr Tseng (曾),” prosecutors said.
The espionage group asked her to provide information such as journalists’ names, make money transfers and gather damaging information about the government in exchange for payments of NT$5,000 per month, some of which was transferred by Lin Chen-you, prosecutors said.
The researcher used an account in another person’s name to receive funds and transferred the money to accounts designated by “Mr Tseng,” they said.
The payments were compensation for military personnel who had been bribed to contravene their official duties, while the arrangement was also used to conceal the source of the proceeds in a money laundering scheme, they added.
On March 10, the researcher allegedly used her cellphone to photograph confidential documents that she sent to “Mr Tseng” through the messaging app Telegram, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said they are seeking a 12-year prison sentence on the charge of accepting bribes in breach of official duties, citing the number and content of the documents allegedly leaked and her long-term cooperation with the hostile force.
Department of Protective Services Director-General Kuo Tsai-jung (郭彩榕) said that the contracted employee worked at the ministry from June last year until her resignation on May 25.
Her primary duties involved administrative tasks for social welfare subsidies to civic groups, such as document distribution and reviewing reimbursement applications, Kuo said, adding that her duties did not involve classified information.
Based on the investigation details released so far, it appears the employee became involved in the alleged illicit activities prior to taking her position at the ministry, Kuo said.
Kuo added that the ministry would enhance its personnel recruitment evaluations.

Tropical Storm Saudel to make a comeback, with little impact on Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:18 UTC
01:47:18 KST

A tropical depression near Hainan that was once Typhoon Saudel may once again strengthen into a tropical storm, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday, but a sea warning for waters around Taiwan is unlikely.
CWA forecaster Huang En-hung (黃恩鴻) said that Saudel would return to being a weak tropical storm by late yesterday or early this morning.
However, as the storm is to gradually weaken again and would head toward China’s Guangdong Province away from Taiwan, the chances that it would affect Taiwan enough for the CWA to issue a sea warning are relatively low, Huang said.
Screengrab from the Central Weather Administration’s Web site
Taiwan’s weather in the coming days is more likely to be affected by the combined effects of an extended low-pressure area and the strengthening of southwesterly winds.
Those conditions are to bring considerable rainfall to Taiwan today and on Thursday, mostly localized around central and southern Taiwan as well as the eastern half of the main island, Huang said.
Today, central, southern and eastern Taiwan should be aware of heavy to extremely heavy rain, while other regions could see thunderstorms in the afternoon and also heavier localized precipitation, Huang said.
Between tomorrow and Thursday, Huang said that central, southern and eastern Taiwan could see short showers or thundershowers throughout the day, and perhaps localized heavy rains.
Mountainous areas throughout Taiwan could also see heavy rain in the afternoon during those days, while on Thursday, the western half of Taiwan plus Yilan County in the northeast could see short showers, thundershowers and localized heavy rain, Huang said.
The weather is to improve in southern Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, and all of Taiwan should see the rainy weather subside by Sunday, Huang said.
In terms of temperatures, Taiwan could expect highs between 30°C and 33°C, with northern Taiwan potentially seeing daytime highs reach 34°C and even 35°C.
Because of the persistent rain in southern Taiwan, highs there could range between 27°C and 28°C, Huang said.

EDITORIAL: Beijing’s corporate tax crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:13 UTC
01:47:13 KST

Beijing has launched a campaign to collect back taxes from large publicly listed companies in China, demanding that businesses return tax benefits they previously enjoyed, Bloomberg News reported last week. In the first half of this year, Chinese tax authorities demanded 7.7 billion yuan (US$1.14 billion) in back taxes and charges for delayed payments from more than 100 listed companies, exceeding the total amount of back taxes recovered in the past 14 years since Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) took office in 2012, it said.
The move indicates that the decades-long model of Chinese provinces offering rebates, subsidies and tax deals to lure investments and meet growth targets could be coming to and end. Chinese companies in emerging industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels had long enjoyed tax perks from provincial governments. Targeted items include the misapplication of tax reductions and exemptions, the over-declaration of value-added tax deductions and the revocation of what were previously deemed compliant tax incentives, Bloomberg reported.
Many listed Chinese companies have been hit with huge tax bills, with some reporting significant declines in profit and even losses in the first half of this year. A shift in a government policy of supporting businesses through tax cuts and the phaseout of the growth-at-all-costs model is at least partially to blame. When unveiling the next five-year blueprint for national development earlier this year, Beijing vowed to maintain taxes at a level relative to GDP.
The strict tax enforcement highlights the growing fiscal pressures facing local and central governments in China. Local governments are facing budget shortfalls because land sales to property developers have collapsed amid a real-estate slump. The central government is dealing with declining tax revenue due to weakening domestic consumption and low corporate profits. This fiscal squeeze on local and central governments, coupled with advanced digital tracking systems such as China’s Golden Tax Phase Four system, gives Chinese authorities more incentives to recover lost revenue wherever they can.
A slowing economy, declining government revenue and continued capital outflows have also prompted Beijing to launch an unprecedented tax enforcement campaign targeting ultra-high-net-worth individuals, several foreign media outlets reported last month. Tax authorities reportedly examined the overseas investments of wealthy Chinese, and, in some cases, demanded taxes on offshore investment gains dating back to 2000, the reports said. The assets under review reportedly include real estate, stocks, insurance policies, cryptocurrencies and offshore trusts.
Central to China’s latest global tax hunt is offshore trusts — which were once a gray area, providing a loophole for wealthy Chinese to avoid taxes — structured in Hong Kong, Singapore or other tax havens. However, the Chinese Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration on July 24 announced that the government would impose a 20 percent flat tax on income generated at every stage of an offshore trust’s life cycle, from establishment to operation and liquidation. Moreover, tax residency is unrelated to nationality. Even if a Chinese citizen holds foreign passports or permanent residency, as long as their primary economic interests remain anchored in China, they are still considered Chinese tax residents and must pay taxes on overseas income and capital gains.
The purpose of Beijing’s aggressive, retroactive enforcement is not just to shore up the country’s severe fiscal shortfalls; it also aims to make its citizens’ overseas assets transparent, traceable and taxable, enabling authorities to tighten control over outbound capital and clamp down on tax evasion. Apparently, China is moving to impose much tighter global tax oversight, aided by the adoption of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Common Reporting Standard and the Golden Tax Phase Four system to cross-check people’s foreign accounts. The bigger picture is not just about collecting unpaid taxes; it is about China expanding its financial oversight beyond its borders.
Under China’s new rules, Chinese citizens’ overseas wealth is no longer beyond the reach of tax authorities. Taken together with Beijing’s new national security rules and stricter exit controls, these developments show a major shift in China’s policy toward treating cross-border movement, private wealth and corporate operations as conditional privileges subject to absolute state control.
However, squeezing private wealth could accelerate capital outflows and weaken investment, while people’s tax compliance could open doors to deeper asset scrutiny and capital controls by authorities. Beijing is trying to get everybody to pay up, but would it solve China’s deeper fiscal crisis? No one knows for sure, yet it is a worrisome development for its wealthy citizens and big companies, and it might reshape global wealth management hubs, particularly Hong Kong and Singapore.

Global chip market to exceed US$2tn by 2030: SEMI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:09 UTC
01:47:09 KST

The global semiconductor market is expected to be worth more than US$2 trillion by 2030 because of growth driven by demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, SEMI senior director of market intelligence Clark Tseng (曾瑞榆) said yesterday.
Earlier projections had put the market at about US$1 trillion by 2030 based on demand for traditional applications such as personal computers, smartphones and consumer electronics, Tseng said at a news conference in Taipei ahead of the opening of Semicon Taiwan trade show today.
Those forecasts have since changed significantly, as AI data centers drive demand for advanced logic chips, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs), he said.
Photo: CNA
The market is expected to surpass US$1.5 trillion this year, but the growth is not broad-based, with PC and smartphone shipments remaining under pressure despite semiconductor demand outpacing overall economic and investment growth, he added.
“AI is reshaping semiconductor growth, driving sustained demand for advanced logic, HBM and DRAM, high-layer-count NAND, testing and advanced packaging equipment,” Tseng said.
SEMI expects the global wafer fab equipment market to grow to US$220 billion in 2028 from US$117 billion last year, up from its previous forecast of US$200 billion.
The association has also raised its 2028 forecasts for testing equipment to US$23.5 billion from US$20.8 billion and for packaging equipment to US$10 billion from US$8.6 billion, Tseng said.
The revisions reflect stronger investment in 2-nanometer and 3-nanometer production capacity, as well as rising demand for HBM, enterprise SSDs, and more complex chip testing and packaging, he said.
The global semiconductor materials market is expected to post double-digit growth this year and next year, reaching US$83 billion and US$92 billion respectively, Tseng said.
Taiwan is expected to account for about 30 percent of the market next year, reflecting its importance in advanced manufacturing and packaging, he said.
On the same occasion, Tien Wu (吳田玉), chair of the SEMI international board of directors and chief executive officer of ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), said the rapid expansion of AI is creating stress on Taiwan’s resources.
The ecosystem required to meet strong AI demand is creating short-term pressure on land, talent, capital and electricity in the nation, while also raising concerns in other countries about the concentration of semiconductor production in Taiwan, Wu said.
However, AI’s long-term value would not come from replacing existing human knowledge, but from enabling cross-disciplinary innovation and replicating successful applications on a much larger scale, he said.
Taiwan should therefore accelerate investment in AI infrastructure while strengthening ties with international partners and explaining the purpose of that investment more clearly, he added.

President William Lai’s (賴清德) administration plans to allocate more than NT$40 billion (US$1.26 billion) next year to develop 10 major artificial intelligence (AI) projects, with a goal of training at least 500,000 AI professionals by 2040.
Lai yesterday met with the VIS Mars robotics team, which represented Taiwan at the FIRST Tech Challenge robotics tournament in Turkey in June. He praised the students for overcoming a major setback when customs detained their competition equipment after they arrived in Turkey.
Unable to access their robot, the team collected discarded components and borrowed tools from other teams to assemble a replacement robot before the competition. They won four qualification matches and earned the tournament’s highest match points.
Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office
Lai said the students’ ability to adapt under pressure reminded him of the fictional character MacGyver.
Team captain Ray Shang (商泱瑞) said their greatest strength was not their equipment, but their ability to rethink, adapt and solve problems regardless of the circumstances.
Lai said technology education and talent development remain key government priorities.
The government launched the AI Talent Ark Project this year to nurture talent through fundamental education, professional development and data-driven approaches. The initiative, together with the 10 major AI projects, aims to build a large AI talent pool, promote smart applications across industries and strengthen Taiwan’s competitiveness.
Shang said the team’s experience showed that perseverance and teamwork were more important than having perfect equipment.
The team had advanced through competitions in Hong Kong and the Netherlands before facing its biggest test in Turkey.
Meanwhile, Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said Taiwan could accumulate computing capacity of at least 10,000 graphics processing units (GPUs) within a year through private investment in AI computing centers under a build-own-operate (BOO) project launched by the ministry.
Technological sovereignty does not mean developing every technology domestically, he said.
Instead, Taiwan should focus on critical technologies, particularly sovereign AI and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite communications, he said.
Sovereign AI means AI systems used in Taiwan should understand Taiwanese perspectives, society and languages. The ministry is therefore developing a Taiwan sovereign AI training corpus by making government-owned datasets available to local and international researchers.
AI computing centers should be located in Taiwan so that AI models can operate under Taiwanese laws and regulations, Lin said, adding that the ministry has designated such centers as major public infrastructure eligible for private investment.
LEO satellite communications are another priority, he said.
Taiwan needs independent communication capabilities, as submarine cables could be disrupted during conflict or “gray zone” harassment.
Although Starlink has shown limited interest in Taiwan’s commercial market because of its strong 4G and 5G coverage, Lin said LEO technology remains essential to Taiwan’s technological sovereignty and national resilience.

Novak Djokovic on Sunday suffered his earliest Grand Slam exit in 20 years and said he does not know the solution to the physical problems he has battled in “pretty much every match” this year.
Argentine Mariano Navone’s 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 victory ended Djokovic’s latest bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title. It also ended his run of 78 Grand Slam first-round victories, a streak stretching all the way back to Djokovic’s 2006 loss to Paul Goldstein at the 2006 Australian Open.
Djokovic vomited on court and struggled with late-match cramps and back pain — an “awful feeling” that he is becoming used to.
Photo: AP
“It’s something that I’ve been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year. Vomiting, throwing up ... then my whole body starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain,” he said.
Although he reached the final of the Australian Open this year and the semi-finals at Wimbledon, Djokovic said he is not equipped right now to go deep in tournaments — and he is not sure what the fix is.
“I’m just trying to address really what’s going on and how far I can go this way,” he said.
Photo: AFP
Despite his struggles, Djokovic appeared to have finally taken control when he broke Navone for a 2-1 lead in the fourth set with a vintage backhand winner down the line.
However, Navone won the next five games, raising his arms in celebration after fighting off two break points for a 5-2 lead and breaking Djokovic again to force the fifth set.
Djokovic took a medical timeout before the final set, receiving massage on his spine and another delivery of medication.
However, Navone jumped to a 3-0 lead in the decisive set, and despite the urging of fans, there was no road back for the Serb.
“It’s unbelievable,” an ecstatic Navone said after triumphing in his first meeting with his longtime idol after 4 hours and 36 minutes.
“It was a tough match, a battle. Playing against Novak the first time in the biggest stage we have in the world of tennis right now... Like, until 20 years he never lose in the first round, so I mean, it’s crazy,” he said.
Navone, ranked 48th, was most pleased with his mental game.
“I was two sets to one down, and then break down also in the fourth, but in that moment, I felt it,” he said.
Djokovic broke Navone in the second game of the match as he rolled to a 3-1 first-set lead.
However, he was clearly struggling and with Navone gaining confidence Djokovic had to claw out of 0-40 hole to hold for 4-1, looking weary as Navone began to extend the rallies.
Djokovic’s double fault on break point allowed Navone to cut the deficit to 4-3, and after a brief pause to close the roof when showers struck, Navone held at love to knot the set at 4-4.
Neither blinked until the tiebreaker, but pills delivered by the trainer did not solve Djokovic’s sluggishness.
He fell behind 4-2 in the tiebreaker and after a cleverly angled forehand winner to make it 5-5, Djokovic hit a forehand long and another weakly into the net to give the set to Navone.
In a tense second set Djokovic missed break chances in the third and fifth games before breaking Navone at love for a 6-5 lead and holding at love to level the match at one set apiece.
The third set was more of the same, with Djokovic looking spent after every long rally.
He let a precious break chance go begging in the fifth game of the third, and after Navone held for 3-2, Djokovic all but collapsed into his courtside chair and buried his face in a towel.
The Serb pressed on and was rewarded with a crucial break for a 5-4 lead. He held for a two sets to one lead, but could not make the advantage stand.
After breaking Navone for a 2-1 lead in the fourth, Djokovic lost the next eight games.
When it was all over, Djokovic embraced Navone, then departed blowing kisses to the crowd that had tried to will him to victory.
“So grateful to experience this,” he said of the crowd support. “They were trying to lift me up in important moments... The love and appreciation they gave me in the end really touched my heart.”

Bruno Fernandes’ hat-trick on Sunday inspired a Manchester United fightback from a goal down to thrash Ipswich Town 5-2 and get their English Premier League season up and running.
After a nightmare 2-0 defeat to Hull City previous weekend, another newly-promoted side had the Red Devils on the ropes when Leif Davis opened the scoring for the Tractor Boys.
However, Fernandes blasted home to level before halftime and then converted from the penalty spot after a Jacob Greaves own-goal put United in front.
Photo: AP
The United captain completed his hat-trick from close range before adding an assist to his fine afternoon for Bryan Mbeumo.
Marcus Rashford was handed his first United start in nearly two years as Michael Carrick made four changes to the side that kicked off the campaign with a woeful display eight days ago.
Rashford and the return of his England international teammate Kobbie Mainoo made a big difference, but United were again reliant on Fernandes as a difference-maker in the final third.
Questions also remain over Carrick’s men at the back.
Senne Lammens had to save one-on-one from Julio Enciso after he broke clear from a United corner before Ipswich took the lead on 29 minutes.
Abdul Fatawu burned Luke Shaw for pace down the wing, and his cross was brilliantly swept high into the net by Davis.
Moments later, the Ipswich left-back had an even better chance to double the visitors’ lead, but his tame effort was saved by Lammens.
Instead, the game swung on an Ipswich error as Marcelino Nunez slipped to gift possession to Matheus Cunha, who fed Fernandes to blast home on his weaker left foot.
Another break went against Gary O’Neil’s men 11 minutes into the second half.
The ball came off Harry Maguire’s arm before he fired a shot, and the goal would have been ruled out had it directly found the net.
However, because the effort was heading off target and deflected in off Greaves, it was allowed to stand as it was not deemed a handball leading directly to a goal.
Greaves was still clearing his head from that setback when he chopped down Cunha as he bore down on goal.
Fernandes, who was this week crowned last season’s player of the year by his fellow professionals, coolly converted the resulting spot-kick.
It was a record 21 Premier League assists last season that powered Fernandes to a haul of individual awards as he only scored nine times.
The Portuguese international is already one-third of the way to matching that tally as he was in the right place to latch onto Mbeumo’s deflected shot and complete his hat-trick.
A fine display going forward was book-ended by United errors at the back as Ipswich were gifted a consolation in stoppage time.
Lisandro Martinez was caught in possession by Enciso, who teed up Chuba Akpom to tap into an empty net.

The (mostly fictional) cockroaches in Japanese markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:07 UTC
01:47:07 KST

You might have read that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has a new friend.
“Japan’s PM: I’m so lonely I befriended a cockroach,” ran the headline in the UK’s Telegraph last week. One tweet of the article had received more than 8 million views.
It is a great story with one problem: It is not remotely true.
The saga stems from a Takaichi tweet in which she said that while her official residence has a reputation for being haunted, it was not a ghost that made her scream, but a cockroach. Citing a belief in reincarnation, she could not bring herself to kill the pest; when she found out that her staff had arranged for an extermination, she expressed mild regret.
Most headlines in Tokyo reported on how bizarre the international coverage was, with one asking “translation error, or ridicule?”
You might well ask, who cares? This is Japan, after all, the country about which you can write anything and worry later if it is true, from fictional eyeball-lickers to supposed post-COVID-19-mask smile coaches. Normally, such stories do not have much impact.
Except, as this episode shows, official communications can be misread, deliberately or not. Consider what that means for increasingly sensitive yen and bond markets.
As the Bank of Japan (BOJ) retreats from the bond market, foreign investors are increasingly dictating prices. They own only about 13 percent of outstanding Japanese government bonds, but account for up to 30 percent of purchases of the benchmark 10-year, and dominate the short-term bill market. The FX market is of course international, with the carry trade and US intervention amplifying that interest.
However, the government still communicates as though domestic institutions are the only audience that matters. It was caught flat-footed earlier this summer when international investors misinterpreted domestic-focused early leaks of a key economic document to mean profligate spending and opposition to BOJ independence. Yields spiked in response.
Communication needs to be tailored with this kind of reaction in mind. Many are just not familiar with the realities of Japan’s debt situation — that while gross debt is high, so are its assets, meaning net debt is far more manageable; that its primary budget deficit is one the lowest among its peers; that forecasts for debt-servicing costs include both interest and principal, unlike the net-interest figures commonly cited for the US.
I have encountered some who think that the entirety of her ￥370 trillion (US$2.32 trillion) public-private investment plan is going to be funded by new Japanese government bond issuance. Not only is this wildly incorrect, even if the administration wanted to spend this much — and it does not — practical constraints mean it would be completely impossible. It is like betting on land prices expecting the first administration of US President Donald Trump to actually build the wall.
Given that the eyes of the world are on Japan in a way they have rarely been before, the old communications model — in which news is leaked first to the domestic press, with the international reaction an afterthought, if it is thought about at all — needs a revamp.
There is a growing narrative that considers the prime minister to be a spendthrift in a country that is already on the fiscal ropes. This supposed imminent collapse is an increasingly prominent explanation for the yen still testing 160, despite the reduced rate gap with the US, the BOJ communicating an increased pace of hikes and prospects of a US Federal Reserve tightening receding.
“Is Japan bust? You’d think so reading recent coverage,” is the accurate summary from Nicholas Smith, a veteran Japan strategist who recently left CLSA, referring to often hyperbolic reports.
The prime minister also faces a powerful domestic perception, deeply entrenched in the Finance Ministry and local commentators, that warns of imminent fiscal calamity. It is simple to grasp, and so travels easily overseas.
If she wants room to pursue her ambitious growth plans, it is one she must fight.
Artificial intelligence (AI) translation might mean that language is increasingly a solved problem. However, while AI can provide context — interpreting that cockroach anecdote or illuminating the realities of Japan’s fiscal situation — it would not do it unless asked. Providing that detail is the job of Takaichi’s government; hoping for understanding to emerge is a fool’s errand.
Thanks to her staff, she might not need to call an exterminator anymore. However, there is someone else she needs: an international communications specialist.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan and the Koreas. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Indigenous energy justice a need
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:06 UTC
01:47:06 KST

The Risk Society and Policy Research Center at National Taiwan University released Taiwan’s first survey on energy justice among indigenous peoples last month. The findings were alarming. Among households surveyed in indigenous communities, 52.2 percent had summer energy expenditures exceeding 10 percent of their work income, meeting the study’s “energy poverty” threshold, and 57.3 percent had at some point paid their electricity bills late because of financial difficulties. Many households could not afford to replace old appliances, leaving them with no choice but to continue using energy-intensive appliances. The poorer the household, the older its appliances, and the higher its electricity bills.
Energy transition policies cannot focus solely on renewable energy and carbon reduction without simultaneously addressing energy justice.
First, the government should launch a household solar program for indigenous communities. Eligible homes should receive full subsidies for the installation of solar power systems, with priority given to economically disadvantaged households and those facing the highest energy burdens. This would allow abundant sunlight in indigenous communities to be an energy asset for local residents, reducing their long-term electricity costs.
Second, the government should introduce a nationwide program to help indigenous households, including those in urban areas, replace old air-conditioners, heating systems and other energy-intensive appliances. Subsidies should be increased, with the most disadvantaged households eligible for full reimbursement. This would prevent a common policy failure in which households receiving a subsidy still cannot afford the required out-of-pocket contribution.
Local governments could consider allowing older indigenous residents to use points from senior citizens’ benefits cards to offset their electricity bills, with particular attention paid to elderly people living alone and those facing financial hardship. Policies for older people should not only enable them to take public transportation and leave their homes. They should protect the basic right to live safely and comfortably, including being able to use air-conditioning and heating during the summer and winter.
Where indigenous communities have abundant sunlight, let that sunlight become an asset for its residents. Energy policy should not just be concerned with generating electricity; it is about its accessibility as a matter of social justice. To this end, the government should introduce a comprehensive action plan for indigenous energy equity, covering everything from solar panels and appliance replacement to electricity-bill assistance for older people. Indigenous communities should no longer be the last group to receive a hand during Taiwan’s energy transition.
Yu Tien-min is an assistant professor at Da-Yeh University.

Opposition drone bill is ineffective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:06 UTC
01:47:06 KST

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan passed an opposition-backed bill that sets aside NT$240 billion (US$7.6 billion) for uncrewed systems over the next six years. At first glance, that looks like a major commitment to Taiwan’s defense and industrial development. However, the headline number does not guarantee the stability that industry needs.
Opposition legislators chose to fund the program through the regular annual budget process. Although the NT$240 billion is earmarked for uncrewed systems, the funding must still return to the Legislative Yuan for approval each year. Unlike a multi-year special budget, it remains subject to annual budget discussions, legislative delays and political disputes. Taiwan saw that risk this year, when the annual budget was not passed until this month.
Industry needs greater certainty. When manufacturers decide whether to build production lines, hire engineers, expand testing capacity or develop domestic supply chains, they need more than a six-year target written into law. They need predictable orders and a credible multi-year procurement pipeline. Annual uncertainty undermines the long-term investment Taiwan needs for rapid industrial expansion.
However, the opposition-backed bill creates an even bigger problem: bureaucratic duplication. The law requires the Executive Yuan to establish a “National Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Strategy Special Committee,” which would coordinate, promote and supervise uncrewed-systems policy and review the national industry development plan.
The Executive Yuan already has a coordination mechanism. Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun (鄭麗君) already leads the “Interagency Task Force on Unmanned Vehicle Industry Development and Management.” Officials from the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA), Ministry of National Defense (MND), Ministry of Transportation, National Science and Technology Council and other agencies use it to coordinate industrial development, defense autonomy, supply chains and regulation.
Individual ministries have clear responsibilities. The MOEA has a dedicated drone-industry development office. The MND has professional planning departments responsible for strategic planning, capability assessment and major defense acquisition.
The Legislative Yuan has the institutions necessary to provide rigorous oversight. Legislators on the Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee oversee defense procurement, force development, drones and uncrewed maritime systems. Legislators on the Economics Committee scrutinize industrial policy. The legislature can question ministers, demand special reports, review budgets, amend laws and examine procurement programs. That is the proper place for oversight.
The opposition-backed legislation instead requires more than half of the new strategy committee’s members to be experts or academics recommended by party caucuses in the Legislative Yuan. This allows caucus-nominated members to participate directly in an Executive Yuan policy coordination and review mechanism. Legislators should not blur those roles.
Legislators should demand transparency, challenge procurement priorities and hold officials accountable when programs fail. However, party caucuses should not need to place their nominees inside an executive policy-making mechanism to exercise oversight.
Clear responsibility produces stronger accountability — and faster execution.
That matters especially for uncrewed systems, where technology evolves far faster than traditional defense procurement cycles. Requirements can change in months, not years. Taiwan needs a process that shortens the path from battlefield requirements to procurement and production. Every additional layer of review creates another source for delays.
The issue is not whether Taiwan should invest more or exercise stronger oversight. It should do both. The question is whether the institutions we create help Taiwan move faster. We should not create new institutions only to make functioning administrative and legislative oversight mechanisms more complicated.
The executive mechanism should be made to work, while the Legislative Yuan should review its results from the legislature. Taiwan does not lack committees. What it cannot afford to waste is time.
Gahon Chiang is a congressional staff member in the office of Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chen Kuan-ting focusing on Taiwan’s national security policy. He is a research fellow at the Taiwan Inspiration Association.

Donovan’s Deep Dives: 823 and two visions of Taiwan’s sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:05 UTC
01:47:05 KST

Every year on the anniversary of the 1958 Kinmen 823 Artillery Bombardment — a central episode in what has become known as the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis — carefully crafted speeches reveal the underlying ideological divide over sovereignty between the Taiwan-centric, pan-green Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the pan-blue Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) stance that Taiwan is ultimately a province of China.
The pan-blue side has the added complication that some are hardcore Republic of China (ROC) nationalists, while others are more accommodating of and willing to work with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to varying degrees.
Different accounts give varying numbers and duration for the conflict, but there were thousands of casualties on both the ROC and PRC sides and as many as 470,000 artillery shells struck Kinmen during the intensive 44-day bombardment.
Photo: Wu Cheng-ting, Taipei Times
For the US, there were fears of a war with the PRC over Quemoy (as Kinmen was then called), with the potential for it to turn nuclear. The US-ROC mutual defense treaty then in force, however, only explicitly covered Taiwan and Penghu. The US Navy provided escort close to Kinmen and provided advanced weaponry, but did not get directly involved in the fighting.
After seizing several islands the ROC held off the coast of China in the years prior, this was the final battle that held off further PRC seizures and preserved the territorial status quo that remains today
This was a pivotal event for Taiwanese in resisting the PRC, and Quemoy became a household name in American Cold War politics.
On the surface, both DPP and KMT politicians’ speeches share much in common. They praise the brave soldiers’ sacrifice in defending the nation, lay wreathes and talk about unity. It is in the details of their speeches that the differences are revealed.
WILLIAM LAI’S LINES ON SOVEREIGNTY
In the pan-green view, Taiwan is a settler and colonial society in much the same way as North America or Australia, and shares a similar timeline of several hundred years. Different colonial rulers, especially the Japanese, and different influences, including American, have created a society and culture different from China.
DPP politicians have complicated feelings about commemorating 823 for two reasons. First, the battle was one of the main justifications for the continuation of KMT-imposed martial law. The other is that most on the pan-green side only reluctantly accept the ROC name, constitution and symbols as a way to maintain independence while avoiding a war with the PRC. Kinmen and Matsu have been part of Fujian for at least a thousand years, and did not share in the Taiwanese settler or colonial experiences.
However, as president of the ROC, William Lai (賴清德) is obligated to maintain sovereignty over the islands and to support the troops. He used his speech to rally support for the military and expanding their role and budgets, a dig at the KMT-led opposition over recent controversies and disagreements over defense spending.
Like most DPP politicians, Lai views China as essentially foreign, which comes out in statements like: “For 68 years, China’s authoritarian forces have never stopped pursuing their ambitions for external expansion.”
Photo: Ou Su-mei, Taipei Times
The presidential office readout of Lai’s speech said that Taiwan must uphold “the spirit of ‘not surrendering a single inch of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen or Matsu.’”
Curiously, it didn’t mention traditional ROC claims in the South China Sea, which suggests that he is not going to fight over real estate there. It moreover seems unlikely that Taiwan is going to fight over other traditional territorial claims, including with the ROC’s 11-dash line that the PRC’s 10-dash (until recently 9-dash) is based on.
CHEN YI-HSIN PARROTS PRC
In response, the KMT issued a press release titled: “KMT Calls for ‘Not Surrendering a Single Inch’ on Aug. 23, Asks William Lai: ‘Why Won’t You Dare Mention Sovereignty Over Scarborough Shoal?’” referring to one of the islands in the South China Sea.
The press release covers a blistering attack by KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chairman Chen Yi-hsin (陳以信) on Lai’s speech. Chen is quoted as saying: “But when the Philippines establishes territorial baselines around Scarborough Shoal (Democracy Reef) in the South China Sea, which is part of our country, and when Japan and the Philippines negotiate over rights and interests in waters east of Taiwan — actions that seriously harm our sovereignty and maritime rights and interests — where is President Lai’s commitment to sovereignty?”
The specific term in the headline and in the quote for Scarborough Shoal is Huangyan Island (黃岩島), which is the official PRC name for it. Did an editor add the official ROC name — Democracy Reef (民主礁) — into the quote?
Since 2012, the shoal has been effectively controlled by the PRC. Scarborough Shoal is only 198km from the Philippines’ Subic Bay harbor and just 345km from the capital, Manila, and is considered a serious threat to their national security.
Chen’s leading use of the PRC-preferred name “Huangyan Island,” rather than Taiwan’s official “Democracy Reef,” strikingly echoes Beijing’s terminology, although he claimed the feature for the ROC rather than the PRC.
CHENG LI-WUN’S POINTED SPEECH
KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun’s (鄭麗文) comments were more sophisticated. She called on Taiwan, Kinmen, Matsu and Penghu to unite under the ROC constitution, reiterated her call for negotiating peace with China and supported a concept popular in some pan-blue circles of using Kinmen as a starting point for peace with China. The theory being that the physical proximity and historical ties with Fujian make it an ideal place to start.
She put the blame on the president entirely for recent constitutional crises, is highly debatable. She also attacked him for having sworn an oath to the ROC constitution, and chastised him: “Don’t say one thing and do another, and don’t try to distort the spirit of the ROC Constitution through the two-state theory.”
In other words, she rejects treating Taiwan and China as two separate countries and instead places both sides within a one-China ROC framework.
LU SHIOW-YEN’S FIERY SPEECH
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) commemorated 823 with a fire-and-brimstone speech that was clearly directed at the pan-blue base. Formerly, when she was a lawmaker, she was deeper blue, but in recent years as mayor has carefully cultivated a more moderate image.
On the softer side of her speech, she spoke about the sacrifices soldiers must make to defend the nation, including by her own father, and her direct experience growing up in a military dependents village.
The rest of the speech was more fiery, and she kept repeating two themes. She said: “Because of their [DPP leaders] ideology, because of their hatred, their goal is to make the Republic of China disappear. Some people are promoting Taiwan independence, putting our country at risk of war and are willing to destroy peace at all costs.”
She added: “We have only one goal: to protect the Republic of China and safeguard peace. We absolutely must win in 2026 and 2028.”
Typically, Lu delivers serious speeches in a calm but resolute tone. This was anything but.
Until recently, she was the frontrunner to be the KMT 2028 presidential candidate, but has been sliding in the polls. She may be pivoting back towards the base to shore up support in the party as she gears up for a run.
Donovan’s Deep Dives is a regular column by Courtney Donovan Smith (石東文) who writes in-depth analysis on everything about Taiwan’s political scene and geopolitics. Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

Ministry maximizing defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:05 UTC
01:47:05 KST

The military is reviewing budget execution trends and postponing non-urgent projects to maximize defense spending, the Ministry of National Defense said yesterday as it submitted its budget for next year and other defense documents to the legislature.
The ministry said China’s “gray zone” harassment of Taiwan has intensified while its military capabilities continue to expand rapidly. The assessment was included in its “Five-Year Force Buildup and Administration Plan Report” (五年兵力整建及施政計畫報告), submitted alongside the defense budget for this year and the “2026 China Military Power Report” (中共軍力報告書).
China continues joint combat-readiness patrols, military exercises and China Coast Guard operations, while using maritime militia forces, legal and psychological warfare, and economic coercion. These activities seek to treat the Taiwan Strait as internal waters and strengthen military deterrence against Taiwan, while improving Beijing’s ability to transition from training to combat, the ministry said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Web site of National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology
The ministry’s domestic priorities include new rifles, night-vision optics, portable counter-drone systems, wheeled combat vehicles and armored fighting vehicles (AFVs).
The military is upgrading submarines and testing the domestically built Hai Kun (海鯤), while developing rescue and replenishment vessels, drones and uncrewed boats.
It is to procure the Strong Bow (強弓) medium-range anti-tactical ballistic missile system and build a multilayered air-defense network under the “Taiwan Shield” (T-Dome) framework. Other priorities include the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK), upgraded air-combat training systems, digitized command and communications networks, and an islandwide fiber-optic backup network.
US procurement priorities include M109A7 self-propelled howitzers and HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems. The military will continue acquiring Altius 600M and Switchblade 300 systems, and add Altius 600ISR and 700M attack drones.
The army has budgeted NT$57.07 billion (US$1.8 billion) from next year to 2033 for 178 domestically developed Cheetah (獵豹) AFVs, armed with 105mm cannons. The D3 prototype has passed evaluation, with procurement to begin next year. The vehicles will have a maximum speed of 100kph, a range of 500km and the ability to fire while moving.
The army is also to spend NT$10.7 billion from next year to 2032 on 4,647 light tactical off-road vehicles. Another NT$79.54 billion from next year to 2034 is budgeted to replace aging CM21 armored personnel carriers with 410 wheeled combat and command vehicles.
The navy has budgeted NT$18.28 billion from next year to 2032 for a follow-on oil and ammunition replenishment ship. It operates the Panshih (磐石) and Wuyi (武夷), which entered service in 2015 and 1990 respectively, with the Wuyi nearing the end of its service life.
It will also spend NT$21.16 billion from next year to 2034 on two follow-on rescue vessels, as existing ships are more than 80 years old. Another NT$13.85 billion is budgeted for a submarine rescue vessel as the Hai Kun and subsequent domestically built submarines enter service.
The air force has budgeted NT$36.04 billion this year to 2032 for the Strong Bow medium-range anti-tactical ballistic missile system, previously funded through classified allocations.
The system is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 1,000km and will be integrated with lower-tier systems to form a multilayered defense network. Delivery is scheduled to begin in 2028, although the number of systems remains classified.
Developed by the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, the Strong Bow is a mobile interceptor designed to work with Patriot and Sky Bow III (天弓三型), military sources said.
The army has budgeted NT$10.73 billion from next year to 2030 for a second phase of night-vision optics procurement, including 41,000 monocular and 10,778 binocular devices.
The procurement follows concerns over shortages after some service members conducting nighttime drills in Taipei were seen without night-vision gear. The army said shortages could affect wartime guard duties.
The army also plans to spend NT$2 billion from next year to 2031 on 129,759 protective masks and 264,278 filters, saying its T3-75 masks, manufactured in 1986, are no longer adequate against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats.
As new equipment enters service, the military will retire equipment that no longer meets operational requirements and adjust force structures and personnel allocations, the ministry said.
Garrison and reserve forces will also be reorganized based on operational scenarios and mobilization requirements.
Drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the ministry said it would prioritize new weapons, communications and intelligence resilience, ammunition, mobilization and training readiness.
It said it has reviewed previous budget execution in line with Executive Yuan guidelines and will postpone non-urgent projects to direct funds toward the military’s most pressing needs.

The coast guard warned of an increasingly severe situation, as analysts say the increased activity is part of China’s bid to map the region for submarine warfare. Religion is shown in how one acts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:04 UTC
01:47:04 KST

Taiwanese entertainer Tsai Yi-chen (蔡頤榛) — known professionally as “Wu Hsiung” (五熊) — was arrested in Japan for allegedly splashing a liquid on a Buddhist artifact displayed in a temple. Tsai failed to set a good example as a Christian.
The Christian Bible says: “Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” However, freedom is not about causing damage as one sees fit.
Confucius said that “I could follow my heart’s desires without overstepping the bonds.” While acting as one wants might seem like freedom, the key actually lies in not breaking the rules. As one accumulates wisdom, their words and actions naturally conform to societal standards. Whether Tsai wants to serve her god, her faith should not serve as an excuse to cross others’ boundaries.
Christianity has a ritual of anointing, lightly applying oil to the body or to objects as a symbol of purification and blessing. However, is the oil essential for the effectiveness in practice? If so, is there still any freedom in this faith, or is it instead trapped by the oil?
The Christian god is supposed to be omnipotent, and yet he chooses not to force people to love him? Jesus did not employ violence or coercion when interacting with people of different religions. If someone’s faith fosters a sense of superiority, they lose the ability to love everyone else. Do some Christians really know what they believe in?
Much of the Bible’s centuries of writings have been interpreted in different ways. An oft-cited passage is: “‘I have the right to do anything,’ you say — but not everything is beneficial; ‘I have the right to do anything’ — but not everything is constructive.” No matter what you believe in, one should have the ability to know what is beneficial or constructive.
If your wisdom is limited, you should first learn not to harm or obstruct others.

Health ministry expands health subsidy categories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:00 UTC
01:47:00 KST

The Ministry of Health and Welfare (MOHW) yesterday announced several health policies that take effect today, including increased subsidies for in vitro fertilization (IVF), inclusion of more therapies under National Health Insurance (NHI) coverage, and expanded eligibility for a children’s dental fluoride treatment subsidy.
The Health Promotion Administration said the subsidies for the second and third courses of IVF treatment for women under 40 years old would be increased from NT$100,000 to NT$150,000 (US$3,158 to US$4,737); and increased from NT$80,000 to NT$130,000 for women aged 40 to 45.
About 20,000 people receive IVF subsidies each year, and about 5,000 people are estimated to be eligible for receiving the increased subsidy each year, it said.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
The NHI Administration (NHIA) said it has revised the NHI coverage criteria for lipid-lowering drugs to align with clinical treatment consensus, added two types of therapies for rare diseases and 20 other treatment items under NHI coverage, and adjusted the NHI payment standards for some medical procedures.
Lipid-lowering drugs, including statins, ezetimibe and combination drugs containing both, would be included into NHI coverage, in line with the latest clinical treatment guidelines revised last year, it said.
The initiative aims to allow people with hyperlipidemia to receive timely and appropriate medication, reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases, the agency said, adding that it is estimated to benefit about 998,000 to 1.11 million patients from the first to fifth year, at an estimated cost of about NT$2.28 billion.
Regarding therapies for rare diseases, drugs containing iptacopan, an oral treatment for adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH), and drugs containing maralixibat chloride, oral solution and tablets used to treat severe itching (cholestatic pruritus) caused by Alagille syndrome (ALGS) in people aged one year or older, would be included for NHI coverage, it said.
Iptacopan has been included in insurance coverage for adult patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). As an oral medication, iptacopan offers clinical convenience, providing PNH patients with more treatment options and helping to enhance treatment accessibility and care quality. It could help about 30 people, with a projected pharmaceutical expenditure of about NT$183 million.
In response to clinical demands, 20 medical procedures, including peripheral atherectomies for treating people with peripheral artery disease, have been added to NHI coverage, the NHIA said, adding that about 11,000 people should benefit from the inclusion.
NHI payments to healthcare providers for operating procedures in pediatric and obstetrics departments have been increased, as well as inpatient nursing services, to address the issue of healthcare provider shortages in certain departments, it said.
The MOHW Department of Oral Health said eligibility for children’s dental fluoride treatment subsidy would be expanded “from birth to until Aug. 31 of the year the child enters elementary school.”
Eligible children can receive the subsidy once every six months when they see a registered dentist for the service before entering elementary school, and children with disabilities, from low-income households, who live in remote areas, outlying islands or indigenous communities, or who are younger than 12 years old, can receive the subsidy once every three months, it said.
The expanded eligibility is expected to benefit about 130,000 people per year, the department said.
Tooth decay in primary teeth among five-year-old children has been reduced from 65.4 percent in 2018 to 46.3 percent in 2024, and the average number of decayed, missing and filled teeth among 12-year-old children has dropped from 3.31 in 2000 to 2.01 in 2020, it said.

Nvidia to invest US$3.5 billion in MediaTek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:59 UTC
01:46:59 KST

Nvidia Corp is investing US$3.5 billion into MediaTek Inc (聯發科), deepening collaboration with the Taiwanese chip designer at a time when it’s working to persuade more companies to build chips that plug into its dominant data center ecosystem.
Nvidia will buy bonds convertible into MediaTek shares, the companies said in a joint statement yesterday.
The investment broadens a partnership between the two chip designers that will see MediaTek using NVLink Fusion and the newly announced NVHBM technology as part of an Nvidia tech suite to help components communicate more seamlessly in data centers. The Taiwanese company is trying to challenge Broadcom Inc and Marvell Technology Inc by helping owners of data centers create their own components.
Photo: CNA
For Nvidia, the new agreement is the latest effort to ensure the future of artificial intelligence (AI) is built around its hardware platform and standards.
The US chip giant has been building data center interconnect systems like NVLink Fusion and partnering with the likes of MediaTek to ensure it maintains a central role in the entire hardware chain, not just with its class-leading AI accelerators.
The MediaTek agreement follows a similar announcement by Amazon.com Inc, which agreed to deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia components. Critically, Amazon also pledged to use Nvidia’s connection technology with its in-house chips.
Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), who was born in Taiwan, is tightening ties with a company working to reduce its reliance on the smartphone market. MediaTek earlier this year secured a partnership with Alphabet Inc’s Google, and is gaining credibility as a design partner to major tech firms that are seeking to build their own AI chips. That momentum has led the chipmaker’s market value to roughly triple in recent months.
The agreements with MediaTek and Amazon give Nvidia the opportunity to retain its central role in the build-out of AI data centers even when companies are deploying chips designed to replace its main offerings. The deal is yet another example of Nvidia’s leadership investing in customers, rivals and other companies involved in the AI industry. Concern about the seemingly circular nature of those investments has percolated in investor circles, though Nvidia has strongly disputed the idea it’s creating false demand.
MediaTek already works with Nvidia on the US chipmaker’s nascent effort to get into the laptop industry. The Taiwanese company is helping with Nvidia’s RTX Spark product for that market.
MediaTek has also signaled that it plans to hire aggressively to better capture business opportunities from the AI boom. Forecasting AI chip revenue of about US$2 billion this year, the company has set the goal of securing as much as 15 percent of an US$80 billion segment of the data center market next year.
