China Focus: Modern tech helps prevent geological risks in China's Three Gorges region
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
17:07:12 CST
18:07:12 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows a drone collecting image data of a collapsed area in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)
WUHAN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Integrated modern technology is helping geologists "tame" the treacherous rock formations of the mountainous Three Gorges Reservoir region, bolstering efforts to prevent and mitigate geological disasters.
Thanks to years of efforts in field investigation and technological exploration, the Wuhan Center of China Geological Survey has established interrelated means to fend off geological disasters in this region, according to Li Ming, a senior engineer at the center.
These technological means include a multi-dimensional rock monitoring system, an integrated information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, as well as a series of ecological restoration techniques for dangerous rock masses.
The Three Gorges project is a vast multi-functional water-control system on the Yangtze River, China's longest waterway.
The Three Gorges Reservoir region is characterized by steep mountains, precipitous slopes, and complex rock formations, making it one of the areas in China most prone to geological disasters. So far, more than 3,000 potential hazard sites have been identified.
To cope with the potential hazards, the center has established an information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, integrating multi-source data including geological base maps, disaster registries and monitoring and early-warning information, Li said.
He noted that one deep rock crevice in Zigui County, central China's Hubei Province, extends more than 110 meters deep. Over 50 crevices cut through the mountain massif, forming an unstable rock body with a total volume exceeding 3 million cubic meters.
The engineer further explained that the upper section of the dangerous rocks consists of hard rock, while its lower section comprises relatively soft coal-bearing strata. The unstable rock body sits right next to the main navigation channel of the Yangtze River.
"Should it collapse and plunge into the river, the surge wave generated instantaneously would pose a severe threat to the safety of passing vessels," Li said, adding this dangerous rock mass is currently stable thanks to multiple engineering measures.
Various devices installed on the cliff face are providing round-the-clock precise monitoring of subtle deformations in the rock mass, summarizing data once every hour and uploading it in real time for monitoring and early warning, Li said.
To address the challenge of dangerous rock masses in the reservoir area, the center has developed a specialized technology by fixing such rock masses with lightweight anchor cable and explored an ecological restoration technique for rock crevices using microorganisms combined with fiber filling, according to Dai Zhenwei, who takes charge of the center's geological disaster monitoring and early warning.
The technological explorations are similar to putting a "safety belt" on the unstable rocks. They provide a new approach to solving the challenge of poor durability of traditional protective structures in water-rich environments, Dai said.
In the meantime, drones and diverse satellite monitoring devices have been put into service to conduct the round-the-clock monitoring works to assess the stability conditions affected by the fluctuations in reservoir water levels, according to Huang Jue, a senior engineer at the Wuhan center.
Huang explained that traditional manual inspections normally take a long period of time and costs are high. The drones can fly close to steep cliffs, dangerous rocks and other areas that are difficult for people to reach.
"Moreover, drones can take off immediately when traffic is disrupted after disasters occur and provide first-hand information for rescue decision-making in a timely manner," he added. ■

This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows an unstable rock body in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)

Ukraine seeks more drones and air defence from Latvia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:00:37 BST
18:00:37 KST

Ukraine has asked Latvia to support the rapid delivery of air defence equipment, unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones and additional strike capabilities as Kyiv sets out its current battlefield priorities, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Mykhailo Drapatyi discussed the requirements during a meeting with Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence announced on 29 August.
The Ukrainian side identified four areas as priorities: unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones, what the ministry described as “middle-strike capabilities”, and air defence assets. Khmara also stressed the need for equipment identified as urgent to reach Ukrainian forces as quickly as possible, making delivery times part of the discussions alongside the type of equipment being sought.
Fibre-optic-controlled drones have taken on a growing battlefield role because the control link is carried through a physical fibre rather than relying on a conventional radio connection. The approach can allow operators to retain control in environments where radio-frequency links are heavily disrupted, although the systems bring their own operational limitations.
Unmanned ground vehicles have similarly been employed for an expanding range of battlefield tasks, including logistics and other activities in areas where exposing personnel carries additional risk. Ukraine has increasingly sought to expand the use of uncrewed systems across land, air and maritime operations.
Air defence remains another continuing requirement for Kyiv as Russian forces employ combinations of missiles and uncrewed attack aircraft against targets across Ukraine. The Ukrainian ministry did not identify particular air defence systems being requested from Latvia in its account of the meeting.
Latvia, meanwhile, intends to continue providing security assistance to Ukraine worth at least 0.25% of its gross domestic product each year. Kyiv said it is also looking to Riga to work with other governments and through multinational initiatives to generate further military assistance. The two defence delegations discussed areas beyond the immediate supply of equipment, including rehabilitation for Ukrainian military personnel, training and the development of cyber capabilities.
Ukraine also offered to share operational experience with Latvia. According to the ministry, this could include lessons from multi-domain operations, territorial defence and the construction and development of modern fortifications.
Latvia has been among the NATO members providing sustained military assistance to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Russia shows off new laser weapon against drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:59:51 UTC
17:59:51 KST

- A Russian military blogger published footage claiming a Russian laser weapon system has destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones near strategic sites in southwestern Russia.
- The claims, including a planned second-generation system for intercepting aircraft and cruise missiles, have not been independently verified.
Footage circulating in Russian pro-military channels this week shows what is claimed to be a Russian laser weapon system engaging aerial drones, according to a Russian military blogger who described the video as an “exclusive.”
The blogger’s post claimed several such systems are now protecting strategic sites in southwestern Russia and that the laser complexes have destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones. The claim has not been independently verified, and no Russian government or military agency has confirmed the figures.
“Only we have sensational footage of the destruction of Ukrainian drones in the sky by a combat Russian laser complex,” the blogger wrote. “Several of these laser installations now cover our strategic facilities in the southwest of the country.”
Based on the footage, the system appears to be a containerized platform combining a laser weapon, a targeting and guidance system, and a command post where an operator controls the unit. The system reportedly includes its own detection setup for tracking aerial threats, combining radar and visual sensors, according to the footage.
The blogger’s post also claimed developers are preparing a second-generation version of the system, intended to intercept faster targets, including tactical aircraft and cruise missiles.
“I am not inclined to overestimate this innovative type of weapon based on ‘new physical principles,’ but combined with traditional air defense systems, a combat laser will definitely be useful for protecting the country from air raids,” the blogger wrote. “It is also gratifying that we not only have such combat ‘purple beams,’ but they have also proven their effectiveness. Now these ‘Jedi swords’ need to be developed and constantly improved. Such is the path.”
Directed energy weapons for counter-drone use have drawn increasing interest from multiple militaries in recent years, though publicly verified operational combat use against drone swarms remains limited across all countries developing the technology. Laser weapons face documented limitations including reduced effectiveness in poor weather, atmospheric interference over longer ranges, and thermal management requirements for sustained operation.
The claims made in the Russian footage, including the number of drones destroyed, the specific location of the systems, and the timeline for a second-generation variant, have not been corroborated by independent sources or confirmed by official Russian military statements.

Hong Kong retail sales rise 4.5% in July, marking 15th straight month of growth

Hong Kong retail sales rise 4.5% in July, marking 15th straight month of growth
Retail sales value for the month reaches HK$31 billion, with momentum remaining ‘resilient’
Hong Kong’s retail sector recorded growth for a 15th consecutive month in July, with the government reporting a 4.5 per cent increase year on year, although the pace of expansion slowed amid adverse weather and continued outbound travel by residents.
Retail sales value for the month reached HK$31 billion (US$4 billion), while sales in the first seven months of the year grew by 8.9 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Monday.
A government spokesman said retail sales growth momentum remained resilient in July, with growth broadly steady from the previous month.
“Looking ahead, continued economic expansion, rising household incomes, and stable labour market conditions should bolster consumer sentiment,” he said.
“A series of coming mega-events is also expected to sustain growth in visitor arrivals, providing further support to retail businesses.”
Sales of jewellery, watches and clocks, and valuable gifts recorded the strongest increase in July, rising by 19.7 per cent year on year, followed by electrical goods and other consumer durables at 11.5 per cent. Other consumer goods not elsewhere classified also grew 10.5 per cent.

Study backs walking blood banks to save wounded troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:36:34 UTC
17:36:34 KST

- Studies cited in the review found fresh whole blood transfusion increased combat casualty survival by up to fivefold compared with component blood therapy.
- The review calls for military units to deploy walking blood banks, prescreened donor networks that supply fresh whole blood near the point of injury during active combat.
Fresh whole blood transfusion can increase combat casualty survival by up to fivefold compared with standard component blood therapy, according to studies cited in a new medical review by Jennifer M. Gurney, a finding that argues for expanding “walking blood banks,” the military’s system for collecting blood directly from screened soldiers near the point of injury during active combat.
The review traces a century of battlefield transfusion history and cites a 2022 study of more than 1,100 combat casualties, co-authored by Gurney, that found a fivefold increase in survival among patients who received warm fresh whole blood, meaning blood transfused shortly after collection from a living donor, compared with those who received only component therapy, blood separated into red cells, plasma and platelets and transfused as separate products. An earlier 2009 study of more than 350 combat casualties similarly found that fresh whole blood was associated with higher survival than component therapy alone.
A walking blood bank works by prescreening soldiers in a unit for blood type and infectious disease risk before deployment, so that when a casualty needs blood urgently, screened donors nearby can be called on to give blood that is transfused within minutes to hours, rather than relying solely on stored blood products shipped from the rear. The review describes this as a “layered approach,” in which fresh whole blood from walking blood banks supplements, rather than replaces, standard blood products already supplied through the military’s blood program.
Hemorrhage remains the leading cause of death from survivable injuries in both military and civilian trauma care, according to the review. A separate 2017 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that combat casualties transfused within 36 minutes of injury had significantly higher survival rates than those transfused later, reinforcing the case for blood delivered as close to the point of injury as possible.
The review traces how this lesson has been learned and lost repeatedly across a century of American wars. By the end of World War I, whole blood transfusion was practiced widely at American military hospitals, with more than 10,000 transfusions performed in 1918 alone. That capability was not carried into World War II, when the U.S. entered the conflict without an established blood banking system. Early in the war, mobile “bleeding teams” collected fresh whole blood from donors near the front, and by March 1945 the U.S. was shipping up to 62,000 units of whole blood per month to the European and Pacific theaters.
The pattern repeated after the war. The Korean War began without an operational military blood program, and the first blood shipments did not arrive until more than two months into the conflict, a delay the review links to preventable deaths among U.S. servicemembers. Whole blood use continued through the Vietnam War, with roughly 600,000 units transfused to more than 330,000 American and allied casualties between 1965 and 1971, before the military shifted toward component therapy in the war’s later years, a change the review attributes to logistics and cost rather than clinical evidence.
The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan prompted the most recent reassessment. The military reintroduced warm fresh whole blood through walking blood banks in 2002, and in 2017 reintroduced low-titer group O whole blood, a universal blood type that can be given to any patient regardless of their own blood type. Low-titer group O whole blood had been recognized as lifesaving as early as World War I but disappeared from military use after Vietnam and was not reintroduced into the U.S. military system until 2016.
Fresh whole blood remains restricted to military use and is not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for routine civilian care, primarily because it cannot undergo the same infectious disease screening required for standard banked blood before transfusion. The review calls for walking blood bank capability to become a standing practice within military units rather than a last resort, arguing that the survival benefit demonstrated in combat casualty data justifies training and rehearsing the capability before it is needed, not after.
Ukraine has provided a live case study of these principles under active combat conditions. A May 2026 study published in Critical Care, drawing on clinical experience at Ukrainian Role 1 and Role 2 battlefield facilities, found that Ukrainian medical teams have at times administered low-titer group O whole blood without full verification of antibody titers under combat pressure, identifying roughly 30 cases between 2024 and 2026 of mixed-field agglutination, a complication linked to massive transfusion of unverified “universal” donor blood. Gurney was a co-author of a separate 2024 paper cited in that Ukrainian study, arguing that type-specific whole blood still has a role in severe trauma care even as low-titer group O blood has become the dominant battlefield product. Separately, U.S. military medical instructors have trained Ukrainian healthcare workers in emergency fresh whole blood transfusion techniques since early in the war, adapting curricula used by U.S. special operations units for Ukrainian frontline conditions, according to a 2024 paper published in Military Medicine.
The review notes that direct clinical comparisons between fresh whole blood and low-titer group O whole blood remain absent from the published academic literature, and calls for further trials to determine which product benefits which patients under which battlefield conditions.

UN committee says countries must consider reparations for slave trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:35:37 UTC
17:35:37 KST

UN committee says countries must consider reparations for slave trade
GENEVA, Aug 31 - A U.N. committee said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other measures to address the enduring legacy of racial discrimination it says persists today.
Guidance published on Monday by the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination stated that the obligations arise from a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.
The committee described the approach as a "paradigm shift" away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations claims.
"States Parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all aspects of remedies," said the U.N. document, which may be cited in courtrooms.
At least 12.5 million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination called the largest forced displacement in history.
Calls for reparations - ranging from official apologies to financial compensation - have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The European Union and Britain abstained from a U.N. resolution on slavery in March.
Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade at the time - the so-called intertemporality principle.
But the U.N. document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.
"Irrespective of the legal characterization of the original historical acts, States Parties remain bound by their present obligations under the Convention to address structural inequalities," the U.N. document states.
Financial compensation alone is not sufficient, it adds, urging "transformative" measures including opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.
Pela Boker-Wilson, a committee expert from Liberia who helped draft the document, said she expects states to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.
"We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action," she told Reuters. "We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten." REUTERS

UN committee presents legal case for broad slavery reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

UN committee presents legal case for broad slavery reparations
GENEVA – Countries are legally obliged to provide broad reparations for harms resulting from both direct and indirect involvement in the transatlantic African slave trade, a United Nations committee said on Aug 31.
Issuing a fresh interpretation of an important international rights treaty, the UN watchdog said the accord obliges countries to work to redress the harms caused by slavery and the continuing consequences.
“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for people of African descent, covering all aspects of remedies,” the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) said in its findings, presented in a document entitled General Recommendation-40.
It stressed that reparatory justice combined “a wide range of measures conceived as monetary, non-monetary and structural”.
The document, which was approved last week but published only on Aug 31, is expected to provide a powerful new tool supporting reparations claims.
This is “a watershed moment”, committee member Pela Boker-Wilson told AFP.
The CERD panel is composed of 18 independent rights experts.
Tasked with monitoring implementation of the 1969 International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, it provided a new interpretation of the treaty’s obligations.
‘Paradigm shift’
The convention counts 182 countries as parties, including the US, Britain, France, Portugal and other nations that were heavily involved in the transatlantic slave trade, which from the 16th to 19th century saw millions of African men, women and children shipped to the Americas to work in brutal – and often deadly – conditions.
In many of those same countries, black people continue to face discrimination and poverty today.
“Confronting historical injustice cannot be separated from the fight against present-day racial discrimination,” Boker-Wilson said.
The Liberian human rights lawyer maintained that the committee’s finding brought about “a paradigm shift” in the framing of reparatory justice from a simple historical responsibility to a present-day legal obligation.
It clarifies that countries are required to take “active measures that are geared towards restoring the dignity, the justice, and equality that people of African descent deserve”.
While the CERD’s findings are not legally-binding, Boker-Wilson stressed that they carry “significant authoritative weight”, and could be used by officials to inform judicial review, by courts as an interpretative tool, as well as to support litigation.
The fresh analysis comes after the UN General Assembly in March adopted a landmark resolution recognising the transatlantic slave trade as “the gravest crime against humanity”, despite opposition from the US and some European countries.
Boker-Wilson said the US and other countries should “welcome” the new findings, noting that the last review of US adherence to the convention on discrimination, in 2022, had found issues with racial profiling and disparities in the criminal justice system.
‘Eliminate structural racism’
While the campaign around reparatory justice has been heavily focused on the US, Boker-Wilson stressed that “it’s a global initiative”.
The transatlantic slave trade “distorted global economic relations by distributing unjustly accumulated wealth across societies and borders, creating shared responsibility for its enduring effects”, the document points out.
Beyond monetary compensation, the required reparations encompass everything from restitution to rehabilitation and memorialisation.
And it pointed to an educational obligation “to investigate and disclose the full truth about transatlantic chattel slavery”. AFP

Taiwan identifies sovereign AI, satellite communications as key technology priorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:32:46 UTC
17:32:46 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-jing (林宜敬) on Monday identified sovereign artificial intelligence and low-Earth orbit satellite communications as two capabilities Taiwan needs to strengthen its technological sovereignty and resilience.
Speaking at the 2026 Technology Sovereignty Summit, Lin said technological sovereignty does not mean developing every technology domestically. Instead, Taiwan must maintain control over capabilities critical to its national autonomy and resilience, per UDN.
Wang Wei-ching (王維菁), chair of the Taiwan Communications Society, said technological sovereignty should not be confused with technological isolation or a rejection of global connectivity. Taiwan should remain open to international cooperation while retaining the ability to make independent decisions and respond to risks, she said.
Wang called for greater transparency, accountability, and fair competition in technology governance. She also warned that local culture should not be sacrificed in pursuit of efficiency.
Lin said sovereign AI has two important implications for Taiwan. AI language models must understand Taiwan's languages, social context, and democratic values rather than rely entirely on foreign data and value systems. Taiwan also needs sufficient domestic computing capacity so that important AI models can operate on infrastructure located in Taiwan and subject to Taiwanese law.
Lin said the Ministry of Digital Affairs is promoting the Taiwan Sovereign AI Training Corps and gradually making government resources available to Taiwanese and international research teams. The initiative is intended to help AI models better understand Taiwan's language, culture, and social context.
Low-Earth orbit satellite communications are another important component of Taiwan's technological resilience, Lin said. Taiwan's extensive 4G and 5G coverage means civilian demand for satellite communications remains limited.
However, alternative communications infrastructure could be crucial during war, gray-zone activity, or disruptions to submarine cables and other infrastructure. Low-Earth orbit satellites could provide backup connectivity and reduce Taiwan's dependence on any single communications system, Lin said.

American C-130 lands on Ramstein taxiway
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:30:56 BST
17:30:56 KST

A US Air Force C-130J Super Hercules has landed on a taxiway at Ramstein Air Base in Germany, marking the first time an aircraft has landed at the installation without using one of its runways, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The landing was carried out on 18 August by an aircrew from the 37th Airlift Squadron during a wing exercise known as Knight LZ. According to the US Air Force, the exercise was intended to test an alternative method of recovering aircraft if Ramstein’s normal runways were unavailable.
The C-130J used an existing taxiway for the landing, allowing aircrew and personnel on the ground to practise operating from a part of the airfield not normally used for aircraft arrivals.
Colonel Matthew Wunderlich, commander of the 86th Operations Group, said: “This capability is more than just landing on a taxiway. It demonstrates our ability to adapt, to work together, and continue generating airpower when conditions change.”
He added: “This creativity and resiliency is essential to maintaining our readiness, increasing strategic options, and fulfilling the mission.”
Several units at Ramstein supported the exercise, including the 86th Security Forces Squadron, 86th Operations Support Squadron, 37th Airlift Squadron and 721st Aerial Port Squadron. The activity required coordination between the aircrew and personnel responsible for airfield operations, security and ground support before the aircraft could conduct the unconventional landing.
Captain Ty Millsap, 86th Operations Support Squadron Chief of Wing Tactics, said: “Exercises like this allow our aircrew and support teams to build the experience and confidence needed to operate in a contingency environment.”
He continued: “It takes coordination across the installation to safely execute an exercise like this, and that coordination is what makes us ready for the unexpected.”
Ramstein Air Base is one of the United States’ largest military aviation installations in Europe and supports airlift, logistics and command activity for US forces operating across the continent and further afield. The 37th Airlift Squadron operates the C-130J from Ramstein as part of the 86th Airlift Wing. The aircraft is used for tactical airlift missions involving personnel and cargo and can operate from shorter and less developed airfields than larger strategic transport aircraft.
The C-130J is the current production version of the Hercules family and incorporates updated engines, avionics and flight systems compared with earlier models. The type is routinely used by the US Air Force for tactical transport missions and can move troops, equipment and supplies into locations where larger aircraft cannot operate. The Knight LZ exercise focused specifically on Ramstein’s ability to continue aircraft operations if its normal runway infrastructure could not be used.
The 18 August flight was the first recorded aircraft landing on a taxiway at the base, according to the 86th Airlift Wing. Following the landing, the participating units used the exercise to validate the procedures required to coordinate airfield access, aircraft movements and support activity around the alternative landing area.

Hong Kong and Singapore property shrug off fund tax breaks
Unknown

Hong Kong and Singapore property shrug off fund tax breaks
While the two cities compete on wealth management incentives to draw talent and capital, the spillover into office and residential real estate remains negligible
Nicholas Spiro is a partner at Lauressa Advisory, a specialist London-based real estate and macroeconomic advisory firm.
The long-standing rivalry between Asia’s two leading financial centres is heating up. As Hong Kong and Singapore compete harder for investment talent, tax incentives for fund managers have emerged as the new battleground.
A government bill working its way through Hong Kong’s Legislative Council would result in sweeping changes to tax rules on carried interest. The legislation, which is expected to be approved later this year, would offer preferential tax treatment to a wider range of alternative investment groups.
The move by Hong Kong prompted a swift response from Singapore. On August 19, Singapore’s central bank announced a package of measures designed to enhance the appeal of the asset management industry, including a proposal that would exempt a share of profits made by fund managers when they deliver strong returns for investors in qualifying funds.
Wall Street banks are already assessing the broader implications of the reforms. In a report on July 31, Citigroup said the changes to Hong Kong’s preferential tax regime were “a structural catalyst for capital and talent inflows into [Hong Kong]” that would support demand in the real estate market.
If 3 per cent of fund managers from mainland China and Singapore relocated to Hong Kong, creating 1,500 new asset management positions, the grade A office market in Central, Admiralty and West Kowloon would benefit from 150,000 sq ft of additional take-up. In the housing market, demand for high-end homes would increase by 2 per cent if the relocations occurred within a year, Citigroup said.
That said, tax competition is not a key determinant of the performance of Hong Kong’s real estate market. “The read-across to the property market is not that clear,” said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL in Hong Kong. The rivalry between Hong Kong and Singapore has had little bearing on the fundamentals of both cities’ property sectors.

Yin became emotional after securing the victory on the 18th green. "It's just been so long since my last win," Yin said. "I know I work hard and also my team, my mom is here. Just everything comes together."
The victory ended a lengthy drought for Yin, who had gone 34 LPGA Tour starts without a win since her breakthrough three-win season in 2024. She had finished runner-up four times during that stretch.
"At that time [in 2024] I was feeling like I'm one of the best players out there," Yin said. "But I didn't win last year, and that made me feel like, 'Am I still one of the best?' I keep questioning myself. I think I've learned a lot this year. I read an article the other day that says some people, their life starts at 40. Some people, their life starts at 24. But life really starts when you don't live in other people's comments, don't live in other people's expectations. That's when your life starts. I get tears in my eyes even when I think about it. I'm just glad I saw that article."
Yin will next represent China to compete at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games in September before returning to Shanghai for the Buick LPGA tournament. ■

BISHKEK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- "See that mountain? That's garbage. The smell is unbearable," local resident Aktan Akylbekov told Xinhua. "But now things are gradually changing for the better."
In December last year, a waste-to-energy plant, built by China's Hunan Junxin Environmental Protection Co., Ltd., was officially commissioned at the foot of Bishkek's "garbage mountain."
Akylbekov, 25, works there as a centralized control operator. From the control room, he monitors operations and flue gas emissions in real time. "We fully comply with environmental standards," he assured.
He said it was a great honor to work with his Chinese colleagues, who built the plant and are now teaching local workers new technologies. "The plant benefits both countries," he said.
Operations at the plant are carried out in a coordinated and well-organized manner. In the unloading area, trucks deposit municipal waste into containers. Operators in the crane control room use large grabs to feed waste into the chute. The incinerator runs at around 1,000 degrees Celsius, with a rotating grate that mixes the waste to ensure complete combustion. Harmful gases are removed through denitrification, desulfurization, and heavy-metal adsorption before emission.
Project General Director Zhang Jinfang said that the company had introduced technologies for generating electricity through waste incineration. By turning "waste" into "treasure," the plant not only helps address environmental problems but also supplies clean electricity to local residents.
The plant currently processes up to 1,000 tons of waste per day and generates about 146 million kWh of green electricity annually, reducing carbon dioxide emissions by up to 100,000 tons per year.
At the commissioning ceremony in December 2025, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said the plant would address waste recycling, generate electricity, and create jobs.
"The construction of this plant will significantly improve the environmental situation in the capital and will also contribute to providing the population with electricity," the president said.
Akylbekov is especially pleased that the second phase is already underway. Two more similar facilities are also being built in the Central Asian country. ■

====================================================================================================

Delaying children's first use of social media may protect mental health: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:18:03 CST
17:18:03 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Delaying the age at which children first use social media may help protect adolescent mental health, new research from Australia's University of New South Wales (UNSW) suggests.
The study found that those who began using social media at a younger age reported more symptoms of anxiety and depression. Simply having a social media account showed a weaker relationship with those symptoms, according to a UNSW statement released Monday.
The study, conducted among Australian adolescents aged 10 to 15 and one of their parents in the six weeks before Australia's social media ban for under-16s took effect in December 2025, found 70 percent of participants had used social media, while about half already had a social media account. The average age at which they first started using social media was 11.
"What surprised us was that the age children first started using social media appeared to matter more for their mental health than simply whether they had an account," said UNSW Associate Professor Susanne Schweizer, the study's chief investigator.
The study showed that only a quarter of 10-to-15-year-olds said they planned to stop using social media after the ban, while 34 percent intended to use it without an account and 35 percent intended to find a way around the restrictions to continue using their accounts, rather than simply waiting until they turn 16.
The findings suggest that delaying children's first exposure may be a promising policy, particularly if combined with education on healthy digital habits. ■

====================================================================================================

Ukraine reveals new details on Russia’s Zircon missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:14:32 UTC
17:14:32 KST

- Ukraine's Defense Intelligence agency published new details on Russia's 3M22 Zircon missile, identifying it as ballistic rather than the hypersonic cruise missile long described by Russian media.
- The disclosure names 70 companies and key personnel involved in the missile's production, along with foreign-made components used in its manufacture.
For years, Russia has bragged about a missile called the Zircon, calling it an unstoppable hypersonic weapon that flies too fast for any air defense system to catch. Ukrainian intelligence just said that’s not quite the full story.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence agency, known as HUR, published a detailed breakdown of the missile this week, saying the Zircon is actually a ballistic missile, not the hypersonic cruise missile Russian state media has described since the weapon first appeared. The distinction matters because the two types of missiles fly very differently and require different defenses to intercept.
“DIU exposes details of russia’s 3M22 Zircon ballistic missile, including its components, production chain, 70 companies involved, key personnel, and foreign equipment used to manufacture the weapon,” the agency wrote on X.
Even the pictures tell a different story than what’s been shown before. The images DIU released show a missile that looks noticeably different from the renderings that have circulated in media coverage for years, with a distinct nose section and a rear assembly built for steering the missile during flight.
According to the newly disclosed details, the 3M22 is a two-stage ballistic missile, using a solid-fuel booster stage to launch the missile and a separate solid-fuel sustainer stage for the remainder of its flight. The missile carries a 120-kilogram (265-pound) warhead and has a maximum range of up to 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). For navigation and targeting, the missile relies on an inertial autonomous navigation system combined with an active radar homing seeker, designated 3B222.
DIU didn’t stop at just describing the missile. The agency published what amounts to a parts catalog, naming specific manufacturers behind individual components. Some of those parts trace back to VPK NPO Mashinostroyeniya, the Russian defense company that developed the Zircon program in the first place, while a countermeasure system was linked to another Russian defense firm called KNIRTI. DIU is also asking the public to send in any additional information they have about where the missile’s parts come from, hoping to fill in more of the supply chain picture over time.
This isn’t the first time analysts have questioned how the Zircon actually flies. Ukrainian outlet Defense Express had previously suggested the missile likely follows what’s called a quasi-ballistic path rather than sustained hypersonic cruising, a description that lines up more closely with DIU’s new “ballistic missile” label than with the hypersonic cruise missile story that’s dominated headlines.
Whatever you call it, Russia has been firing a lot more of them lately. Ukrainian intelligence estimated Russia had around 40 Zircon missiles in its stockpile back in 2024. That number has reportedly grown to roughly 230. For two years after the missile’s first confirmed use in a February 2024 strike on Kyiv, Russia only fired six of them total. This year alone, Russia has launched around 40, including 15 in July and eight during a single massive combined attack on Kyiv in early June.
The Zircon was originally designed to fire from the 3S14 vertical launch system used on Russian Navy frigates, including the Admiral Gorshkov, and has since been adapted for launch from land. Russia has increasingly fired the missile from the K300P Bastion coastal defense system, a mobile launcher originally built to fire the P-800 Oniks anti-ship missile at ships. Ukrainian forces have targeted Bastion launchers in occupied Crimea specifically to prevent Zircon strikes, including a March 2026 drone strike that destroyed one launcher and triggered an unintended missile launch during the attack.
Part of the reason Zircon strikes are relatively rare comes down to cost. Each missile runs about $5.6 million, according to Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi, citing Russian purchasing records, making it one of the most expensive conventional missiles Russia builds, cheaper only than its Oreshnik missile.

Kenya airport staff strike delays thousands of passengers
NAIROBI, Aug 31 - Flight delays at Kenya's main international airport on Monday affected thousands of travellers as airport workers' go-slow strike action continued into its second day, with the main union saying negotiations were ongoing.
The Kenya Aviation Workers' Union (KAWU) said the strike at the Jomo Kenyatta International Airport was due to a range of grievances, including the inability to conclude a collective bargaining agreement with the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority and lack of cooperation from the Kenya Airports Authority (KAA) and Kenya Airways subsidiary Jambojet.
KAA on Sunday said some flights were experiencing delays without disclosing reasons for the delays. It did not respond to a request for comment on Monday. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority and Jambojet did not respond to requests for comment.
Rwanda's national carrier RwandAir said in an X post on Sunday that it had cancelled two flights as a result of what it said were air traffic control challenges at the airport in Nairobi.
Passengers told Reuters they had spent hours at the airport waiting for news about their flights.
"When I got here, the flight was delayed till 1 a.m. So it was an hour and a half delay, and then there was another delay till 4:30 a.m. And then at about 3 o'clock, I went to the check-in. They told me that the flight's been cancelled," said rabbi Mendel Goldman, who is travelling to a wedding in Florida.
"The earliest flight they can get us is only tomorrow night, so we've got to wait," Goldman said on Monday. "We're going to try and make most of it, but in the meantime, I've been here for 12 hours now, waiting in the airport."
KAWU Secretary General Moss Ndiema said the union and government officials met on Sunday to resolve issues but without success.
"We have agreed to proceed with the engagements tomorrow, as from 11 o'clock in the morning. In the meantime, the strike action is still on," he said in comments broadcast on KTN Television on Sunday. REUTERS

NATO deputy chief visits Dublin for defence talks
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:00:38 BST
17:00:38 KST

NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska is visiting Dublin for two days of engagements, including a public discussion on security issues and an informal meeting of European Union defence ministers, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Shekerinska will appear at the Institute of International and European Affairs in Dublin on 31 August for a one-hour event beginning at 14:30. The discussion will also be livestreamed for online participants.
Her visit runs from 31 August to 1 September and will also include participation in an informal meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council in its Defence Ministers’ format on Tuesday.
The Foreign Affairs Council is the principal forum through which EU member states coordinate foreign, security and defence policy. Meetings in Defence Ministers’ format bring together national defence ministers to discuss issues affecting the Union’s Common Security and Defence Policy, military support initiatives and wider European security.
Ireland is an EU member but is not a member of NATO, retaining a longstanding policy of military neutrality. It nevertheless maintains formal cooperation with the Alliance through NATO’s Partnership for Peace programme, which Ireland joined in 1999, and participates in a range of peace support, training and interoperability activities.
Shekerinska took office as NATO Deputy Secretary General on 2 December 2024. Before joining the Alliance’s senior leadership, she served as North Macedonia’s defence minister from 2017 to 2020 and again from 2020 to 2022. She was the first woman to serve as North Macedonia’s defence minister and became the country’s longest-serving holder of the position since independence. She has also previously served as deputy prime minister. Her IIEA appearance is expected to provide a broader discussion of NATO’s current priorities and the security environment facing Europe, while the following day’s EU meeting will place her alongside defence ministers from across the bloc.
The visit takes place as NATO and the European Union continue to work through overlapping questions of European defence capacity, military readiness and the division of responsibilities between national governments, the EU and the Alliance.
Recent NATO discussions have placed increased emphasis on European members assuming a larger share of conventional defence responsibilities, alongside higher defence expenditure and expanded industrial capacity. Those debates also affect EU states outside NATO, including Ireland, because many questions around infrastructure protection, resilience, maritime security and military mobility extend beyond formal Alliance membership.

What do China’s new housing presale rules mean for real estate developers?

What do China’s new housing presale rules mean for real estate developers?
Beijing aims to restore buyer confidence, trading near-term financial pain for some developers for long-term market stability, analysts say
With China rolling out a stronger-than-expected package of measures to transition the housing market away from a presales model, analysts said the shift is a double-edged sword for real estate developers: tighter regulations are poised to squeeze cash inflows, even as the reforms aim to stimulate sales and stabilise prices over time.
“From structural topping out through practical completion, residential projects take six to 12 months, depending on building height,” said a private developer on condition of anonymity, citing the sensitivity of the matter. “This will substantially delay fund disbursements and weigh heavily on our cash flow.”
Official data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed funds secured by property developers totalled 4.57 trillion yuan (US$679.98 billion) in the January-July period. Deposits and advance receipts and mortgage proceeds stood at 2.04 trillion yuan, accounting for 44.6 per cent of the total funding pool. The share surpassed the 36.1 per cent coming from self-raised funds.
“The PBOC’s new rules serve as a major near-term negative catalyst for developers across the country,” said Fang Chengqi, chief analyst at Zhejiang province-based Caitong Securities, who estimated that developers’ average levered return on investment could drop by about 60 per cent.
“Going forward, the market will increasingly be dominated by large-scale central and local government-owned developers with low leverage and solid financing access. Small regional players carrying very low leverage will also survive. Aggressive mid-tier private developers – such as Sichuan-based Bontop Group – are likely to fall by the wayside,” Fang noted.

homo faber 2026 brings 500 craft artists to venice in es devlin’s ‘island of light’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:45:15 UTC
16:45:15 KST

es devlin turns homo faber 2026 into ‘an island of light’ in venice
Homo Faber returns to Venice from September 1st–30th, 2026, with its fourth edition, titled An Island of Light. Taking place across Fondazione Giorgio Cini on San Giorgio Maggiore, the biennial brings together more than 500 artisans from over 70 countries. Es Devlin, serving as artistic director, develops the exhibition as a sequence of immersive installations that respond directly to the island, its architecture, gardens, and relationship with the surrounding lagoon. Across 15 installations, light becomes a recurring material. Water reflects the Palladian architecture, mirrors alter the scale of objects and spaces, and projections, movement, and sound introduce another layer to the experience of craft.
The title An Island of Light begins with Devlin’s own experience of arriving in Venice and seeing San Giorgio from above. ‘When I look at an aerial view of this place, if I’m lucky enough to have a clear day when I’m landing, I can see this island like an object, like a jewel, like a fragile egg, like something I might pick up and hold very carefully so I don’t break it.’ she shares during the opening of Homo Faber 2026, where designboom was present. ‘And yet, when I’m on the island, I have a very different sensation. I feel held by the stone, by the architecture, by the garden, by the cypresses. They call this island the lungs of Venice. I want you to hold the taste of the word ”light” and the word ”island” while you walk through the trees and through the architecture.’
The opening follows our earlier conversation with Alberto Cavalli, executive director of the Michelangelo Foundation, who spoke with us ahead of this year’s biennial about Homo Faber’s wider effort to bring the handmade object and the people behind it back into focus. An Island of Light now gives that idea a physical form, using Devlin’s installations to move attention beyond the finished object and toward the materials, tools, hands, and knowledge involved in its making.
A Great Turning | all images by Giulio Ghirardi © Michelangelo Foundation, unless stated otherwise
from the artisan’s studio to an index of hands
The exhibition opens with A Language of Hands, an installation conceived as an artisan’s studio. Es Devlin introduces the visitor to the atmosphere of making. Multimedia projections and sound evoke a workshop after its inhabitants have left, placing the emphasis on the people and gestures behind the work. ‘The first thing you encounter is a studio, an atelier, and I hope you will feel like you’ve walked in just as 500 artisans have finished their work for the day. As any of you who have spent time in an artisan studio or an artist’s studio know, I’ve never seen anyone not smile when they walk into mine. I think you feel vividly happy when you’re surrounded by the quality of time passing when people are making things,’ the British artist and designer notes. ‘One thing this exhibition is inviting us to remember is that consciousness in humans is important. I read recently that if we understood the body better, there wouldn’t be a word for a mind. We are conscious from the soles of our feet, we make decisions with the hair on the back of our necks, and we think with the tips of our fingers. When you enter the first room, I hope you’ll have a feeling of an environment of people who do just that,’ she adds.
This focus on the body runs through the exhibition design. In most cases, craft is encountered through its finished form, as a glass vessel, a textile, a piece of furniture, or an object placed on a plinth. In An Island of Light, the route begins with the conditions of making. The hand, the workshop, the passing of time, and the physical knowledge involved in working with a material become part of the exhibition.
The following rooms continue this shift in perspective. An Index of Artisans presents black-and-white portraits of the makers participating in Homo Faber, bringing the people behind the objects into view. In An Alphabet of Objects, more than one hundred works are transformed into projected silhouettes. A large moving cylindrical structure casts their forms across the space, creating a changing visual language of shadows. Devlin moves between the maker and the object, between physical material and projected image, repeatedly changing the scale and conditions through which craft is seen.
a large kinetic mirror responds to changing daylight | image © designboom
using water, wood, and light as exhibition materials
The exhibition then extends into the gardens and historic spaces of the Fondazione Giorgio Cini, where A Library of Lungs introduces curved wooden structures inspired by Devlin’s paper sculptures. Installed in relation to the gardens of San Giorgio, the work refers to the description of the island as one of the ‘lungs of Venice.’
Water becomes the central element of A Full Moon Rising, installed in the former Piscina Gandini. A semicircular structure holding moon jars and vessels rises from the pool, while light and reflections move across the water. The installation brings together the history of containers made to hold and transport water with water itself, turning the former swimming pool into a part of the display.
In A Rooted Ascent, a multi-level cork structure organizes works made from wood alongside objects produced through the weaving of natural materials. The installation is accompanied by makers working live in the space, bringing process into direct contact with the finished pieces.
A Full Moon Rising | image by Sophia Bennett © Michelangelo Foundation
devlin works with the architecture of san giorgio maggiore
The historic architecture of Fondazione Giorgio Cini becomes increasingly present as the exhibition develops.
In An Infinite Birdsong, shaped and backlit mirrors create a nocturnal Venetian environment. Handmade birds and insects emerge from the windows of the room, while jewelry inspired by similar forms is displayed at the center. Porcelain, metal, glass, and paper appear alongside reflections and shadows, creating a space where the objects and the architecture are visually intertwined.
One of Devlin’s most direct interventions is A Great Turning, installed in the Palladian cloister. A long pool of water reflects the arches of the portico and a large kinetic mirror responds to changing daylight. The installation works with the existing geometry of the cloister, using reflection to alter the visitor’s perception of its symmetry and depth.
In the Ambulatory of the Palladian Refectory, A Luminous Ark introduces illuminated paper sculptures of Venetian wildlife. Designed by Devlin and made by Chinese paper artist Wen Qiuwen, the suspended birds appear throughout the space like lanterns.
a semicircular structure holding moon jars and vessels rises from the pool | image © designboom
from white light to a rainbow of forms
Inside the Palladian Refectory, Devlin develops two contrasting installations around light and color. The first one, dubbed A Feast of Light, gathers white objects made from porcelain, glass, textiles, paper, and other materials around a large illuminated table. A vertical beam of light moves through the monumental room, while the reflective surface of the table amplifies the monochrome arrangement. White objects that might otherwise appear visually similar reveal different degrees of opacity, texture, reflection, and translucency.
The following installation, A Rainbow of Forms, takes the opposite approach. Color becomes the central element. Objects made from materials including plastic, enamel, resin, and glass are arranged on reflective shelves and rotating structures beneath a mirrored ceiling. The space produces a kaleidoscopic environment in which objects, colors, and reflections continually multiply.
Before the route reaches the Borges Labyrinth, Twenty Silent Songs occupies the Cypress Cloister. The installation consists of 20 rectangular panels framing circular works inspired by the sound waves of 20 imaginary bells. Each work is interpreted by a different artisan or atelier from five continents. The project draws on the history of the cloister as a place of study and prayer and on the bells of the Basilica di San Giorgio, translating an imagined acoustic experience into form.
light and reflections move across the water | image © designboom
ALBERTO CAVALLI ON CREATIVITY, COMMUNITY, AND THE JOY OF MAKING
The fourth edition of Homo Faber brings together more than 700 objects by more than 500 artisans from 70 countries. For Alberto Cavalli, Executive Director of the Michelangelo Foundation, the numbers only tell part of the story. Organizing the biennial, he says, is challenging ‘creatively, humanly, financially,’ but this difficulty is also connected to the ethos of the artisans whose work the event celebrates. ‘The work that slips out easily from your fingers is not worth pursuing,’ Cavalli says. ‘The fruits that you can pick up on low-hanging branches are maybe not the most interesting ones.’ For him, the effort involved in building Homo Faber reflects the wider idea behind homo faber, the human being capable of shaping the world around them through talent, vision, and creativity. ‘Now more than ever, proclaiming the importance of homo faber matters and makes a difference,’ he adds.
Behind the scale of An Island of Light, Cavalli identifies a set of values that shape the Michelangelo Foundation’s wider vision. The first concerns human creativity, individuality, and freedom of expression. Speaking about younger generations and the increasing influence of digital systems, Cavalli jokes that while Grace Jones once sang Slave to the Rhythm, today’s generation risks becoming ‘a slave to the algorithm.’ His concern is mainly about the pressure to conform to systems that increasingly shape how people see themselves and present their ideas. In contrast, he sees making as a space in which individual experience and creativity can take a more direct form. Working with one’s hands, materials, and personal knowledge allows makers to develop and communicate a vision that is not reduced to a predetermined image. The second value is community. Cavalli points to a contradiction in contemporary life, mentioning that digital technologies have made constant communication possible, yet isolation continues to grow. ‘The more you feel alone and left to your own devices, the more you feel weak,’ he highlights. At Homo Faber, the ambition is to create a community in which makers, students, collaborators, and visitors can come together and ‘feel accompanied, heard, seen, embraced, appreciated.’ The final value is joy. For Cavalli, the artisans gathered in Venice demonstrate a form of satisfaction that comes directly from making and transforming the world around them. ‘The artisans are here to teach us the joy that comes from making, from shaping the world according to your vision, according to your hopes, dreams and expectations,’ he comments.
A Rainbow of Forms
a movement beyond objects
The mayor of Venice, Simone Venturini, describes the event as something larger than an exhibition. ‘Homo Faber is not an exhibition, it’s a movement, and right now we need to push for a movement in favor of beauty, harmony and authenticity, in a world that is very material but also troubled. Beauty, authenticity, craftsmanship, heritage can heal the wounds of a very troubled world, and we can do it here, in a neutral space, in an old monastery, in the most important city for art, culture, intercultural value, and dialogue,’ he shares. ‘I think that’s not just about Homo Faber, or only about a product or craftsmanship. It’s about soul and humanity. This is not an exhibition about things, goods, or objects; it’s a movement about humanity, and about soul.’
Devlin’s direction gives this idea a physical form. An Island of Light organizes 700 works through a series of changing environments. Objects appear alongside the materials, tools, gestures, and processes connected to their making, while the architecture of San Giorgio Maggiore becomes part of the experience. Light moves through the exhibition in different ways. It reflects off water in the former swimming pool, enters the Palladian cloisters, catches mirrored surfaces, and transforms objects into silhouettes and shadows. Color and material also shape the route, moving visitors between different atmospheres and spaces. The exhibition design places the objects within a wider context without taking attention away from the makers themselves. Throughout the 15 installations, Devlin returns to the relationship between the finished work and the hand, the material, the workshop, and the accumulated knowledge behind each practice.
objects made from materials including plastic, enamel, resin, and glass are arranged on reflective shelves

2 women in Iran sentenced to death over protests, rights groups say
Iranian courts have issued death sentences for two women charged over anti-government protests in January, rights groups said Monday, as Tehran ramps up executions of people arrested in the demonstrations.
The two women were sentenced in separate cases but both were related to incidents in the central city of Isfahan, which was a hub of the nationwide protest activity that peaked on the nights of Jan. 8 and 9.
Against the backdrop of the war, Iran has already executed 29 men on charges related to the demonstrations, according to the Norway-based nongovernmental organization Iran Human Rights.
So far, no woman has been executed over the unrest, although Iran has hanged at least 16 women this year on other charges, according to Iran Human Rights.
Taraneh Rahimi, 20, was sentenced to death along with nine men over incidents during the protests in a square in Isfahan that saw two people killed, including a member of the security forces, the Norway-based Hengaw group and U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency said Monday.
Other defendants in the case were given sentences of up to 36 years in prison, including Taraneh's sister Romina, they added.
"Defendants' lawyers did not have access to a substantial portion of the case file and objected that they had not been given sufficient time to review the documents and evidence," Human Rights Activists News Agency said.
In the other case, Leila Abolhasani, a 43-year-old mother of two teenagers, was convicted by a court in Isfahan of setting fire to a store during the protests, the Dadban legal affairs monitor and Human Rights Activists News Agency said.
Her relatives have denied the accusation, saying she was only present at the scene and was filming the burning store, the groups said.

Meloni's big reforms flounder but security bills flourish in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31

16:40:37 KST

Meloni's big reforms flounder but security bills flourish in Italy
ROME, Aug 31 - Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government took office in October 2022 and will become the longest-serving administration in the history of the Italian Republic on September 4.
Here are some of the main legislative efforts undertaken by her coalition, which have achieved varied results.
JUDICIAL REFORM
One of its flagship initiatives sought to revamp Italy's fiercely independent judiciary. Because this involved a change to the constitution, it went to a referendum, which the government lost decisively in March.
PREMIERSHIP
The government said it would introduce the direct election of the prime minister by voters. Meloni called this the "mother of all reforms", however it has not progressed after initial approval in the Senate in June 2024. Critics said it could trigger political chaos and undermine the role of the president. The reform will not be enacted before the next elections.
DIFFERENTIATED AUTONOMY
The law grants greater powers to the regions and has been aggressively promoted by the far-right coalition League party. The legislation was approved in 2024, but the Constitutional Court subsequently struck down key parts of it. The legislation is now in limbo, but the League has said the problems will be resolved before the next election.
IMMIGRATION
The government tightened asylum and anti-smuggling rules, struck migration agreements with North African states and expanded repatriations. However, its flagship scheme, building two detention centres in Albania, was delayed by legal challenges and is now operating mainly as a repatriation facility for migrants already transferred from Italy, not as the offshore asylum-processing system originally promoted by Meloni.
SECURITY AND LAW AND ORDER
Meloni's government has been particularly active on security, repeatedly responding to high-profile incidents with tougher laws and penalties. Measures have included new offences targeting illegal raves, stricter anti-smuggling rules after a migrant shipwreck, tougher penalties for wildfire arson, youth crime and a sweeping 2025 security decree covering protests, prison riots, squatting and other public-order offences.
TAX AND WELFARE
Meloni has pursued a targeted tax-cutting agenda: reducing income tax bands to three from four and pushing measures to benefit the self-employed. However, Italy's total tax burden has barely changed over the past four years, with some tax cuts counterbalanced by tighter limits on deductions for higher-income taxpayers. The government abolished a "Citizens' Income" welfare scheme, replacing it with more restrictive benefits and stricter work requirements. Figures show it also reduced tax evasion by promoting the use of digital payments. REUTERS

Irish warships open fire with main guns
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:40:18 BST
16:40:18 KST

Irish Naval Service patrol ships LÉ Samuel Beckett and LÉ George Bernard Shaw have taken part in a Ship Training Period involving live-fire gunnery, manoeuvring, maritime interdiction and replenishment-at-sea training, according to the Irish Naval Service.
Footage released by the service shows one of the vessels conducting a gun exercise at sea, with its main naval gun firing during the training period. The Naval Service described the activity as a demanding package intended to exercise several of the core skills required during operations.
The training included Gun Exercises, known as GUNEX, alongside manoeuvring exercises, Maritime Interdiction Operations and Replenishment at Sea training. Together, those activities cover weapons employment, ship handling, interception procedures and the ability of vessels to operate in close coordination while underway.
The Naval Service said: “This week the Naval Service conducted a Ship Training Period (STP). This was a demanding period of training which involved Gun Exercises (GUNEX), Manoeuvring Exercises, Maritime Interdiction (MIO) and Replenishment at Sea training (RAS).”
LÉ Samuel Beckett and LÉ George Bernard Shaw are both Samuel Beckett-class offshore patrol vessels.
The class is fitted with a 76mm main gun mounted forward, providing a substantially heavier weapon than the smaller-calibre systems carried elsewhere on the ships. Gunnery training allows crews to practise the procedures surrounding weapon operation, fire control and safe engagement while maintaining proficiency with the ship’s principal armament. Maritime Interdiction Operations exercise a different part of a ship’s crew. Such training can involve identifying and approaching vessels of interest, establishing communications, controlling their movement and preparing boarding teams for inspection or enforcement activity.
For a navy whose routine work includes monitoring maritime activity across Ireland’s extensive area of responsibility, those procedures form part of the practical skills required for patrol and security operations. Replenishment at Sea training is intended to develop the close-quarters ship handling and coordination required when vessels transfer stores or other supplies while remaining underway. Even when no material is physically transferred, crews can practise the approach, station keeping, communications and safety procedures involved.
Manoeuvring exercises similarly allow bridge teams to work through coordinated changes of course, formation movements and close navigation with other vessels. Such activity is particularly important when several ships are operating together or when conducting interception and boarding tasks.
LÉ Samuel Beckett was the first ship of the class to enter Irish service, while LÉ George Bernard Shaw is the fourth and final vessel of the design. The ships were built as larger and more capable replacements for older Irish patrol vessels, with an emphasis on endurance and operations in the North Atlantic environment.

New stability record for Italy's Meloni may prove fleeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:36:04 UTC
16:36:04 KST

New stability record for Italy's Meloni may prove fleeting
ROME, Aug 31 - In a country famed for political instability, Giorgia Meloni is poised to lead Italy's longest-lasting government since World War Two, overtaking a record of 1,412 consecutive days set by Silvio Berlusconi in 2005.
Meloni, who has tempered her populist instincts with pragmatism since taking power in October 2022, plans a rally on Friday, September 4 to celebrate the milestone, framing the durability of her coalition as one of its crowning achievements.
After cycling through 68 governments in 80 years, Italy has proved much steadier during a period of global conflict than France, which has had five prime ministers since the autumn of 2022, while Britain has got through four.
But just as Italy has shaken off its reputation for volatility, opinion polls suggest that the 2027 parliamentary elections could usher in a more fragmented and potentially less stable political landscape.
"There is a genuine risk that we could return to the worst kind of a splintered parliament next time around," said Roberto D'Alimonte, a professor of Italian politics at Rome's Luiss university.
While Berlusconi's single-term record is about to be eclipsed, he will remain the longest-serving Italian prime minister overall, with a tenure of about nine years over four terms between 1994 and 2011.
BUDGET DISCIPLINE
Worried about the prospect of renewed political turbulence, coalition allies are quick to tout the dividends of four years of uninterrupted rule.
Deputy Foreign Minister Edmondo Cirielli, of Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, said the government had kept deficits and debt under control, while adding 1.2 million workers to the jobs market, pushing unemployment to under 6%.
"The record figures on employment and unemployment are indisputable," he told Reuters.
Analysts broadly agree that Meloni's strongest achievement has been restoring confidence in Italy's shaky public finances, blighted by a hefty debt mountain.
Lorenzo Codogno, a former chief economist at the Treasury and now head of LC Macro Advisors, said the cabinet had convinced investors it was committed to budget discipline and had curtailed costly policies of past administrations, notably the "Superbonus" home renovation scheme.
"In terms of fiscal responsibility, I think the government has done a decent job. In terms of promoting growth and reforming the economy, not much has been done," he said.
Little effort was made to shake up an inefficient public administration, the health service and education system, while all the government's institutional reforms, including handing more powers to the prime minister, have floundered.
"Part of the reason Meloni has been able to stay in power for four years is that she did not try to change much or upset voters," said Lorenzo Pregliasco, head of YouTrend pollster.
"This is perhaps the most sobering lesson we can draw from this period."
LOSING TRUMP
While ducking ambitious change, Meloni focused on law and order, boosting police powers and cracking down on irregular immigration — a key electoral pledge — cutting the number of new arrivals to 66,316 last year from 157,651 in 2023.
"There has been the paradigm shift imposed by Giorgia Meloni in the management of illegal immigration," Francesco Filini, the head of Brothers of Italy's policy programme, told Reuters, saying much of Europe was now looking to emulate her.
Although she has forged good relations with many European leaders, Meloni's standing abroad has been bruised by the collapse of her once-close ties with Donald Trump after the U.S. president accused her in April of lacking courage and letting the United States down in its war with Iran.
The diplomatic setback, which destroyed any pretence that Meloni could serve as a bridge between Europe and Washington, came within weeks of a stinging domestic defeat, when Italians rejected her flagship judicial reform in a referendum.
The loss punctured the aura of invincibility that had surrounded Meloni's coalition, and while her party remains the most popular in Italy, the standing of her main allies — most notably the far-right League — has dropped steadily.
With time running out, the government has embarked on one last-gasp legislative push, seeking to redraw the electoral law by introducing a system that would give a majority bonus to any bloc winning more than 42% of the vote.
Critics say the change is designed to strengthen the conservative bloc's chances of staying in power. Meloni says it is aimed at providing renewed stability, whoever wins.
NEW PARTY DISRUPTS OUTLOOK
However, the political landscape has changed since the law was devised, thanks to the emergence of a new far-right party led by an ex-general, Roberto Vannacci, who has tapped into anxieties over immigration, security and cultural change with language that is markedly blunter than Meloni's.
A poll published by BiDiMedia on August 26 put the coalition partners on just 38.5%, while the broad centre-left camp, which is deeply divided over foreign policy and prone to relentless infighting, is hovering close to the vital 42% threshold.
Support for Vannacci has surged to 8%, suggesting he could win it for Meloni, if she agreed to bring him into her alliance.
That would be a risky move which might alienate moderate voters and alarm EU allies concerned by Vannacci's extremism. Alternatively, she could hope for an inconclusive vote and seek a post-election pact with Vannacci to give her a working majority.
Either way, the path to another stable government appears narrower than before. The opposition is disunited, while Vannacci's rise risks turning a previously disciplined conservative alliance into a more fractious bloc.
"The markets have liked stability and got used to it, but this is Italy, it won't last for ever," said Codogno. REUTERS

Italy's revolving-door governments — the numbers behind the instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:35:51 UTC
16:35:51 KST

Italy's revolving-door governments — the numbers behind the instability
ROME, Aug 31 - Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is due to set a record as leading Italy's longest-serving administration on September 4. Yet the country's revolving-door cabinets have often masked a more stable political system than first meets the eye.
Below are some facts and figures about Italy's post-war governments:
HOW MANY GOVERNMENTS AND PRIME MINISTERS?
Meloni's administration is Italy's 68th government since 1946, led by the country's 31st prime minister of the republican era. Unlike in some countries, a new government is said to have been created after a major cabinet reshuffle, even if the prime minister remains the same.
AVERAGE LIFESPAN
Across the 80 years from the formation of Alcide De Gasperi's government in July 1946 to Meloni's record in 2026, the average cabinet has lasted roughly 14 months. The figure varies according to methodology: calculating only the period from a government's swearing-in to its resignation produces a shorter average, because outgoing cabinets often remain in office in a caretaker capacity.
THE SHORTEST AND THE LONGEST
The briefest tenure was Amintore Fanfani's first government, which lasted 22 days in 1954. Before Meloni, only four administrations lasted more than 1,000 days: Silvio Berlusconi's 2nd government (1,412 days, from 2001 to 2005), Berlusconi's 4th government (1,287 days, 2008 to 2011), Bettino Craxi (1,093 days, 1983 to 1986) and Matteo Renzi (1,024 days, 2014 to 2016). Altogether, Berlusconi served about nine years over four terms.
WHY SO MANY SHORT-LIVED GOVERNMENTS?
Italy's post-war system combined proportional representation, which encouraged a fragmented party landscape, with coalition governments vulnerable to disputes. The constitution also requires a government to retain the confidence of both the lower house and the Senate — two houses with equal powers, giving small coalition partners considerable leverage.
However, the turnover did not always mean a wholesale change of political direction. During much of the post-war era, the Christian Democrats remained at the centre of power, while prime ministers and coalition formulas revolved around them.
Despite frequent changes of government, nine of Italy's 18 post-war legislatures ran broadly to the end of their normal five-year term, while five lasted for four years.
ELECTORAL LAWS: A FREQUENTLY CHANGING RULEBOOK
Italy has deployed three different electoral systems in general elections in the past 22 years, with Meloni promising to introduce a fourth ahead of the 2027 vote, saying it will bring greater stability. REUTERS
